== Aftermath ==
{{see also|List of members of the twenty-fifth Knesset}}
[[File:Isaac Herzog in the Knesset, November 2022 (KBG GPO175541 2).jpeg|thumb|The swearing-in ceremony of the members of the newly elected 25th Knesset, 15 November 2022.]]
With 86% of the vote counted, the right-wing bloc led by [[Benjamin Netanyahu]], known in Israel as the [[national camp]], was forecast to win a majority of seats at 65, while both leftist [[Meretz]] and [[Balad (political party)|Balad]] parties were under the [[electoral threshold]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Bachner |first=Michael |date=2 November 2022 |title=With 86% of votes tallied, Netanyahu headed for decisive comeback victory |work=[[The Times of Israel]] |url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/with-85-of-votes-tallied-netanyahu-on-verge-of-breaking-deadlock-regaining-power/ |access-date=6 November 2022}}</ref> As all the votes were counted, they remained under the threshold;<ref name="IEF">{{cite news |date=2 November 2022 |title=Israel election: Final results announced for election 2022 |work=[[The Jerusalem Post]]|url=https://www.jpost.com/israel-elections/live-updates-721259 |access-date=6 November 2022 }}</ref> far-right parties saw a surge in their vote share.<ref name="IEF" /><ref>{{cite news |last=Berg |first=Raffi |date=1 November 2022 |title=Netanyahu set for comeback with far right's help |work=[[BBC News]]|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-63459824 |access-date=6 November 2022}}</ref> In terms of votes, both blocs were neck-and-neck, with the anti-Netanyahu bloc achieving 49.5% but not gaining enough seats due to Meretz and Balad narrowly missing the electoral threshold,<ref>{{cite news |last=Tibon|first=Amir|date=2 November 2022|title=The Two Left-wing Politicians Who Crowned Netanyahu |work=Haaretz |url=https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/haaretz-today/2022-11-02/ty-article/.highlight/the-two-left-wing-politicians-who-crowned-netanyahu/00000184-393e-d52c-a1cf-f9ff6eec0000 |access-date=4 November 2022}}</ref> as 289,000 anti-Netanyahu votes went wasted in terms of seats share.<ref>{{cite news |last=Sharon |first=Jeremy |date=3 November 2022 |title=Netanyahu won 8-seat majority over his opponents despite near-parity in raw votes |work=[[The Times of Israel]] |url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/netanyahu-won-8-seat-majority-over-his-opponents-despite-near-parity-in-raw-votes/ |access-date=6 November 2022}}</ref> Orly Ades, head of Israel's election panel [[Central Elections Committee]], said Netanyahu's party [[Likud]] tried to undermine voting supervision, and described their actions as "something we've never seen before".<ref>{{cite news |last=Maanit |first=Chen |date=3 November 2022 |title=Election Panel Says Likud Sought to Undermine Supervision of Voting on Election Night |work=[[Haaretz]] |url=https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2022-11-03/ty-article/.premium/election-panel-says-likud-sought-to-undermine-supervision-of-voting-on-election-night/00000184-3e4d-de59-a5f4-bf7fd53f0000 |access-date=6 November 2022}}</ref>

Netanyahu's bloc went on to win 64 seats, while the coalition led by the incumbent prime minister [[Yair Lapid]] won 51 seats.<ref>{{cite news |last=Fitoussi |first=Olivier |date=3 November 2022 |title=Israel election: Final results show Netanyahu bloc at 64 seats |work=[[i24NEWS]] |publisher= |url=https://www.i24news.tv/en/news/israeli-elections/1667497728-israel-election-final-results-show-netanyahu-bloc-at-64-seats |access-date=6 November 2022}}</ref> In addition to Meretz and Balad, the right-wing party [[The Jewish Home]] also failed to cross the electoral threshold.<ref name="Haaretz results"/> The new majority was variously described as the most right-wing government in Israeli history,<ref>{{cite news |last1=Kershner |first1=Isabel |last2=Kingsley |first2=Patrick |date=1 November 2022 |title=Israel Election: Exit Polls Show Netanyahu With Edge in Israel's Election |newspaper=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/live/2022/11/01/world/israel-election |access-date=6 November 2022 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> as well as its most religious government.<ref>{{cite news |last=Maltz |first=Judy |date=3 November 2022 |title=Will Israel Become a Theocracy? Religious Parties Are Election's Biggest Winners |work=[[Haaretz]] |url=https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/elections/2022-11-03/ty-article/.highlight/will-israel-become-a-theocracy-religious-parties-are-elections-biggest-winners/00000184-3db9-dc3c-a1ac-bfbb83b40000 |access-date=6 November 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Gross |first=Judah Ari |date=4 November 2022 |title=Israel poised to have its most religious government; experts say no theocracy yet |work=[[The Times of Israel]] |url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/with-85-of-votes-tallied-netanyahu-on-verge-of-breaking-deadlock-regaining-power/ |access-date=6 November 2022}}</ref>

Lapid conceded to Netanyahu,<ref>{{cite news |last=Raice |first=Shayndi |date=3 November 2022|title=Benjamin Netanyahu Wins Another Shot at Leading Israel as Lapid Concedes |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/israels-benjamin-netanyahu-edges-closer-to-election-win-11667470853 |access-date=4 November 2022 |work=The Wall Street Journal}}</ref> and congratulated him,<ref>{{cite web |last=Ravid |first=Barak |date=3 November 2022 |title=Israel's Lapid congratulates Netanyahu on election win|url=https://www.axios.com/2022/11/01/israeli-elections-early-exit-polls-show-netanyahus-bloc-winning-narrow-majority |access-date=3 November 2022 |website=Axios}}</ref> wishing him luck "for the sake of the Israeli people".<ref>{{cite news |date=3 November 2022|title=Final results give Likud bloc 64 seats; ADL: Far right will hurt Israel globally |url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog-november-03-2022/ |access-date=3 November 2022 |work=The Times of Israel }}</ref> Netanyahu received congratulatory messages from leaders around the world, including those of Canada, France, Hungary, India, Italy, Jordan, Sudan, Ukraine, the United Arab Emirates, the United States, and the United Kingdom, among others.<ref>{{cite web | title=International congratulations start coming in for Netanyahu | website= The Jerusalem Post| date=3 November 2022 | url=https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article-721417}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Biden calls Netanyahu to congratulate him on his election victory | website= The Jerusalem Post| date=7 November 2022 | url=https://www.jpost.com/breaking-news/article-721707}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=World leaders congratulate Netanyahu on his election victory|website=Israel National News |date=10 November 2022 | url=https://www.israelnationalnews.com/news/362624}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Jordanian king, Sudanese military ruler congratulate Netanyahu on election win | website=The Times of Israel | date=14 November 2022 | url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/jordanian-king-sudanese-military-ruler-congratulate-netanyahu-on-election-win/}}</ref>

On 15 November, the swearing-in ceremony for the newly elected [[List of members of the twenty-fifth Knesset|members of the 25th Knesset]] was held during the opening session. The incoming Knesset includes 29 female lawmakers, 7 less than the last Knesset, and 28 new parliamentarians. The vote to appoint a new [[List of Knesset speakers|Speaker of the Knesset]], which is usually conducted at the opening session, and the swearing in of cabinet members were postponed since ongoing coalition negotiations had not yet resulted in agreement on these positions.<ref>{{cite web | website=Israel HaYom | date=15 November 2022 | title=Israel to swear in 25th Knesset ahead of Netanyahu's 6th term as PM|last1= Ettinger|first1= Amir|last2= Shlezinger|first2= Yehuda| url=https://www.israelhayom.com/2022/11/15/Israel-to-swear-in-25th-parliament-inaugurating-netanyahus-6th-term-as-prime-minister/}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last=Bachner | first=Michael | title=As 25th Knesset sworn in, president urges MKs to end 'addiction' to toxic discourse | website=The Times of Israel | date=20 November 2022 | url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/as-25th-knesset-sworn-in-president-urges-mks-to-end-addiction-to-toxic-discourse/}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last= Reich |first=Eleanor H.|title=Israel swears in new parliament, most right-wing in history |url=https://apnews.com/article/middle-east-religion-israel-benjamin-netanyahu-347e906749a862ffcf905ee0056e068f |access-date=15 November 2022 |work=Associated Press |date=15 November 2022 |language=en-US}}</ref>

The vote to replace incumbent Knesset speaker [[Mickey Levy]] was scheduled for 13 December, after Likud and its allies secured the necessary number of signatures for it.<ref>{{cite news|date=12 December 2022|author=Carrie Keller-Lynn|title=Key vote on Knesset speaker pushed to Tuesday after Lapid camp threatens filibuster|url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/key-vote-on-knesset-speaker-pushed-to-tuesday-after-lapid-camp-threatens-filibuster/|access-date=12 December 2022|work=The Times of Israel}}</ref> [[Yariv Levin]] of Likud was elected as a temporary  speaker by 64 votes, while his opponents [[Meirav Ben-Ari]] of Yesh Atid and [[Ayman Odeh]] of Hadash got 45 and five votes respectively.<ref>{{cite news|date=13 December 2022|author=Abdelraouf Arnaout|title=Israeli lawmakers elect interim Knesset speaker|url=https://www.aa.com.tr/en/middle-east/israeli-lawmakers-elect-interim-knesset-speaker/2762642|access-date=14 December 2022|work=Anadolu Agency}}</ref> He resigned on 29 December and [[Amir Ohana]] of Likud was elected as the speaker by 63 votes.<ref>{{cite news|date=29 December 2022|author=Carrie Keller-Lynn|url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/likuds-amir-ohana-becomes-israels-first-openly-gay-knesset-speaker/|title=Likud's Amir Ohana becomes Israel's first openly gay Knesset speaker|access-date=29 December 2022|work=Times of Israel}}</ref>

=== Government formation ===
{{main|Thirty-seventh government of Israel}}

[[File:Israeli legislative election, November 2022 (KBG GPO1 4).jpeg|thumb|President Herzog consulting with MKs [[Orit Strook]], [[Ohad Tal]] and [[Moshe Solomon]] ahead of nominating a prime minister-designate, 10 November 2022.]]
[[File:Isaac Herzog assigned the task of forming a government to Benjamin Netanyahu MK, November 2022 (KBG GPO3232).jpg|thumb|President Herzog assigns the task of forming a new government to Likud leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, 13 November 2022.]]

On 3 November 2022 Netanyahu told his aide [[Yariv Levin]] to begin informal coalition talks with allied parties after 97% of the vote was counted.<ref>{{cite news|date=3 November 2022|title=With 97% of votes tallied, Netanyahu launches government talks|url=https://www.ynetnews.com/article/ojd1zycgk|access-date=6 November 2022|work=Ynet}}</ref>

Netanyahu himself started holding talks on 6 November. He first met with [[Moshe Gafni]], the leader of the [[Degel HaTorah]] faction of [[United Torah Judaism]], and then with [[Yitzhak Goldknopf]], the leader of the United Torah Judaism alliance and its [[Agudat Yisrael]] faction. Meanwhile, the [[Religious Zionist Party]] leader [[Bezalel Smotrich]] and the leader of its [[Otzma Yehudit]] faction [[Itamar Ben-Gvir]] pledged that they would not enter the coalition without the other faction. Gafni later met with Smotrich for coalition talks.<ref name="Spiro 2022">{{cite news|last=Spiro|first=Amy|date=6 November 2022|title=As Netanyahu begins coalition talks, Smotrich and Ben Gvir vow to remain united|url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/as-netanyahu-begins-coalition-talks-smotrich-and-ben-gvir-vow-to-remain-united/|access-date=6 November 2022|work=The Times of Israel}}</ref> Smotrich then met with Netanyahu. On 7 November, Netanyahu met with Ben-Gvir.<ref>{{cite news|date=7 November 2022|title=Ben Gvir after talks, 1st picture with Netanyahu: 'Full right' coalition on its way|url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/ben-gvir-sits-with-netanyahu-for-post-election-coalition-talks-first-joint-photo/|access-date=8 November 2022|work=The Times of Israel}}</ref> A major demand from the UTJ was that the Knesset be allowed to [[Override clause (Israel)|override]] the rulings of the Supreme Court.<ref>{{cite news|date=8 November 2022|title=UTJ insisting no government without High Court override commitment first — reports|url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/utj-insisting-no-government-without-high-court-override-commitment-first-reports/|access-date=12 November 2022|work=The Times of Israel}}</ref> Netanyahu met with the [[Noam (political party)|Noam]] faction leader and its sole MK [[Avi Maoz]] on 8 November.<ref>{{cite news|date=8 November 2022|last=Breuer|first=Eliav|title=Anti-LGBTQ+ MK Avi Maoz, Netanyahu meet ahead of coalition negotiations|url=https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/politics-and-diplomacy/article-721784|access-date=9 November 2022|work=The Jerusalem Post}}</ref>

President [[Isaac Herzog]] began consultations with heads of all political parties on 9 November after the election results were certified.<ref>{{cite news|date=9 November 2022|title=Israel's Election Results Certified, President Begins Consultations|url=https://themedialine.org/headlines/israels-election-results-certified-president-begins-consultations/|access-date=9 November 2022|work=The Media Line}}</ref> [[Shas]] met with Likud for coalition talks on 10 November.<ref>{{cite news|date=10 November 2022|last=Breuer|first=Eliav|title=Shas, Likud meet for coalition negotiation talks|url=https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/politics-and-diplomacy/article-722022|access-date=12 November 2022|work=The Jerusalem Post}}</ref> By 11 November, Netanyahu had secured recommendations from 64 MKs, which constituted a majority.<ref name="mandate">{{cite news|date=11 November 2022|title=Netanyahu to be mandated to form new Israeli government|url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2022/11/11/netanyahu-mandated-to-form-new-israeli-government|access-date=13 November 2022|work=Al Jazeera}}</ref> He was given the mandate to form the thirty-seventh government of Israel by President Herzog on 13 November.<ref>{{cite news|first=Dov|last=Lieber|date=13 November 2022|title=Israeli President Hands Mandate to Benjamin Netanyahu to Form Government|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/israeli-president-hands-mandate-to-benjamin-netanyahu-to-form-government-11668337197|access-date=13 November 2022|work=The Wall Street Journal}}</ref> Otzma Yehudit and Noam officially split from Religious Zionism on 20 November as per a pre-election agreement.<ref>{{cite news|date=20 November 2022|title=Separating from Religious Zionism, Otzma Yehudit and Noam now independent parties|url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/separating-from-religious-zionism-otzma-yehudit-and-noam-now-independent-factions/|last1=Keller-Lynn|first1=Carrie|access-date=20 November 2022|work=The Times of Israel}}</ref>

Likud signed a coalition agreement with Otzma Yehudit on 25 November,<ref>{{cite news|date=25 November 2022|title=Ben Gvir to get newly created role of national security minister in deal with Likud|url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/likud-said-to-make-progress-in-coalition-talks-with-otzma-yehudit-shas/|access-date=25 November 2022|work=The Times of Israel}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|date=25 November 2022|title=אחרי ההסכם: מי יכהן כשר ומי יו"ר ועדה? כל הפרטים|url=https://www.srugim.co.il/734646-%D7%90%D7%97%D7%A8%D7%99-%D7%94%D7%94%D7%A1%D7%9B%D7%9D-%D7%9E%D7%99-%D7%99%D7%9B%D7%94%D7%9F-%D7%9B%D7%A9%D7%A8-%D7%95%D7%9E%D7%99-%D7%99%D7%95%D7%A8-%D7%95%D7%A2%D7%93%D7%94-%D7%9B%D7%9C-%D7%94|access-date=25 role|url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/gantz-blasts-netanyahu-for-making-ben-gvir-the-real-pm-with-expanded-security-role/|access-date=27 November 2022|work=The Times of Israel}}</ref> with Noam on 27 November,<ref>{{cite news|author=Carrie Keller-Lynn|date=27 November 2022|title=Netanyahu puts extremist homophobic politician in charge of Israel's Jewish identity|url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/netanyahu-puts-extremist-homophobic-politician-in-charge-of-israels-jewish-identity/|access-date=27 November 2022|work=The Times of Israel}}</ref> the Religious Zionist Party on 1 December,<ref>{{cite news|author=Carrie Keller-Lynn|date=1 December 2022|title=Netanyahu gives Smotrich broad powers over settlements, Palestinian construction|url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/netanyahu-gives-smotrich-broad-powers-over-settlements-palestinian-construction/|access-date=3 December 2022|work=[[The Times of Israel]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=Elia Breur|date=1 December 2022|title=Smotrich gets finance ministry, authority over West Bank in coalition deal|url=https://www.jpost.com/breaking-news/article-723877|access-date=4 December 2022|work=[[The Jerusalem Post]]}}</ref> United Torah Judaism on 6 December,<ref>{{cite news|date=6 December 2022|title=As Netanyahu's coalition deadline nears, Likud signs interim deal with UTJ|url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/as-netanyahu-closes-in-on-coalition-deadline-likud-signs-interim-deal-with-utj/|access-date=8 December 2022|work=The Times of Israel}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|date=8 December 2022|title=Israel's incoming government will be a bureaucratic puzzle - Analysis|url=https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/politics-and-diplomacy/article-724358|author=Eliav Breuer|access-date=8 December 2022|work=The Jerusalem Post}}</ref> and with Shas on 8 December.<ref>{{cite news|date=8 December 2022|title=Likud inks deal with Shas, finishes doling out government posts to coalition allies|url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/inking-deal-with-shas-likud-finishes-divvying-out-govt-posts-to-coalition-partners/|access-date=8 December 2022|work=The Times of Israel}}</ref>

Netanyahu asked Herzog for a 14-day extension after the agreement with Shas in order to finalise the roles his allied parties would play.<ref>{{cite news|date=8 December 2022|title=Netanyahu secures parliament majority, seeks more time to form government|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/israels-netanyahu-secures-parliament-majority-closer-forming-government-2022-12-08/|author=Henriette Chacar|access-date=8 December 2022|work=Reuters}}</ref> Herzog on 9 December extended the deadline to 21 December.<ref>{{cite news|date=9 December 2022|title=Israeli President grants Netanyahu 10-day extension to form government|url=https://www.thenationalnews.com/mena/2022/12/09/israeli-president-grants-netanyahu-10-day-extension-to-form-government/|access-date=9 December 2022|work=The National}}</ref> On that date, Netanyahu informed Herzog that he had succeeded in forming a coalition.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Keller-Lynn |first=Carrie |title='I've done it': Netanyahu announces his 6th government, Israel's most hardline ever |url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/netanyahu-announces-his-sixth-government-israels-most-hardline-yet/ |date=21 December 2022 |access-date=22 December 2022 |work=The Times of Israel}}</ref> The coalition government was sworn in on 29 December.<ref name="BBCswearing">{{Cite web |last1=Knell |first1=Yollande |last2=Gritten |first2=David |title=Netanyahu's hard-line new government takes office in Israel |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-64115141 |date=29 December 2022 |access-date=29 December 2022 |work=BBC}}</ref>

===Satisfaction with results===
At the end of November and the beginning of December, the [[Israel Democracy Institute]] polled Israelis on their satisfaction with the results of the election. 43% were found to be satisfied, 52% unsatisfied, and 5% were undecided.<ref>{{cite web |author=Tamar Hermann, Or Anabi |title=Supreme Court Should Retain Power – Survey |url=https://en.idi.org.il/articles/46635 |publisher=Israeli Democracy Institute |access-date=14 January 2024 |date=6 December 2022}}</ref>

of the [[Althing]]. The [[Centre-left politics|centre-left]] [[Social Democratic Alliance]], led by [[Kristrún Frostadóttir]], outperformed the ruling [[Independence Party (Iceland)|Independence Party]] to win the most seats, at 15.{{Cite web |url=https://apnews.com/article/iceland-election-results-social-democrats-989773ec8a24cddef7ba78d5aa933df2 |title=Social democrats gain and incumbents are punished in Iceland’s election |date=1 December 2024 |access-date=1 December 2024 |website=Associated Press |language=en |archive-date=1 December 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241201150818/https://apnews.com/article/iceland-election-results-social-democrats-989773ec8a24cddef7ba78d5aa933df2 |url-status=live }} The election saw the worst performance by the [[Independence Party (Iceland)|Independence Party]], [[Progressive Party (Iceland)|Progressive Party]], the [[Left-Green Movement]], and the [[Pirate Party (Iceland)|Pirate Party]] in each of the parties' histories, while [[Viðreisn]], the [[People's Party (Iceland)|People's Party]], and the [[Centre Party (Iceland)|Centre Party]] saw their best performance in each of the parties' histories. This follows a trend of Icelanders voting against every post–[[Great Recession|2008 recession]] government except during the [[2021 Icelandic parliamentary election|2021 election]].{{Cite web |url=https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20241201-social-democrats-set-to-overtake-ruling-party-in-iceland-snap-election |title=Social Democrats overtake PM's party in Iceland vote |date=1 December 2024 |access-date=1 December 2024 |website=France 24 |language=en |archive-date=1 December 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241201121640/https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20241201-social-democrats-set-to-overtake-ruling-party-in-iceland-snap-election |url-status=live }} The Left-Green Movement and the Pirate Party lost all of their parliamentary representation, with each failing to obtain a seat for the first time since their foundation in the [[1999 Icelandic parliamentary election|1999]] and [[2013 Icelandic parliamentary election|2013 elections]], respectively.{{Cite web |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/12/1/social-democrats-win-icelands-snap-election-as-incumbents-punished |title=Social Democrats win Iceland’s snap elections as incumbents punished |date=1 December 2024 |access-date=2 December 2024 |website=Al Jazeera |language=en}} ==Background== ===Previous election=== {{main|2021 Icelandic parliamentary election}} The [[2021 Icelandic parliamentary election|2021 parliamentary election]] took place on 25 September, a month before the latest date allowed by law. The government coalition of the [[Left-Green Movement]], the [[Progressive Party (Iceland)|Progressive Party]] and the [[Independence Party (Iceland)|Independence Party]], led by prime minister [[Katrín Jakobsdóttir]], had been in place since the [[2017 Icelandic parliamentary election|2017 elections]]. This unusual coalition of parties from the left wing, the center and the right wing of Icelandic mainstream politics maintained its majority in parliament in the elections as the Independence Party had the same number of seats as before while the Progressive Party added 5 seats and the Left-Green Movement lost 3. As for the opposition parties, the [[People's Party (Iceland)|People's Party]] gained two seats and [[Viðreisn]] gained 1 seat. The Pirate Party held steady but the [[Social Democratic Alliance]] lost 1 seat and the [[Centre Party (Iceland)|Centre Party]] lost 4 of its seats in parliament. The [[Icelandic Socialist Party]] received 4.1% of the vote but no seats as 5% of the national vote is needed to be eligible for the allocation of [[leveling seat]]s. The coalition partners from the previous term soon decided that the first option for coalition talks should be to renew their coalition. The [[second cabinet of Katrín Jakobsdóttir]] was then formed on 28 November.{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/icelands-left-right-coalition-agrees-take-another-term-2021-11-28/|title=Iceland's left-right coalition agrees to take another term|work=Reuters|date=28 November 2021|access-date=3 December 2021|archive-date=30 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211130052716/https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/icelands-left-right-coalition-agrees-take-another-term-2021-11-28/|url-status=live}}{{cite web |title=Katrin Jakobsdottir, Iceland's Staunch Feminist PM, Begins Second Term |url=https://www.voanews.com/a/katrin-jakobsdottir-iceland-staunch-feminist-pm-begins-second-term/6331139.html |date=28 November 2021 |work=[[Voice of America]] |access-date=15 December 2021 |archive-date=29 November 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211129092320/https://www.voanews.com/a/katrin-jakobsdottir-iceland-staunch-feminist-pm-begins-second-term/6331139.html |url-status=live }} ===Fall of government=== In April 2024, Katrín Jakobsdóttir resigned to contest the [[2024 Icelandic presidential election]], which she lost. She was succeeded as prime minister by [[Bjarni Benediktsson (born 1970)|Bjarni Benediktsson]].{{cite news |date=13 October 2024 |title=Iceland PM calls new election as coalition government collapses |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/10/13/iceland-pm-calls-new-election-as-coalition-government-collapses |access-date=14 October 2024 |work=Al Jazeera |archive-date=10 November 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241110003614/https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/10/13/iceland-pm-calls-new-election-as-coalition-government-collapses |url-status=live }} On 13 October, prime minister Bjarni Benediktsson announced that the government had collapsed due to disputes over foreign policy, asylum seekers, and energy, prompting him to call for new elections and ask President [[Halla Tómasdóttir]] the next day to dissolve the [[Althingi]] and set the elections for 30 November.{{cite news |url=https://apnews.com/article/iceland-snap-election-coalition-government-9d170f37de3228506de93444668c416a |title=Iceland appears headed for a snap election after governing coalition collapses |work=[[Associated Press]] |date=14 October 2024 |access-date=14 October 2024 |archive-date=10 November 2024 cited "how different the Movement's vision for the future is, compared to what I want to stand for".{{cite web |url=https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2024/10/13/iceland-s-government-coalition-collapses-new-elections-to-be-held-in-november_6729282_4.html |title=Iceland's government coalition collapses, new elections to be held in November |work=[[Le Monde]] |date=13 October 2024 |access-date=14 October 2024 |archive-date=10 November 2024 |url-status=live }} ==Issues== In November 2024, a [[Gallup, Inc.|Gallup]] poll found that more than 60% of voters regarded healthcare, economic issues and housing as a top concern. Immigration was regarded as a key issue by 32% of those surveyed while asylum issues accounted for 18% of respondents. The public broadcaster [[RÚV]] said that an [[AI chatbot]] set up to answer election-related questions received mostly queries on housing and taxation.{{Cite web |date=30 November 2024 |title=Icelanders head to the polls after government collapse |url=https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20241130-icelanders-head-to-the-polls-after-government-collapse |access-date=30 November 2024 |website=France 24 |language=en}} == Electoral system == {{further|Elections in Iceland}} The 63 members of the [[Althing]] are elected by [[open list]] [[proportional representation]] in six multi-member [[Constituencies of Iceland|constituencies]], with 54 seats allocated to parties at the constituency level with no [[electoral threshold]], and 9 [[leveling seat]]s assigned to party lists at the national level in order to ensure proportionality with the election result, with a threshold of 5 percent required.{{cite report|title=Ísland, Alþingiskosningar, 27. April 2013: Úttektarskýrsla|url=http://www.osce.org/is/odihr/elections/iceland/103314?download=true|publisher=OSCE/ODIHR|date=24 June 2013|access-date=30 October 2017|archive-date=14 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160914235149/http://www.osce.org/is/odihr/elections/iceland/103314?download=true|url-status=live}} The 54 constituency seats are distributed within each constituency according to the [[D'Hondt method]].{{cite web|title=Útreikningar við úthlutun jöfnunarsæta|url=http://www.kosning.is/upplysingar/jofnunarsaeti/|publisher=Kosningavefur Dómsmála- og Mannréttindaráðuneytisins|date=27 April 2013|access-date=30 October 2017|archive-date=2 November 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171102015341/http://www.kosning.is/upplysingar/jofnunarsaeti/|url-status=live}} Election lists are determined by parties; although voters have the option of altering the order of candidates or striking out particular candidates entirely, this rarely has any effect on the result. The number of voters per parliamentary seat varies significantly between the constituencies of Iceland. The number of seats per constituency was determined by law in 1999 and is not updated before each election except when the number of voters per representative in the most represented constituency reaches half the number of voters per representative in the least represented constituency. The [[Constitution of Iceland|constitution]] stipulates that in this case, a constituency seat should be transferred from the most represented constituency to the least represented constituency. This has happened twice since 1999, in both cases transferring a constituency seat from the [[Northwest (Althing constituency)|Northwest]] constituency (a large rural constituency) to the [[Southwest (Althing constituency)|Southwest]] constituency (a relatively small constituency in area, adjoining the capital city). In the 2021 election, the number of eligible voters for each seat in the Southwest was 5671.5, more than double the 2693.5 eligible voters for each seat in the Northwest. According to the constitution, this means another transfer of a constituency seat from the Northwest to the Southwest before this election.{{Cite web |date=15 September 2025 |title=General elections to the Althingi 30 November 2024 |url=https://hagstofas3bucket.hagstofa.is/hagstofan/media/public/2025/9572a72b-76f3-481b-ba87-217bdf8858b5.pdf |access-date=17 Mar 2026}} ===Date=== Per Article 23 in Chapter V of Act No. 112 from the 25 June 2021 Elections Law, elections must be held no later than the same weekday of the month four years after the previous elections, counting from the turn of the month;{{cite web |title=112/2021: Kosningalög |url=https://www.althingi.is/lagas/nuna/2021112.html |access-date=28 May 2022 |publisher=Alþingi |archive-date=28 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220528200058/https://www.althingi.is/lagas/nuna/2021112.html |url-status=live }} therefore, because the [[2021 Icelandic parliamentary election|2021 election]] took place on the fourth Saturday in September, the latest possible date for the election was 27 September 2025.{{cn|date=December 2024}} Following the collapse of the government in October 2024, the election was held on 30 November. ==Political parties== {{see also|List of political parties in Iceland}} The table below lists political parties participating in the election. style="background:#FEF4AE;"| 2 | 1 ! style="background:#C5F7CA;"| 2 | 10 |} == Government formation == {{Main|Cabinet of Kristrún Frostadóttir}} [[People's Party (Iceland)|People's Party]] leader [[Inga Sæland]] expressed an interest in joining a governing coalition and said she favored a coalition consisting of her own party, the [[Social Democratic Alliance]], and [[Viðreisn]]. However, she did not explicitly rule out any party. This followed with praise from the leader of the Social Democratic Alliance [[Kristrún Frostadóttir]] for Inga's work on repairing issues affecting the elderly and disabled.{{Cite news|date=2024-12-01 |access-date=2024-12-02|title=Inga Sæland hallar sér upp að Kristrúnu|url=https://www.mbl.is/frettir/innlent/2024/12/01/inga_saeland_hallar_ser_upp_ad_kristrunu/|website=mbl.is}} Kristrún Frostadóttir also expressed interest in forming a government, but did not rule out any party, but signaled that if she formed a coalition with the [[Independence Party (Iceland)|Independence Party]], she said they would need to change their policies. However, she said she preferred a coalition with those who were ideologically closer to her party. There was talk also about the possibility of forming the biggest parliamentary majority between the three largest parties (S, D, and C), similarly to what was done in the last parliamentary session. Viðreisn's leader [[Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir]] also expressed an interest in forming a government and said she was interested in joining a "coherent" government and was not seeking to become Prime Minister. Election results showed that her party could play a kingmaker role in who forms the next government and would be able to provide a majority (if it comes down) to either a possible centrist left-leaning coalition with the Social Democrats and People's or possibly with Independence and the [[Centre Party (Iceland)|Centre Party]], which is more right-leaning. Centre Party leader [[Sigmundur Davíð Gunnlaugsson]] met with President [[Halla Tómasdóttir]] on 2 December. He stated that he believed that Social Democratic Alliance leader Kristrún Frostadóttir should get the first mandate to form a government, as her party won first and said he did not rule out joining a government with any party. He stated he would implement "real changes", if he does enter a coalition.{{Cite news|date=2 Dec 2024 |access-date=2024-12-02|title=Eðlilegt að Kristrún fái umboðið|url= https://www.mbl.is/frettir/innlent/2024/12/02/edlilegt_ad_kristrun_fai_umbodid/|website=mbl.is}} Independence Party leader and Prime Minister [[Bjarni Benediktsson (born 1970)|Bjarni Benediktsson]] also met with Halla and stated that he would not be making any special effort in asking for a mandate to forming a government, stating nothing was achieved in getting it and not being able to do anything with it, if received. He also stated he intended to meet with his party to decide on how to proceed, following the elections.{{Cite news|date=2 Dec 2024 |access-date=2024-12-02|title= Discussed the possibilities in the situation|url= https://icelandmonitor.mbl.is/news/news/2024/12/02/discussed_the_possibilities_in_the_situation/ |website=mbl.is}} On 3 December, Halla gave Kristrún the first mandate and expressed interest in trying to form a government with her own party, Viðreisn, and the People's Party.{{Cite news|date=3 Dec 2024 |access-date=2024-12-03|title= Kristrún Frostadóttir Receives The Mandate To Form Government|url= https://grapevine.is/news/2024/12/03/kristrun-frostadottir-receives-the-mandate-to-form-government/ |website=grapevine.is}} On 4 December, Kristrún Frostadóttir began the formal process of forming a government consisting of Social Democratic Alliance, Viðreisn and the People's Party. If successfully formed, the government would have 36 of the 63 seats in the [[Althing]]. The coalition leaders were dubbed as "[[valkyrie]]s", citing that the three parties are led by women.{{Cite web |date=2024-12-04 |title=From Iceland — Kristrún Frostadóttir Begins Formal Government Formation |url=https://grapevine.is/news/2024/12/04/kristrun-frostadottir-begins-formal-government-formation/ |access-date=2024-12-04 |website=The Reykjavik Grapevine |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |date=2024-12-03 |title=Valkyrie Coalition: Iceland's New Political Era |url=https://www.devdiscourse.com/article/politics/3179905-valkyrie-coalition-icelands-new-political-era?amp |access-date=2024-12-17 |website=www.devdiscourse.com |language=en-US}} On 21 December, Kristrún Frostadóttir formed [[Cabinet of Kristrún Frostadóttir|her cabinet]] and was appointed prime minister. The cabinet consists of four ministers from Kristrún's Social Democratic Alliance, four from Þorgerður's Viðreisn, and three from Inga's People's Party.{{cite web |url=https://icelandmonitor.mbl.is/news/news/2024/12/21/these_are_the_ministers_of_the_government/ |title=These are the ministers of the government |language=en |website=Iceland Monitor.is |author=Iceland Monitor|access-date=21 December 2024}} == Notes == {{notelist}} == References == {{reflist}} {{Icelandic elections}} [[Category:2024 elections in Iceland|Parliamentary]] [[Category:November 2024 in Europe|Icelandic parliamentary election]] [[Category:Parliamentary elections in Iceland]] [[Category:Opinion polling in Iceland]]

All 300 members of the [[National Assembly (South Korea)|National Assembly]] were elected, 254 from [[first-past-the-post]] [[South Korean Legislature Constituencies|constituencies]] and 46 from [[party-list proportional representation|proportional party lists]].{{Cite web |date=20 February 2024 |title=Political parties in full-fledged election mode as April 10 voting nears |url=https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/www/nation/2024/05/113_369101.html |access-date=29 February 2024 |website=[[The Korea Times]] |language=en |archive-date=29 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240229214704/https://m.koreatimes.co.kr/pages/article.asp?newsIdx=369101 |url-status=live }}{{cite web |script-title=ko:선거일정 |url=https://www.nec.go.kr/site/nec/ex/bbs/View.do?cbIdx=1104&bcIdx=192949 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231125194511/https://www.nec.go.kr/site/nec/ex/bbs/View.do?cbIdx=1104&bcIdx=192949 |archive-date=25 November 2023 |access-date=25 November 2023 |website=National Electoral Commission}} The two largest parties, the liberal [[Democratic Party (South Korea, 2015)|Democratic Party]] and the conservative [[People Power Party]], once again set up [[Decoy list#South Korea|satellite parties]] to take advantage of the electoral system. The election served as a "mid-term evaluation" for the administration of President [[Yoon Suk-yeol]] as it approached its third year. Additionally, there was significant interest in whether the ruling party could surpass the constraints of the ruling coalition, which did not secure a majority in the previous general election, and gain the necessary momentum to govern effectively during the remainder of its term.{{Cite web |last=김 |first=연정 |date=2024-04-11 |title=[4·10 총선] 또 무너진 與…野 협조 없이 입법·예산 불가능 |url=https://www.yna.co.kr/view/AKR20240410039700001 |access-date=2024-04-21 |website=[[Yonhap News Agency]] |language=ko}} The election saw opposition parties, primarily the [[Democratic Party (South Korea, 2015)|Democratic Party]], retain their majority in the National Assembly.{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/south-korea-opposition-wins-landslide-parliamentary-vote-resounding-blow-yoon-2024-04-10/|title=Opposition win in South Korea election to deepen policy stalemate for Yoon|first1=Hyunsu|last1=Yim|first2=Jack|last2=Kim|publisher=Reuters|date=11 April 2024|accessdate=11 April 2024}} The new legislators had their first meeting on 30 May.{{cite news|url=https://en.yna.co.kr/view/PYH20240530131600315|title=1st meeting of 22nd parliament's DP lawmakers|publisher=[[Yonhap News Agency]]|date=30 May 2024|accessdate=2 June 2024}} ==Background== ===Redistricting=== On 28 February 2024, the ruling and opposition parties reached a consensus to redraw the electoral districts.{{Cite web |last=안 |first=윤학 |date=2024-02-29 |script-title=ko:[속보] 여야, 선거구획정 극적 합의..."오늘 본회의서 처리" |url=https://www.ytn.co.kr/_ln/0101_202402291206004957 |access-date=2024-04-21 |website=[[YTN]] |language=ko}} Subsequently, the National Assembly's plenary session passed an amendment to the Public Offices Election Act, resulting in the reformation of the electoral districts. In comparison to the 21st National Assembly elections, there was an increase of one constituency, bringing the total to 254, while the seats for proportional representation decreased by one, totaling 46.{{Cite web |last=김 |first=연정 |date=2024-02-29 |title=4·10총선 선거구 획정안 국회 통과…전북 대신 비례 1석 축소 |url=https://www.yna.co.kr/view/AKR20240229146100001 |access-date=2024-04-21 |website=[[Yonhap News Agency]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240410124404/https://en.yna.co.kr/view/AEN20240410005651315?section=national/politics |url-status=live }} ==Results== {{See also|List of members of the National Assembly (South Korea), 2024–2028}} Exit polls indicated that the Democratic Party and its partner, the [[Democratic Alliance of Korea]], would win between 168 and 197 seats in the National Assembly, while the People Power Party and its partner, the [[People Future Party]], were expected to win between 85 and 111 seats. The [[Rebuilding Korea Party]], which only contested proportional representation seats, was projected to win 15 seats. Democratic Party leader Lee Jae-myung was projected to keep his seat in [[Gyeyang B]] of [[Incheon]] against People Power Party candidate and former land minister [[Won Hee-ryong]], winning 56.1% and 42.8% of the vote respectively.{{Cite web |date=10 April 2024 |title=(4th LD) Opposition forecast to win landslide victory: exit polls |url=https://en.yna.co.kr/view/AEN20240409006054315?section=national/politics |website=[[Yonhap News Agency]] |access-date=10 April 2024 |archive-date=10 April 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240410123546/https://en.yna.co.kr/view/AEN20240409006054315?section=national/politics |url-status=live }} The [[Justice Party (South Korea)|Justice Party]] failed to win seats for the first time since its foundation in 2012. Among the elected candidates in proportional representation seats was Park Choong-kwon (representing the People Future Party), a North Korean defector who previously worked in the [[North Korean nuclear weapons programme]] before fleeing to the South in 2009.{{Cite web |date=12 April 2024 |title=How a North Korean missile researcher became a South Korean MP proportional representation seats since its introduction in [[2004 South Korean legislative election|2004]], with the National Electoral Commission tallying 1,309,931 such ballots, equivalent to 4.4% opposition bloc (including the [[Rebuilding Korea Party]] and [[New Future Party (South Korea)|New Future]], which are both led by former members of the [[Democratic Party (South Korea, 2015)|Democratic Party]] and are considerably anti-Yoon){{cite web |last1=Kim |first1=Sang |last2=Young Kim |first2=Joo |last3=Jeong |first3=Hyeonseung |title=A Guide to South Korea's 2024 National They won a combined total of 189 against the government alliance and [[Reform Party (South Korea)|Reform]] (who are more moderately conservative and big tent) total of 111. Nevertheless, the election result, and overwhelming majority in favor of the governmental opposition, was enough to effectively block any government plans going into the future. ''[[The Diplomat (magazine)|The Diplomat]]'' described [[Yoon Suk-yeol]] as a "lame duck" for his remaining three years in office.{{cite web |last1=Shin |first1=Mitch |title=In South Korea, President Yoon's Lame Duck Era Officially Begins |url=https://thediplomat.com/2024/04/in-south-korea-president-yoons-lame-duck-era-officially-begins/ |publisher=The Diplomat |access-date=17 April 2024 |archive-date=16 April 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240416130903/https://thediplomat.com/2024/04/in-south-korea-president-yoons-lame-duck-era-officially-begins/ |url-status=live }} Chae Jin-won of Humanitas College at [[Kyung Hee University]] stated that "If Yoon can't find a way to work with the opposition, there is a likelihood of impeachment, which some factions in the ruling party may comply with for the sake of their own political futures."{{cite web |title=Election rout makes Yoon's 'lame duck' fears reality |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2024/04/11/asia-pacific/politics/election-rout-yoon-lame-duck/ |website=[[The Japan Times]] |date=11 April 2024 |publisher=Jiji Press |access-date=17 April 2024 |archive-date=11 April 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240411094953/https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2024/04/11/asia-pacific/politics/election-rout-yoon-lame-duck/ |url-status=live }} ==See also== *[[List of members of the National Assembly (South Korea), 2024–2028]] *[[2024 North Korean parliamentary election]] ==Notes== {{Notelist}} ==References== {{Reflist}} {{South Korean elections}} [[Category:2024 elections in South Korea|Legislative]] [[Category:April 2024 in South Korea|Legislative election]] [[Category:Legislative elections in South Korea]] [[Category:Presidency of Yoon Suk Yeol]]

coalition of the [[Democratic Party (Luxembourg)|Democratic Party]] (DP), the [[Luxembourg Socialist Workers' Party]] (LSAP) and [[The Greens (Luxembourg)|The Greens]]. ==Electoral system== The 60 members of the [[Chamber of Deputies (Luxembourg)|Chamber of Deputies]] are elected by [[proportional representation]] in four [[Constituencies of Luxembourg|multi-member constituencies]]; nine in [[North (Chamber of Deputies of Luxembourg constituency)|North]] constituency, seven in [[East (Chamber of Deputies of Luxembourg constituency)|East]], 23 in [[South (Chamber of Deputies of Luxembourg constituency)|South]] and 21 in [[Centre (Chamber of Deputies of Luxembourg constituency)|Centre]]. Voters can vote for a party list or cast multiple votes for as many candidates as there are seats. Seat allocation is calculated in accordance with the [[Hagenbach-Bischoff quota]].[http://www.ipu.org/parline-e/reports/2191_B.htm Electoral system] IPU Only [[Luxembourgish nationality law|Luxembourgish citizens]] may vote in general elections. A proposal to extend voting rights to foreigners who have lived in Luxembourg for at least ten years and have previously voted in a European or local election in Luxembourg, was rejected in a [[2015 Luxembourg constitutional referendum|2015 referendum]]. Voting is [[Compulsory voting|mandatory]] for eligible Luxembourg citizens who live in Luxembourg and are under 75 years of age.{{Cite web|url=https://guichet.public.lu/citoyens/en/citoyennete/elections/elections-legislatives/vote-elections-legislatives/index.html|title=Voting in legislative elections - Citoyens // Luxembourg|website=Government of Luxembourg|language=en|access-date=2018-06-04}} Luxembourg citizens who live abroad may vote by post at the [[Communes of Luxembourg|commune]] in which they most recently lived in Luxembourg.{{Cite news|url=https://elections.public.lu/fr/systeme-electoral/legislatives-mode-emploi/vote-correspondance.html|title=Vote par correspondance|access-date=2018-06-04|language=fr}} Luxembourg citizens who were born in Luxembourg but have never lived there may vote by post at the commune in which they were born. Luxembourg citizens who were not born in Luxembourg and have never lived there may vote by post at the commune of [[Luxembourg City]]. ==Contesting parties== {| class=wikitable ! rowspan=2| List

Incumbent Prime Minister [[Krišjānis Kariņš]] led his [[New Unity]] party and allies to a decisive win in the election which was seen as a decisive victory for pro-Western parties in the country.{{Cite web |date=2022-10-02 |title=Victory for pro-Western over pro-Moscow parties in Latvia's election |url=https://www.euronews.com/2022/10/02/latvia-prime-ministers-new-unity-party-wins-general-election-early-results |access-date=2024-11-20 |website=euronews |language=en}} Karinš went on to form the [[Second Kariņš cabinet]] with [[National Alliance (Latvia)|National Alliance]] and [[United List (Latvia)|United List]].{{Cite web |date=2022-12-14 |title=Three Latvian parties sign coalition deal to form government |url=https://apnews.com/article/russia-ukraine-latvia-government-and-politics-a1bcb8d018e6c8b5c31975911fb881ad |access-date=2024-11-20 |website=AP News |language=en}} ==Electoral system== The 100 members of the Saeima are elected by [[open list]], [[proportional representation]] from five multi-member constituencies ranging in size from 12 to 36 seats and based on the [[regions of Latvia]], with overseas votes included in the Riga constituency. Seats are allocated using the [[Sainte-Laguë method]] with a national [[electoral threshold]] of 5%. Voters may cast "specific votes" for candidates on the list that they have voted for. This involves drawing a plus sign (+) next to the candidate's names to indicate preference (positive votes), or by crossing out names to indicate disapproval (negative votes). The number of votes for each candidate is the number of votes cast for the list, plus their number of positive votes, minus their number of negative votes. The candidates with the highest vote totals fill their party's seats.[http://archive.ipu.org/parline-e/reports/2177_B.htm Electoral system] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180806184537/http://archive.ipu.org/parline-e/reports/2177_B.htm |date=6 August 2018 }} IPU ===Seat redistribution === The Central Electoral Commission is required to determine the number of Members of Parliament (MPs) to be elected using the number of eligible voters four months before the election. On 2 June 2022, the Central Electoral Commission has announced the new distribution of MPs. [[Riga (Saeima constituency)|Rīga]] and [[Livonia (Saeima constituency)|Vidzeme]] constituencies have both gained one seat compared to the 2018 election, while [[Latgallia (Saeima constituency)|Latgale]] and [[Semigallia (Saeima constituency)|Zemgale]] constituencies have both lost one.{{Cite web |date=2 June 2022 |title=Rudenī 14.Saeimas vēlēšanās par vienu deputātu vairāk ievēlēs Rīgā un Vidzemē |trans-title=One more MP will be elected in Rīga and Vidzeme in the fall |url=https://www.tvnet.lv/7536773/rudeni-14-saeimas-velesanas-par-vienu-deputatu-vairak-ieveles-riga-un-vidzeme |access-date=2 June 2022 |website=TVNET |language=lv |archive-date=2 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220602164934/https://www.tvnet.lv/7536773/rudeni-14-saeimas-velesanas-par-vienu-deputatu-vairak-ieveles-riga-un-vidzeme |url-status=live }} {| class="wikitable" style="align=center;" ! In a speech after the election, Kariņš stated that Latvia would continue to support Ukraine against Russia and he stated his preference to maintain the current [[First Kariņš cabinet|coalition government]].{{Cite web |date=2 October 2022 |title=Latvia PM's New Unity party wins general election — early results |url=https://www.euronews.com/2022/10/02/latvia-prime-ministers-new-unity-party-wins-general-election-early-results |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221002080642/http://www.euronews.com/2022/10/02/latvia-prime-ministers-new-unity-party-wins-general-election-early-results |archive-date=2 October 2022 |access-date=2 October 2022 |website=euronews |language=en}} The [[Union of Greens and Farmers]] placed second, receiving 13% of the vote, despite leader [[Aivars Lembergs]] being sentenced to five years in prison in 2021 and under sanction by the United States.{{Cite web |title=Verdict: Saeima elections 2022 winners and losers |url=https://eng.lsm.lv/article/politics/politics/verdict-saeima-elections-2022-winners-and-losers.a476213/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221002091503/https://eng.lsm.lv/article/politics/politics/verdict-saeima-elections-2022-winners-and-losers.a476213/ |archive-date=2 October 2022 |access-date=2 October 2022 |website=eng.lsm.lv |language=en}} The other parties which placed above the 5% threshold to receive a seat in parliament were the [[United List (Latvia)|United List]] with 11%, the [[National Alliance (Latvia)|National Alliance]] with 9.3%, [[For Stability!]] with 7%, [[Latvia First]] with 6%, and [[The Progressives (Latvia)|The Progressives]], who entered parliament for the first time with 6% of the vote.{{Cite web |date=3 October 2022 |title=Saeima election results: Seven lists win seats in Latvian parliament |url=https://news.err.ee/1608736561/saeima-election-results-seven-lists-win-seats-in-latvian-parliament |access-date=9 October 2022 |website=[[Eesti Rahvusringhääling]] |language=en}} The [[wasted vote]] in this election was 29.09%. [[Social Democratic Party "Harmony"|Harmony]], who had placed first in the previous three general elections, was unable to secure any parliamentary seats, being slightly under the 5% threshold (of all votes, including invalid) with 4.9% of the vote. This has been attributed to many reasons, including internal disputes on the [[2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine]], pushing away both ethnic Latvians and ethnic [[Russians in Latvia|Russians]]. General elections were held in [[Malta]] on 26 March 2022 to elect all members of the [[Parliament of Malta|House of Representatives]]. 

The [[Labour Party (Malta)|Labour Party]], which had governed Malta since [[2013 Maltese general election|2013]], won a second term in [[2017 Maltese general election|2017 election]] under [[Joseph Muscat]]. [[Simon Busuttil]], the leader of the opposition [[Nationalist Party (Malta)|Nationalist Party]], resigned after the 2017 election and was replaced by [[Adrian Delia]]. Following the assassination of journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia, Muscat was faced with a [[2019 Malta political crisis|political crisis]] and [[2019–2020 Maltese protests|mass protests]] in 2019 and resigned in January 2020. [[Robert Abela]] succeeded him as prime minister and leader of the Labour Party in January 2020, while [[Bernard Grech]] succeeded Delia later that year.

Journalists noted that the campaign was overshadowed by the [[2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine|Russian invasion of Ukraine]] and that it was the "quietest in decades". Six political parties nominated their candidates for the 2022 general election. The Labour Party and its leader campaigned on investing in [[green urbanism]] and [[environmental issues]], while the Nationalist Party pledged a one billion <!-- one billion what? -->  investment in ten new economic sectors. The [[AD+PD]] campaigned on proposals for [[LGBT rights in Malta|LGBT rights]], while the [[People's Party (Malta)|People's Party]] campaigned on increasing the [[minimum wage]] and abolishing [[EU Digital COVID Certificate|green passes]]. Additionally, [[ABBA (political party)|ABBA]] supported the investigation into [[Abortion-rights movements|abortion-rights]] activists, while [[Volt Malta]] supported the [[Abortion in Malta|legalisation of abortion]]. [[Opinion polling for the 2022 Maltese general election|Opinion polls]] in the run-up to the election indicated another victory for Labour Party.

The Labour Party retained its majority in parliament, winning a third consecutive election for the first time since [[1981 Maltese general election|1981]] with 55.11% of the popular vote, the largest share since [[1955 Maltese general election|1955]], marginally surpassing the 55.04% it scored in [[2017 Maltese general election|2017]]. Voter turnout was 86%. As a result of a constitutional amendment, Article 52(A), passed before the elections, twelve seats were added to the House of Representatives and were given to women from both parties, so as to limit male dominance.<ref name="genderbonus">{{Cite web |date=12 April 2022 |title=General Election 2022 - elected to fill the additional seats |url=https://electoral.gov.mt/pr2-12-04-22-en |access-date=14 April 2022 |website=Electoral Commission of Malta |archive-date=30 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220430095713/https://electoral.gov.mt/pr2-12-04-22-en |url-status=live }}</ref> Abela formed his [[Maltese Government 2022–2027|new cabinet]] four days after the election.

==Electoral system==
{{Politics of Malta}}
Most Maltese MPs are elected from 13 five-seat constituencies by [[single transferable vote]] using [[optional preferential voting]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=How Malta Votes: An Overview - Malta Elections |url=https://www.um.edu.mt/projects/maltaelections/stvsystem/howmaltavotes |access-date=19 November 2021 |website=University of Malta |archive-date=8 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220308062851/https://www.um.edu.mt/projects/maltaelections/stvsystem/howmaltavotes |url-status=live }}</ref> Candidates who pass the [[Hagenbach-Bischoff quota]] in the first round are elected, and any surplus votes transferred to the remaining candidates, who will be elected if this enables them to pass the quota.<ref name=":0" /> The lowest ranked candidates are then eliminated one-by-one with their preferences transferred to other candidates, who are elected as they achieve the quota, until all five seats are filled.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Malta, electoral system |url=http://archive.ipu.org/parline-e/reports/2203_B.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171012044754/http://archive.ipu.org/parline-e/reports/2203_B.htm |archive-date=12 October 2017 |access-date=19 November 2021 |website=Inter-Parliamentary Union}}</ref>

Other seats are filled to achieve other types of fairness. If a party wins a majority of first preference votes but fails to achieve a parliamentary majority, they are awarded seats to ensure a one-seat majority, if they are one of only two parties to obtain seats.<ref name=":1" /> As well, 12 seats are awarded to unsuccessful candidates of the "under-represented gender" if it receives less than 40 percent of the seats.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://constitutionnet.org/news/maltas-proposed-gender-top-system-good-intentions-questionable-means | title=Malta's proposed gender top-up system: Good intentions, questionable means?|date=2021-02-19 |author=Victor Paul Borg|website=[[ConstitutionNet]] }}</ref> Thus the Maltese parliament in total has 79 members.

Candidates are allowed to run in two different constituencies, and if elected in both, they must vacate one of the seats. Their replacement is chosen by a "casual election", in which the votes for the vacating candidate are redistributed.<ref name="x147">{{cite web | title=Marking your ballot | website=Times of Malta | date=2013-03-08 | url=https://timesofmalta.com/article/Marking-your-ballot.460689 | access-date=2026-05-05}}</ref>

In 2018 the [[government of Malta]] lowered the national voting age to 16.<ref>{{Cite web |date=5 March 2018 |title=16-year-olds granted the vote in national elections |url=https://timesofmalta.com/articles/view/16-year-olds-granted-the-vote-in-national-elections.672453 |access-date=4 March 2022 |website=Times of Malta |language=en-GB |archive-date=26 March 2022 legislature a gender-corrective mechanism was introduced, with Article 52A of the Constitution stating that provides for up to 12 additional seats for unelected candidates from "the under-represented === Party campaigns ===
==== Labour Party ====
[[File:Malta Flimkien campaign logo.png|thumb|upright=0.6|alt="Malta Together", a slogan used by the Labour Party during the campaign period|"Malta Together", a slogan used by the Labour Party during the campaign period]]
The [[Labour Party (Malta)|Labour Party]] began its campaign in late February, during which the party stated its pledge to convert [[Floriana]]'s St Anne Street into a public garden.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Zammit |first=Mark Laurence |date=21 February 2022 |title=Labour pledges to convert Floriana's St Anne Street into public garden |url=https://timesofmalta.com/articles/view/labour-pledges-to-convert-florianas-st-anne-street-into-public-garden.935951 |access-date=25 March 2022 |website=Times of Malta |language=en-GB |archive-date=25 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220325184520/https://timesofmalta.com/articles/view/labour-pledges-to-convert-florianas-st-anne-street-into-public-garden.935951 |url-status=live }}</ref> In mid-March, the Labour Party released its election manifesto, which included investments in [[Green urbanism|green urban areas]], an extension to free [[child care]] to all, and slashing [[corporate tax]] rates.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Borg |first=Bertrand |date=11 March 2022 |title=Labour's election manifesto at-a-glance: What is the party proposing? |url=https://timesofmalta.com/articles/view/labours-election-manifesto-at-a-glance-what-is-the-party-proposing.940737 |access-date=25 March 2022 |website=Times of Malta |language=en-GB |archive-date=25 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220325184521/https://timesofmalta.com/articles/view/labours-election-manifesto-at-a-glance-what-is-the-party-proposing.940737 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Borg |first=Amy |date=21 February 2022 |title='Se ninvestu €700 miljun fi spazji ħodor' – Abela |url=https://newsbook.com.mt/live-abela-jindirizza-konferenza-tal-ahbarijiet/ |access-date=25 March 2022 |website=Newsbook |language=mt |archive-date=21 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220321233218/https://newsbook.com.mt/live-abela-jindirizza-konferenza-tal-ahbarijiet/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Abela primarily campaigned on [[environmental issues]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Xuereb |first=Matthew |date=11 March 2022 |title=Labour manifesto is a 'blueprint for Malta's future' - PM |url=https://timesofmalta.com/articles/view/labour-manifesto-is-a-blueprint-for-maltas-future-pm.940794 |access-date=25 March 2022 |website=Times of Malta |language=en-GB |archive-date=25 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220325184437/https://timesofmalta.com/articles/view/labour-manifesto-is-a-blueprint-for-maltas-future-pm.940794 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=de Gaetano |first=Elizabeth |date=23 February 2022 |title=Where have we heard these before? PM launches election campaign with rehashed electoral pledges |url=https://theshiftnews.com/2022/02/23/where-have-we-heard-these-before-prime-minister-launches-election-campaign-with-rehashed-electoral-pledges/ |access-date=25 March 2022 |website=The Shift News |archive-date=7 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220407031724/https://theshiftnews.com/2022/02/23/where-have-we-heard-these-before-prime-minister-launches-election-campaign-with-rehashed-electoral-pledges/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Joseph Muscat, the former prime minister, also participated in Labour Party campaigns.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Martin |first=Ivan |date=26 February 2022 |title=Enthusiasm for Joseph Muscat as he hits the campaign trail |url=https://timesofmalta.com/articles/view/watch-enthusiasm-for-joseph-muscat-as-he-hits-the-campaign-trail.937179 |access-date=25 March 2022 |website=Times of Malta |language=en-GB |archive-date=27 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220327052452/https://timesofmalta.com/articles/view/watch-enthusiasm-for-joseph-muscat-as-he-hits-the-campaign-trail.937179 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Bonnici |first=Julian |date=23 February 2022 |title=Joseph Muscat Is Lending Support To Labour Candidates On Campaign Trail |url=https://lovinmalta.com/news/joseph-muscat-labour-party-candidate/ |access-date=25 March 2022 |website=Lovin Malta |language=en-GB |archive-date=8 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220408005610/https://lovinmalta.com/news/joseph-muscat-labour-party-candidate/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== Nationalist Party ====
The election program of the [[Nationalist Party (Malta)|Nationalist Party]] was released on 24 February, which had included 540 proposals in total.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Borg |first=Jacob |date=24 February 2022 |title=PN election programme at-a-glance: What is the party proposing? |url=https://timesofmalta.com/articles/view/pn-election-programme-at-a-glance-what-is-the-party-proposing.936849 |access-date=25 March 2022 |website=Times of Malta |language=en-GB |archive-date=25 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220325184527/https://timesofmalta.com/articles/view/pn-election-programme-at-a-glance-what-is-the-party-proposing.936849 |url-status=live }}</ref> The party also pledged a one billion investment in ten new economic sectors.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Berger |first=Shona |date=20 February 2022 |title=PN pledges €1 billion for 10 new economic sectors in its first campaign rally - Voting stations were opened from 07:00 to 22:00, and in total, there were 355,075 citizens that had the right to vote in the general election.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Orland |first=Kevin Schembri |date=26 March 2022 |title=Maltese vote in general election with some firsts for nation |url=https://apnews.com/article/europe-elections-voting-general-elections-malta-4e3b0cc428e69f8803f347ca8bcdb4d9 |access-date=26 March 2022 |website=Associated Press |archive-date=26 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220326212809/https://apnews.com/article/europe-elections-voting-general-elections-malta-4e3b0cc428e69f8803f347ca8bcdb4d9 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=26 March 2022 |title=Voting begins in Malta's general election |url=https://timesofmalta.com/articles/view/voting-begins-in-maltas-general-election.944094 |access-date=26 March 2022 |website=Times of Malta |language=en-GB |archive-date=26 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220326130157/https://timesofmalta.com/articles/view/voting-begins-in-maltas-general-election.944094 |url-status=live }}</ref> The turnout at 14:00 was reported at 44.8%, which was eight points lower than in 2017.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Sansone |first1=Kurt |last2=Vella |first2=Matthew |date=26 March 2022 |title=Election Day: Voting in Malta comes to an end with prospect of lowest turnout ever |url=http://www.maltatoday.com.mt/news/election-2022/115941/live_blog_election_voting_day_1 |access-date=26 March 2022 |website=MaltaToday |archive-date=27 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220327104933/https://www.maltatoday.com.mt/news/election-2022/115941/live_blog_election_voting_day_1 |url-status=live }}</ref> According to the Electoral Commission of Malta, a total of 304,050 citizens voted, which made it the lowest turnout since the [[1955 Maltese general election|1955 election]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=26 March 2022 |title=Electoral Commission of Malta General Election 2022 - Approximate percentage of votes cast over the 4 voting days 2022 |url=https://electoral.gov.mt/Contents/Item/Display/72635 |access-date=27 March 2022 |website=Electoral Commission of Malta |archive-date=28 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220328062602/https://electoral.gov.mt/Contents/Item/Display/72635 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Bonnici |first=Julian |date=27 March 2022 |title=Breaking: Labour Party Wins General Election |url=https://lovinmalta.com/news/election-2022/labour-party-win-general-election-2022/ |access-date=27 March 2022 |website=Lovin Malta |language=en-GB |archive-date=28 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220328061605/https://lovinmalta.com/news/election-2022/labour-party-win-general-election-2022/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In addition to the 65 regularly elected members, two seats were awarded to the Nationalist Party to restore proportionality between votes obtained and parliamentary representation and twelve more women were appointed (six for each of the parties with elected members) to comply with the gender-corrective mechanism.<ref>{{cite web |last=Sansone |first=Kurt |date=6 May 2022 |title=Malta's new parliament: fresher, younger faces and a larger House... |url=https://www.maltatoday.com.mt/news/national/116310/maltas_new_parliament_fresher_younger_faces_and_a_larger_house#.Yv9NqHZBzIU |access-date=19 August 2022 |website=Malta Today |archive-date=8 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220608082619/https://www.maltatoday.com.mt/news/national/116310/maltas_new_parliament_fresher_younger_faces_and_a_larger_house#.Yv9NqHZBzIU |url-status=live }}</ref>

|access-date=5 January 2025 |work=Brújula Política |date=12 November 2024}} == Background == === Political background === In the [[2018 Mexican general election|2018 election]], [[Andrés Manuel López Obrador]], a three-time presidential candidate and founder of the [[Morena (political party)|National Regeneration Movement]] (Morena), ran as the candidate of the [[Juntos Haremos Historia]] alliance, which included Morena, the [[Labor Party (Mexico)|Labor Party]] (PT), and the [[Social Encounter Party]] (PES). He won in a landslide, securing 54.71% of the vote and defeating his closest rival, [[Ricardo Anaya]] of the [[Por México al Frente]] coalition, by nearly 31 percentage points. The Juntos Haremos Historia alliance also secured majorities in the [[Chamber of Deputies (Mexico)|Chamber of Deputies]] and the [[Senate of the Republic (Mexico)|Senate]]. As president, López Obrador expanded the Mexican welfare state with programs aimed at the elderly and low-income students, raised the minimum wage significantly, and invested heavily in infrastructure projects such as the [[Tren Maya]] and the [[Felipe Ángeles International Airport]]. He combatted corruption by implementing [[austerity]] measures, including salary caps, budget cuts across the government, and the dismissal of numerous government employees.{{Cite web |last=Romero |first=Luis Gómez |date=2019-02-09 |title=López Obrador Takes on Corruption and Poverty in Mexico Through Austerity |url=https://psmag.com/economics/combatting-corruption-in-mexico-through-austerity/ |access-date=2025-01-14 |website=Pacific Standard |language=en-US}}{{Cite news |last=Agren |first=David |date=2020-04-24 |title='He's Mr Scrooge': Mexican president unveils severe cuts amid coronavirus |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/apr/24/mexico-amlo-severe-cuts-amid-coronavirus |access-date=2025-01-14 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}} While his administration achieved a poverty reduction, it faced accusations of [[democratic backsliding]] and undermining institutional independence, including frequent attacks on journalists and judges during his morning press conferences and questioning the necessity of independent public agencies such as the INE and INAI.{{Cite journal |last1=Berg |first1=Ryan C. |last2=Moraveg |first2=Leonardo |date=2024-05-31 |title=An Uncertain Future: Democratic Backsliding through Executive Aggrandizement under AMLO |url=https://www.csis.org/analysis/uncertain-future-democratic-backsliding-through-executive-aggrandizement-under-amlo |journal=Center for Strategic and International Studies |language=en}} The country’s murder rate fell from 30 per 100,000 people in 2018 when AMLO entered office, to 28 per 100,000 people in 2021 according to [[World Bank]] data. Between 2019 and 2023 there was a 15 percent decrease in the number of murders according to public data.{{Cite web |last=Osgood |first=Brian |title=What is the legacy of Mexico's President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador? |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/9/30/what-is-the-legacy-of-mexican-president-andres-manuel-lopez-obrador |access-date=2024-11-29 |website=Al Jazeera |language=en}}{{Cite web |date=2024-10-02 |title=Termina el sexenio de AMLO con 199 mil 619 asesinatos, la cifra más alta en la historia reciente |url=https://www.elfinanciero.com.mx/nacional/2024/10/02/termina-el-sexenio-de-amlo-con-199-mil-619-asesinatos-la-cifra-mas-alta-en-la-historia-reciente/ |access-date=2025-01-14 |website=El Financiero |language=es}} During the [[2021 Mexican legislative election|2021 elections]], party alliances shifted significantly. The [[National Action Party (Mexico)|National Action Party]] (PAN), the [[Institutional Revolutionary Party]] (PRI), and the [[Party of the Democratic Revolution]] (PRD) formed [[Va por México|a big-tent coalition]] to challenge Morena's growing dominance.{{Cite web |date=2020-12-23 |title=Sí por México formaliza alianza PRI-PAN-PRD: "Nos une la amenaza que hoy vivimos todos", aseguró Marko {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180707182242/http://www.electionguide.org/elections/id/2246/|date=7 July 2018}} IFES Article 83 of the [[Mexican Constitution]] limits the president to a Estados Unidos Mexicanos. Artículo 83. 1917 (México).'' ==== Polling indicated that crime and violence ranked high on voters' concerns in the election.{{Cite web |date=30 January 2024 |title=¿Qué le preocupa al mundo y a los mexicanos en 2024? |url=https://businessinsider.mx/que-le-preocupa-al-mundo-a-los-mexicanos-2024-estudio-ipsos/ |access-date=1 March 2024 |website=Business Insider México |language=es |archive-date=1 March 2024 [[Andrés Manuel López Obrador]], Mexico experienced one of its bloodiest periods. From 2018 to 2022, the number of [[List of countries by intentional homicide rate|intentional homicides]] surpassed 30,000, with the peak in 2020 at 36,773 homicides.{{Cite web |title=México – Homicidios Intencionados 2022 |url=https://datosmacro.expansion.com/demografia/homicidios/mexico |access-date=2 March 2024 |website=Datosmacro.com |language=es |archive-date=2 March 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240302062315/https://datosmacro.expansion.com/demografia/homicidios/mexico |url-status=live}}{{Cite web |title=Informe de Seguridad |url=http://www.gob.mx/sspc/galerias/informe-de-seguridad-358359?idiom=es |access-date=1 March 2024 |website=gob.mx |language=es |archive-date=3 March 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240303033536/https://www.gob.mx/sspc/galerias/informe-de-seguridad-358359?idiom=es |url-status=live}} However, since 2020, homicide rates have decreased. In 2023, homicides fell below 30,000 for the first time since 2018, totaling 29,675.{{Cite web |date=16 January 2024 |title=Los homicidios dolosos caen un 4.18% en 2023 en México, primera vez por debajo de los 30,000 |url=https://www.forbes.com.mx/los-homicidios-dolosos-caen-un-4-18-en-2023-en-mexico-primera-vez-por-debajo-de-los-30000/ |access-date=1 March 2024 |website=Forbes México |language=es-MX |archive-date=1 March 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240301202535/https://www.forbes.com.mx/los-homicidios-dolosos-caen-un-4-18-en-2023-en-mexico-primera-vez-por-debajo-de-los-30000/ |url-status=live}} Despite this decrease, the numbers remain higher than recorded between 1990 and 2017. López Obrador tackled this issue by endorsing the "[[Abrazos, no balazos|hugs, not bullets]]" slogan and establishing the civilian-led [[National Guard (Mexico)|National Guard]]. Some have raised suspicions that López Obrador's administration is underreporting intentional homicides, with some cases possibly being reclassified as having undetermined intentions to bring the figure down.{{Cite web |date=25 January 2024 |title=Mexico marks another record-breaking year for murders |url=https://houstonherald.com/2024/01/mexico-marks-another-record-breaking-year-for-murders/ |access-date=1 March 2024 |website=Houston Herald |language=en-US |archive-date=1 March 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240301202534/https://houstonherald.com/2024/01/mexico-marks-another-record-breaking-year-for-murders/ |url-status=live}} Xóchitl Gálvez highlighted that security would be a top priority in her government. She opposed López Obrador's "hugs, not bullets" approach. She proposed several measures to strengthen state police forces nationwide, including raising their salaries to MXN 20,000 per month, building a university for aspiring police officers, and providing state governments with increased economic resources and advanced technology to combat crime.{{Cite web |last=Figueroa |first=Héctor |date=5 March 2024 |title=Xóchitl Gálvez construirá la Universidad Nacional para la Seguridad |url=https://www.excelsior.com.mx/nacional/xochitl-galvez-construira-la-universidad-nacional-para-la-seguridad/1639417 |access-date=6 March 2024 |website=Excélsior Claudia Sheinbaum has expressed her commitment to replicating her success as [[Head of Government of Mexico City]], where, in 2023, her policies brought down intentional homicides to their lowest
