==Filing of nomination papers==
Thirty-nine candidates from 12 political parties and 27 independent candidates indicated their intention to contest the 2024 presidential election. They collected nomination forms from the Electoral Commission.<ref>{{cite web |title=Here are the 39 aspirants who have picked up presidential nomination forms - Official |url=https://www.ghanaweb.com/GhanaHomePage/NewsArchive/Here-are-the-39-aspirants-who-have-picked-up-presidential-nomination-forms-Official-1949307 |website=GhanaWeb |access-date=12 September 2024 |date=5 September 2024}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |author1=Michael Quaye |author2=Samuel Duodu |title=As 39 pick presidential forms on the road to Election 2024, is it an issue of misrule or competition? |url=https://www.graphic.com.gh/news/politics/ghana-news-road-to-election-2024-issue-of-misrule-or-competition-as-39-pick-presidential-forms.html |location=Accra, Ghana|newspaper=[[Daily Graphic (Ghana)|Daily Graphic]]|access-date=12 September 2024 |date=9 September 2024}}</ref> The filing of nomination papers started on 9 September 2024.<ref>{{cite web |author1=Joseph Odotei |title=2024 election: Exclusive photos as 8 presidential aspirants file nomination forms - Adomonline.com |url=https://www.adomonline.com/2024-election-exclusive-photos-as-8-presidential-aspirants-file-nomination-forms/ |website=Adom Online |access-date=12 September 2024 |date=9 September 2024}}</ref> At the close of nominations on 13 September 2024, 24 of the candidates had successfully filed their nomination papers with the Commission.<ref name="cnr">{{cite web |author1=Hamdiad Mohammed |title=Election 2024: Meet the 24 Presidential candidates |url=https://citinewsroom.com/2024/09/2024-polls-meet-the-24-presidential-candidates-who-have-filed-nomination-forms/ |website=citinewsroom.com |access-date=16 September 2024 |date=16 September 2024}}</ref> Twelve candidates submitted forms as representatives of political parties and the other 12 were independent candidates. ==Final list of presidential candidates==
On 20 September 2024, the Electoral Commission released the final list of candidates who would be on the ballot for the presidential election. Thirteen of the 24 applicants made the final list while 11 were disqualified.<ref>{{cite web |title=Outcome of the filing of nominations for the 2024 presidential election |url=https://ec.gov.gh/outcome-of-the-filing-of-nominations-for-the-2024-presidential-election/ |website=Electoral Commission |access-date=23 September 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240923194634/https://ec.gov.gh/outcome-of-the-filing-of-nominations-for-the-2024-presidential-election/ |archive-date=23 September 2024 |date=20 September 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> The disqualifications were based on the candidates not having fulfilled all the requirements or discrepancies noticed on their forms.<ref>{{Cite news |author1=Enoch Darfah Frimpong |author2=Dickson Worlanyo Dotse |title=Why EC disqualified PNC's Bernard Mornah, Janet Nabla and 9 others |url=https://www.graphic.com.gh/news/politics/why-ec-disqualified-pncs-bernard-mornah-janet-nabla-and-9-others.html |location=Accra, Ghana|newspaper=[[Daily Graphic (Ghana)|Daily Graphic]]|access-date=21 September 2024 |date=20 September 2024}}</ref> Nine of the 12 candidates of political parties and four of the 12 independent candidates made the final list. Candidates of the People's National Convention (PNC), Progressive Alliance for Ghana (PAG) and the [[Progressive People's Party (Ghana)|Progressive People's Party]] (PPP) were not listed.<ref>{{Cite news |author1=Enoch Darfah Frimpong |title=EC clears 13 presidential candidates for Election 2024, PNC's Bernard Mornah and 10 others disqualified |url=https://www.graphic.com.gh/news/politics/ec-clears-13-presidential-candidates-for-election-2024.html |location=Accra, Ghana|newspaper=[[Daily Graphic (Ghana)|Daily Graphic]]|access-date=21 September 2024 |date=20 September 2024}}</ref> The order of candidates on the ballot paper was determined by a ballot conducted by the Electoral Commission on 20 September 2024.<ref>{{Cite news |author1=Enoch Darfah Frimpong |title=Bawumia is number 1, Mahama number 8 on ballot paper for 2024 presidential election |url=https://www.graphic.com.gh/news/politics/presidential-election-2024-balloting.html |location=Accra, Ghana|newspaper=[[Daily Graphic (Ghana)|Daily Graphic]]|access-date=21 September 2024 |date=20 September 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Alan Kyerematen reacts to being last on 2024 presidential ballot paper |url=https://www.ghanaweb.com/GhanaHomePage/politics/Alan-Kyerematen-reacts-to-being-last-on-2024-presidential-ballot-paper-1951761 |website=GhanaWeb|access-date=21 September 2024 |date=21 September 2024}}</ref>

On 28 October 2024, Akua Donkor, the presidential candidate for the Ghana Freedom Party, died after a sudden illness.<ref>{{Cite news |author1=Enoch Darfah Frimpong |title=CONFIRMED: GFP's presidential candidate Akua Donkor passes on |url=https://www.graphic.com.gh/news/politics/gfps-presidential-candidate-akua-donkor-passes-on.html |location=Accra, Ghana|newspaper=[[Daily Graphic (Ghana)|Daily Graphic]]|date=29 October 2024 |access-date=29 October 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author1=Ernest K. Arhinful |title=Akua Donkor, Presidential Candidate of Ghana Freedom Party dies at age 83 |url=https://www.myjoyonline.com/akua-donkor-presidential-candidate-of-ghana-freedom-party-dies-at-age-72/ |website=Joy Online |access-date=29 October 2024 |date=29 October 2024}}</ref> The GFP was given ten days to nominate a replacement for Akua Donkor. They submitted forms for Philip Appiah-Kubi who was her running mate. The Electoral Commission found that the forms submitted had irregularities and as the GFP could not correct them promptly, they were disqualified from presenting a candidate for the Presidential election. The Commission however went ahead with printing the ballot papers citing inadequate time and to reduce costs if they had to start all over again.<ref>{{cite web |title=Why Akua Donkor's image will remain on the presidential ballot on December 7 - EC clarifies |url=https://www.ghanaweb.com/GhanaHomePage/politics/Why-Akua-Donkor-s-image-will-remain-on-the-presidential-ballot-on-December-7-EC-clarifies-1959682 |website=GhanaWeb|access-date=12 November 2024 |date=12 November 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=2024 Election: EC resumes printing of presidential ballot papers |url=https://www.ghanaweb.com/GhanaHomePage/politics/2024-Election-EC-resumes-printing-of-presidential-ballot-papers-1959675 |website=GhanaWeb|access-date=12 November 2024 |date=12 November 2024}}</ref>

==Results==
Turnout was relatively low at 60.9% (approximately 18.8 million votes),<ref name="3news-results1">{{cite news |last1=Effah |first1=Evans |title=Full details of 2024 election results announced by Jean Mensa |url=https://3news.com/news/full-details-of-2024-election-results-announced-by-jean-mensa/ |access-date=12 December 2024 |work=3 News Ghana |date=10 December 2024}}</ref> a sharp drop from the 79% turnout in [[2020 Ghanaian general election|the 2020 election]].<ref name="bloomberg-turnout">{{cite news |last1=Dontoh |first1=Ekow |title=Ghana Election Turnout Shows Extent of Voter Apathy to Politics |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2024-12-08/ghana-elections-voter-turnout-likely-plunged-to-61 |access-date=13 December 2024 |work=Bloomberg |date=7 December 2024}}</ref> The National Democratic Congress saw a significant victory, winning both the office of President and a majority of parliamentary seats,<ref name=3newsdetail>{{cite news |title=2024 Election Results |url=https://3news.com/elections/ |access-date=13 December 2024 |work=3 News |date=2024}}</ref> ending eight years of power for the NPP.<ref name="Guardian-results">{{cite news |agency=Agence France-Presse |date=8 December 2024 |title=Ghana's former president John Dramani Mahama wins election |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2024/dec/08/ghana-former-president-john-dramani-mahama-wins-election |access-date=13 December 2024 |work=The Guardian}}</ref>

In nine constituencies, political party supporters showed up en masse to collation centers and caused damage to election materials, delaying presidential and parliamentary results from those locations. Margins in the presidential race were large enough for an official winner to be declared prior to reporting from these constituencies.<ref name="3news-results1"/>

===President===
Former president [[John Mahama]] (NDC) won with 57% of the vote. [[Mahamudu Bawumia]] conceded defeat on 8 December, congratulating Mahama on his victory.<ref name=":1" /> The results were officially certified on 9 December.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-12-09 |title=Ghana opposition leader Mahama officially wins election |url=https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20241209-ghana-opposition-leader-mahama-officially-wins-election |access-date=2024-12-10 |website=France 24 |language=en-US}}</ref>

[[Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang]], became the nation's first female vice president when she was sworn in with Mahama on 7 January 2025.<ref name="bbc-dec10">{{cite web |last1=Nunoo |first1=Favour |last2=Nesta Kupemba |first2=Danai |last3=Booty |first3=Natasha |title=Victorious John Mahama promises new beginning for Ghana |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cqjzv9k8zjjo |publisher=[[BBC]] |access-date=13 December 2024 |date=10 December 2024}}</ref>

===Parliament===
A total of 801 people contested for the 276 seats in parliament.<ref name="totalcandidates">{{cite web |last1=Otchere |first1=Gertrude Owireduwaah |title=Election 2024: Check out full list of 801 parliamentary candidates - Adomonline.com |url=https://www.adomonline.com/election-2024-check-out-full-list-of-801-parliamentary-candidates/ |access-date=11 February 2025 |date=7 December 2024}}</ref> Preliminary results show that the National Democratic Congress won a two-thirds majority of the nation's 276 parliamentary seats.<ref name="aa-9dec">{{cite news |last1=Fiifi Forson |first1=Enoch |title=Voters return Ghana's ex-President Mahama to office after 8 years out of power |url=https://www.aa.com.tr/en/africa/voters-return-ghanas-ex-president-mahama-to-office-after-8-years-out-of-power/3419583 |access-date=13 December 2024 |work=Anadolu Agency |date=9 December 2024}}</ref> Parliamentary control before the election was with the New Patriotic Party, with 137 seats held by each of the two largest parties and one independent caucusing with the NPP.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.myjoyonline.com/npp-asks-speaker-bagbin-to-remain-impartial-as-it-maintains-majority/|title=NPP asks Speaker Bagbin to remain impartial as it maintains majority|date=21 January 2021|website=Joy Online|language=en|access-date=21 January 2021}}</ref> On 13 December, the Deputy Chairperson of the Electoral Commission announced that the results of 12 constituencies needed re-collation but only three had been completed and these were results for Suhum, Akwatia and Fanteakwa North. The results for Ablekuma North, Dome-Kwabenya, Okaikwei Central, Tema Central, all in the Greater Accra region were yet to be collated. In the Ashanti Region, results were still pending for Ahafo Ano North, Ahafo Ano South West, Obuasi East. In the Bono East Region results were still pending for Techiman South. Nsawam-Adoagyiri, a ninth constituency in the Eastern Region is also pending.<ref>{{cite web |title=EC declares parliamentary results for Dome, Okaikwei Central, Ablekuma North, Tema Central illegal |url=https://www.ghanaweb.com/GhanaHomePage/NewsArchive/EC-declares-parliamentary-results-for-Dome-Okaikwei-Central-Ablekuma-North-Tema-Central-illegal-1964020 |website=GhanaWeb|access-date=15 December 2024 |date=14 December 2024}}</ref>

====By constituencies====
The result for [[Ablekuma North]] in the Greater Accra Region is still pending as the collation of the results could not be completed before the inauguration of the 9th Parliament.<ref name="provisionalregionalresult">{{Cite news |author1=Enoch Darfah Frimpong |title=NPP 88 seats; NDC 183 seats; 4 Independent MPs in 9th Parliament, Ablekuma North outstanding |url=https://www.graphic.com.gh/news/politics/npp-88-seats-ndc-183-seats-4-independent-mps-in-9th-parliament-ablekuma-north-outstanding.html |location=Accra, Ghana|newspaper=[[Daily Graphic (Ghana)|Daily Graphic]]|access-date=8 January 2025 |language=en-gb |date=5 January 2025}}</ref> The result for the Ablekuma North constituency in the Greater Accra Region was eventually determined following a [[2025 Ablekuma North parliamentary election rerun]] held on 11 July 2025, after the Electoral Commission was unable to complete collation before the inauguration of the 9th Parliament. [[Ewurabena Aubynn]] of the National Democratic Congress (NDC) won the seat, marking the first time the NDC had secured the constituency since the beginning of the Fourth Republic.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NDC’s Ewurabena Aubynn wins Ablekuma North seat in crucial rerun - MyJoyOnline |url=https://www.myjoyonline.com/ndcs-ewurabena-aubynn-wins-ablekuma-north-seat-in-crucial-rerun/ |access-date=2025-07-12 |website=www.myjoyonline.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

Parliamentary elections were held in [[Iraq]] on 10 October 2021.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.al-monitor.com/pulse/originals/2021/01/iraq-baghdad-early-elections-vote-kadhimi-electoral-system.html|title=Iraq's general elections pushed to October|author=[[Staff writer]]|date=22 January 2021|work=[[Al-Monitor]]|access-date=22 January 2021|archive-date=30 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210130024405/https://www.al-monitor.com/pulse/originals/2021/01/iraq-baghdad-early-elections-vote-kadhimi-electoral-system.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The elections determined the 329 members of the [[Council of Representatives of Iraq|Council of Representatives]] who in turn elected the Iraqi [[President of Iraq|president]] and confirmed the [[Prime Minister of Iraq|prime minister]]. These were Iraq's fifth parliamentary election since the [[2003 invasion of Iraq|2003 US-led invasion]] and the first since the [[2019 Iraqi October Revolution]].<ref>{{cite web|date=10 October 2021|title=Infographic: All you need to know about Iraq's election|url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2021/10/10/infographic-all-you-need-to-know-about-iraqs-elections|url-status=live|website=Al Jazeera|access-date=10 October 2021|archive-date=10 October 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211010175936/https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2021/10/10/infographic-all-you-need-to-know-about-iraqs-elections}}</ref> 

The election results would result in [[2021 Baghdad clashes|protests in Baghdad]] and an [[2021–2022 Iraqi political crisis|11 month-long political crisis]].

==Background==
The elections were originally due to be held in 2022, but were brought forward to June 2021 amidst the [[2019–2021 Iraqi protests]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=US urges Iraqi government formation as stalemate drags on - Al-Monitor: The Pulse of the Middle East |url=https://www.al-monitor.com/originals/2022/04/us-urges-iraqi-government-formation-stalemate-drags |access-date=2022-04-24 |website=www.al-monitor.com |date=22 April 2022 |language=en}}</ref> They were then delayed until October as the [[Independent High Electoral Commission]] asked for more time to organize "free and fair elections", which the [[cabinet of Iraq]] approved on 19 January 2021.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2021/1/19/iraqi-cabinet-votes-to-delay-general-election-until-october-10|title=Iraqi cabinet votes to delay general election until October 10|date=19 January 2021|work=[[Al Jazeera English|Al Jazeera]]|access-date=22 January 2021|archive-date=11 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210211062119/https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2021/1/19/iraqi-cabinet-votes-to-delay-general-election-until-october-10|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Electoral system ==
The electoral system was changed following the [[2018 Iraqi parliamentary election|last parliamentary elections]] amid the [[2019–2021 Iraqi protests]]. Previously conducted under [[proportional representation]] calculated using the [[Webster/Sainte-Laguë method]] with the governorates as constituencies, the 2021 elections were conducted under [[single non-transferable vote]].<ref>{{cite web|title=تعليمات توزيع المقاعد لانتخابات مجلس النواب العراقي 2021|url=https://ihec.iq/seat_distribution/|url-status=live|access-date=2021-09-22|website=Independent High Electoral Commission|language=ar|archive-date=11 September 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210911092721/https://ihec.iq/seat_distribution/}}</ref>{{Efn|The distribution of the number of electoral districts in each governorate relies on the number of quota seats for women multiplied by 3 or 5 seats for the electoral district depending on the governate’s population size.}} Of the 329 total seats, 320 were elected in 83 multi-member constituencies ranging in size from 3 to 5 seats. One seat in each constituency is reserved for the most voted woman. Nine seats are reserved for minorities (5 for [[Christianity in Iraq|Christians]] and 1 each for [[Yazidis]], [[Shabaks]], [[Mandaeans]] and [[Feyli Kurds]]).<ref>{{cite web|title=Iraq's Electoral Preparations and Processes Report No. 4 (10 December 2020)|date=11 December 2020 |url=https://reliefweb.int/report/iraq/iraq-s-electoral-preparations-and-processes-report-no-4-10-december-2020|url-status=live|access-date=2021-09-21|publisher=UN Assistance Mission for Iraq|language=en|via=Reliefweb|archive-date=21 September 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210921212845/https://reliefweb.int/report/iraq/iraq-s-electoral-preparations-and-processes-report-no-4-10-december-2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|date=11 May 2020|title=قانون انتخابات مجلس النواب العراقي : رقم (٩ (لسنة ٢|url=https://moj.gov.iq/upload/pdf/4603.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210813042243/https://moj.gov.iq/upload/pdf/4603.pdf|archive-date=2021-08-13|website=Ministry of Justice|language=ar}}</ref>

==Boycott threats==
On 15 July 2021, [[Muqtada al-Sadr]] announced the [[Sadrist Movement]] intended to boycott the October 10th election, citing corruption and voter fraud and claiming that free and fair elections were impossible in the wake of the ongoing political crisis.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://epc.ae/whatif-details/91/muqtada-al-sadrs-boycott-of-iraq-elections-a-political-tactic-or-a-strategic-decision|title=Muqtada al-Sadr's Boycott of Iraq Elections: A Political Tactic or a Strategic Decision?|work=Emirates Policy Center|date=2 August 2021|access-date=10 October 2021|archive-date=11 October 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211011104029/https://epc.ae/whatif-details/91/muqtada-al-sadrs-boycott-of-iraq-elections-a-political-tactic-or-a-strategic-decision|url-status=live}}</ref> On 24 July, the [[Iraqi Communist Party]] (which ran with the Sadrist Movement as the [[Alliance Towards Reforms]] in 2018), announced they were boycotting the elections, stating "In the absence of conditions for free and fair elections, participation in them would only mean collusion in reproducing the same corrupt political system that is responsible for the catastrophic state of affairs in the country."<ref>{{cite web|title=Iraq's Communist Party pulls out of election race|url=https://www.rudaw.net/english/middleeast/iraq/24072021|date=24 July 2021|work=[[Rudaw Media Network|Rudaw]]|access-date=10 October 2021|archive-date=17 December 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211217201503/https://www.rudaw.net/english/middleeast/iraq/24072021|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Louis Raphaël I Sako]], Patriarch of the [[Chaldean Catholic Church]], also called on Christians to boycott the election.<ref>{{cite web |author1=Sura Ali |title=Christians will not participate in Iraqi elections: Cardinal Sako |url=https://www.rudaw.net/english/middleeast/iraq/160720211 |date=16 July 2021 |access-date=10 October 2021 |work=[[Rudaw Media Network|Rudaw]] |archive-date=11 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211011114036/https://www.rudaw.net/english/middleeast/iraq/160720211 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The boycotts have been condemned by the [[United Nations Assistance Mission for Iraq]], as well as by other Iraqi political parties and leaders, including former Prime Minister [[Nouri al-Maliki]], leader of the [[State of Law Coalition]], and the [[Kurdistan Democratic Party]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Boycotting Iraqi elections will not solve anything: UNAMI chief|url=https://www.rudaw.net/english/middleeast/iraq/250820212|date=25 August 2021|work=[[Rudaw Media Network|Rudaw]]|access-date=10 October 2021|archive-date=11 October 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211011121039/https://www.rudaw.net/english/middleeast/iraq/250820212|url-status=live}}</ref>

On 27 August, al-Sadr reversed his decision to boycott and announced his party would take part in the election.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2021/8/27/iraq-sadr-says-he-will-participate-in-general-election|title=Moqtada al-Sadr says he will participate in Iraq general election|work=[[Al Jazeera English|Al Jazeera]]|date=27 August 2021|access-date=10 October 2021|archive-date=9 October 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211009155425/https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2021/8/27/iraq-sadr-says-he-will-participate-in-general-election|url-status=live}}</ref>

On 9 October, Kurdistan Socialist Democratic Party announced that they would withdraw their candidates from the elections in Dohuk, Erbil and Sulaymaniyah governorates (10 constituencies) and declared their support for the Kurdistan Democratic Party.<ref>{{Cite news|date=9 October 2021|title=حزبی سۆسیالیست كاندیده‌كانی خۆی له‌ چه‌ند بازنه‌كه‌یه‌ك له‌ به‌رژه‌وه‌ندی پارتی ده‌كشێنێته‌وه|language=ku|work=Kurdistan24|url=https://www.kurdistan24.net/ckb/story/211281-حزبی-سۆسیالیست-كاندیده%E2%80%8Cكانی-خۆی-له%E2%80%8C-چه%E2%80%8Cند-بازنه%E2%80%8Cكه%E2%80%8Cیه%E2%80%8Cك-له%E2%80%8C-به%E2%80%8Cرژه%E2%80%8Cوه%E2%80%8Cندی-پارتی-ده%E2%80%8Cكشێنێته%E2%80%8Cوه|access-date=9 October 2021|archive-date=9 October 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211009080506/https://www.kurdistan24.net/ckb/story/211281-%D8%AD%D8%B2%D8%A8%DB%8C-%D8%B3%DB%86%D8%B3%DB%8C%D8%A7%D9%84%DB%8C%D8%B3%D8%AA-%D9%83%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%AF%DB%8C%D8%AF%D9%87%E2%80%8C%D9%83%D8%A7%D9%86%DB%8C-%D8%AE%DB%86%DB%8C-%D9%84%D9%87%E2%80%8C-%DA%86%D9%87%E2%80%8C%D9%86%D8%AF-%D8%A8%D8%A7%D8%B2%D9%86%D9%87%E2%80%8C%D9%83%D9%87%E2%80%8C%DB%8C%D9%87%E2%80%8C%D9%83-%D9%84%D9%87%E2%80%8C-%D8%A8%D9%87%E2%80%8C%D8%B1%DA%98%D9%87%E2%80%8C%D9%88%D9%87%E2%80%8C%D9%86%D8%AF%DB%8C-%D9%BE%D8%A7%D8%B1%D8%AA%DB%8C-%D8%AF%D9%87%E2%80%8C%D9%83%D8%B4%DB%8E%D9%86%DB%8E%D8%AA%D9%87%E2%80%8C%D9%88%D9%87|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Results==
=== National results ===
Soldiers, prisoners, and displaced people voted early on 8 October.<ref>{{Cite news |date=8 October 2021 |title=Soldiers, prisoners, displaced people vote early ahead of Iraq election |work=[[Reuters]] |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-iraq-election-special-voting/soldiers-prisoners-displaced-people-vote-early-ahead-of-iraq-election-idUSKBN2GY152 |url-status=live |access-date=8 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211008180909/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-iraq-election-special-voting/soldiers-prisoners-displaced-people-vote-early-ahead-of-iraq-election-idUSKBN2GY152 |archive-date=8 October 2021}}</ref>

The Independent High Electoral Commission announced partial preliminary results on 11 October. The Sadrist political bloc received the most seats after the initial count, with 73.<ref>{{cite news |author=<!--Staff writer(s)/no by-line.--> |date=11 October 2021 |title=High-caliber surprises emerge after the announcement of the Iraqi elections' preliminary results |url=https://shafaq.com/en/Report/High-caliber-surprises-emerge-after-the-announcement-of-the-Iraqi-elections-preliminary-results |work=Shafaq News |access-date=14 October 2021 |archive-date=11 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211011235332/https://shafaq.com/en/Report/High-caliber-surprises-emerge-after-the-announcement-of-the-Iraqi-elections-preliminary-results |url-status=live }}</ref> The political [[Fatah Alliance]], a coalition of the pro-Iran [[Badr Organisation]] and [[Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq]] (AAH), won 17 seats, down from the 48 it had won in the prior election. [[Hadi al-Amiri]] and [[Qais al-Khazali]], leaders of Badr Organisation and AAH respectively, rejected the results, alleging "fraud" in the elections. They took their case to court seeking "to have the results annulled" because of "serious violations".<ref>{{Cite news|last=Faraj|first=Salam|title=Iraq's top court rejects fraud claims, ratifies election results|work=[[Agence France-Presse|AFP]]|url=https://news.yahoo.com/iraqs-top-court-rejects-fraud-154228735.html}}</ref> On 12 October, the commission announced a manual count of polling stations that were not electronically counted in the initial canvass.<ref>{{cite news |last=Shakir |first=Layal |date=13 October 2021 |title=Iraqi parties tense as electoral commission does manual count |url=https://www.rudaw.net/english/middleeast/iraq/131020212 |work=Rudaw |location=Erbil |access-date=14 October 2021 |archive-date=13 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211013141123/https://www.rudaw.net/english/middleeast/iraq/131020212 |url-status=live }}</ref> Of the total 57,944 polling stations, 45,716 uploaded electronic results. 8,547 stations were selected by lottery to be manually counted, while the remaining 3,681 stations experienced technical difficulties necessitating a manual count as well.<ref>{{Cite tweet |user=IHECOfficial |number=1448024651079237636 |date=12 October 2021 |title=🔻👈 مجموع محطات الاقتراع الكلي 🟢عدد المحطات المحجورة (3681) بانتظار عدها وفرزها يدوياً وامام وسائل الاعلام . 🟢 عدد المحطات التي نقلت الكترونياً وتمت مطابقتها مع عصي الذاكرة (45,716) . 🟢 عدد المحطات المختارة في قرعة العد اليدوي (8,547) يجري الآن رفعها مع بقية النتائج . |access-date=14 October 2021}}</ref> This manual count is expected to modify the overall allocation of seats.

On 15 October, the commission noted it had received 356 complaints about the preliminary election count by the 14 October deadline. The complaints division must address the complaints within seven days, which may then be reviewed by the judiciary within ten days. Final results will not be released until the complaints are resolved.<ref>{{cite news |author=<!--Staff writer(s)/no by-line.--> |date=15 October 2021 |title=Iraq electoral commission investigating 356 complaints |url=https://www.rudaw.net/english/middleeast/iraq/15102021 |work=Rudaw |access-date=15 October 2021 |archive-date=15 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211015101616/https://www.rudaw.net/english/middleeast/iraq/15102021 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Late on 16 October, the commission announced its updated preliminary results after completion of manual recounts.<ref name="K24Oct17">{{cite news |author=<!--Staff writer(s)/no by-line.--> |date=17 October 2021 |title=Iraqi election authority reports preliminary vote result |url=https://www.kurdistan24.net/en/story/25940-Iraqi-election-authority-reports-preliminary-vote-result |work=Kurdistan24 |access-date=17 October 2021 |archive-date=17 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211017043540/https://www.kurdistan24.net/en/story/25940-Iraqi-election-authority-reports-preliminary-vote-result |url-status=live }}</ref> The updated results triggered another opportunity to file election complaints with a deadline of 19 October. The commission had received over 1,000 complaints by 18 October, but a spokesperson stated it was unlikely the appeals will change the outcome.<ref>{{cite news |last=Shakir |first=Layal |date=18 October 2021 |title=Iraq electoral commission received more than 1,000 complaints |url=https://www.rudaw.net/english/middleeast/iraq/181020211 |work=Rudaw =location=Erbil |access-date=19 October 2021 |archive-date=18 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211018123129/https://www.rudaw.net/english/middleeast/iraq/181020211 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Official final results, after recounting by The High Electoral Commission were shared on November 30.<ref>{{cite news |last=Jiyad |first=Sajad |date=30 November 2021 |title=Final results announced by IHEC presser |url=https://twitter.com/SajadJiyad/status/1465683037312716808 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211130234947/https://twitter.com/SajadJiyad/status/1465683037312716808 |archive-date=30 November 2021 |access-date=30 November 2021}}</ref>

On 27 December, the Iraqi Supreme Court ratified the parliamentary election results after rejecting a complaint of irregularities filed by al-Amiri and al-Khazali.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Faraj |first=Salam |date=27 December 2021 |title=Iraq's top court rejects fraud claims, ratifies election results |work=[[Agence France-Presse|AFP]] |url=https://news.yahoo.com/iraqs-top-court-rejects-fraud-154228735.html}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Alkhaldi|first=Celine|date=28 December 2021|title=Iraq's supreme court ratifies contested election results|work=[[CNN]]|url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/12/28/middleeast/iraq-court-election-intl/index.html}}</ref>

The [[Alliance Towards Reforms]] won 73 seats, with the [[Progress Party (Iraq)|Progress Party]] winning 37, the [[State of Law Coalition]] winning 34, the [[Kurdistan Democratic Party]] with 32, the [[Fatah Alliance]] winning 17 seats, the [[Patriotic Union of Kurdistan]] gaining 16 seats, the Azem Alliance with 12 seats, while the [[Emtidad Movement]] and the [[New Generation Movement]] received nine seats each, and political independents gained 40 seats.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aa.com.tr/en/middle-east/iraq-announces-full-results-of-parliamentary-elections/2394814|title=Iraq announces full results of parliamentary elections|date=17 October 2021|access-date=19 October 2021|author=Ali Jawad|work=[[Anadolu Agency]]|archive-date=18 October 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211018091133/https://www.aa.com.tr/en/middle-east/iraq-announces-full-results-of-parliamentary-elections/2394814|url-status=live}}</ref>

As for the seats reserved for minorities, the [[Babylon Movement]] won 4 seats out of 5 reserved for Christians, while 1 seat was gained by an independent candidate. The Yazidi single seat was won by the [[Yazidi Movement for Reform and Progress]]. Likewise, one seat each reserved for the Yezidi and Shabak communities were won by Nayef Khalaf Sido of the Yezidi Progress Party, and independent candidate Waad Mahmoud Ahmed respectively.<ref name="kurdistan24.net">{{cite web |url=https://www.kurdistan24.net/en/story/25973-Minority-quota-candidates-received-over-96,000-votes-in-Iraqi-election |title=Minority quota candidates received over 96,000 votes in Iraqi election |website=www.kurdistan24.net |first=Mustafa |last=Shilani |date=2021-10-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211020112648/https://www.kurdistan24.net/en/story/25973-Minority-quota-candidates-received-over-96,000-votes-in-Iraqi-election |archive-date=20 October 2021}}</ref>

==Aftermath==
{{Main|2022 Iraqi political crisis}}

=== Conduct ===
The [[United Nations Security Council]] issued a statement congratulating the people and Government of Iraq on the smooth conduct of a “technically sound election” and deploring related threats of violence. [[Jeanine Hennis-Plasschaert]], Special Representative of United Nations, said the vote was generally peaceful and well-run. She added that “there is much for Iraqis to be proud of in this election.” She acknowledged that elections and their outcomes can provoke strong feelings, in Iraq or in any democracy across the globe and called for all groups to accept the outcome of the electoral process.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-11-23 |title=Importance of sound, inclusive elections in Iraq 'cannot be overstated' |url=https://news.un.org/en/story/2021/11/1106412 |access-date=2022-04-10 |website=UN News |language=en}}</ref>

{{Politics of Kenya}}

General elections were held in [[Kenya]] on 9 August 2022. Voters elected the [[President of Kenya|president]], governors, [[Senate of Kenya|senators]], members of the [[National Assembly (Kenya)|National Assembly]], and members of county assemblies. 

This was the third general election and the fourth presidential one since the promulgation of the [[Constitution of Kenya|2010 constitution]]. Incumbent president [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] was not eligible for a third term according to the constitution, nor county governors who had served two terms. The 2022 general election saw the lowest number of presidential candidates cleared since the multi-party system was implemented in 1992. Parliamentarians were elected to sit in the [[13th Parliament of Kenya]].

[[William Ruto]] was elected President of Kenya with 50.5% of the vote, defeating [[Raila Odinga]] who received 48.85% of the vote.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-08-15 |title=Kenya election result: William Ruto wins presidential poll |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-62554210 |url-status=live |access-date=2022-08-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220815164106/https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-62554210 |archive-date=15 August 2022}}</ref> On 22 August, Odinga filed a petition with the [[Supreme Court of Kenya]] challenging the results announced by [[Wafula Chebukati]], the chairman of the [[Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=22 August 2022 |last=Kimeu |first=Caroline |location=Nairobi |title=Kenya opposition leader files court challenge to election result |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/aug/22/kenya-opposition-leader-files-court-challenge-election-result-raila-odinga |access-date=23 August 2022 |website=The Guardian |language=en |archive-date=23 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220823063023/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/aug/22/kenya-opposition-leader-files-court-challenge-election-result-raila-odinga |url-status=live }}</ref> On 5 September, the Supreme Court rejected the challenge and upheld Ruto's victory.<ref>{{cite ==Background==
The [[Constitution of Kenya]] requires that a general election of members of parliament be held on the second Tuesday of August on every fifth year, which meant that the general election was scheduled for 9 August 2022. If Kenya is at war, the election can be delayed if a resolution is passed in each House of Parliament by at least two-thirds of all the members of the House. Such a resolution can delay the election by up to six months, and may be passed multiple times provided that the delays do not cumulatively exceed 12 months.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.klrc.go.ke/index.php/constitution-of-kenya/123-chapter-eight-the-legislature/part-2-composition-and-membership-of-parliament/269-101-election-of-members-of-parliament |title=Constitution of Kenya – 101. Election of members of Parliament |work=[[Kenya Law Reform Commission|KLRC]] |access-date=21 March 2022 |archive-date=10 December 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171210144249/http://www.klrc.go.ke/index.php/constitution-of-kenya/123-chapter-eight-the-legislature/part-2-composition-and-membership-of-parliament/269-101-election-of-members-of-parliament |url-status=live }}</ref>

The constitution requires that a presidential election take place at the same time as the general election. In the event that prior to the next general election the position of president falls vacant and the office of deputy president is also vacant (who otherwise would assume the office of president), a presidential election could be held at an earlier date. According to the constitution, in such circumstances, an election needs to be held within sixty days after the vacancy arose in the office of president.

Incumbent president [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] was not eligible to pursue a third term due to the two-term limit in the constitution.<ref>{{cite web|title=Kenya's Uhuru Kenyatta pledges to respect term limit in 2022|url=https://www.theeastafrican.co.ke/tea/news/east-africa/kenya-s-uhuru-kenyatta-pledges-to-respect-term-limit-in-2022-1443496|accessdate=29 July 2022|date=19 June 2020|work=The East African|archive-date=29 July 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220729213031/https://www.theeastafrican.co.ke/tea/news/east-africa/kenya-s-uhuru-kenyatta-pledges-to-respect-term-limit-in-2022-1443496|url-status=live}}</ref> County governors who had served two terms at the helms of their respective counties were also ineligible for a third term.<ref>{{cite web|first1=Justus|last1=Wanga|date=28 March 2021|title=Why experts can't agree on governors county limits|url=https://nation.africa/kenya/news/politics/why-experts-can-t-seem-to-agree-on-term-limits-for-governors--3339044|work=[[Daily Nation|Nation]]|accessdate=29 July 2022|archive-date=29 July 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220729212921/https://nation.africa/kenya/news/politics/why-experts-can-t-seem-to-agree-on-term-limits-for-governors--3339044|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Electoral system==
[[File:Kenyan parliament.jpg|thumb|[[Parliament Buildings (Kenya)|Parliament Buildings]], [[Nairobi]]]]
The [[President of Kenya]] is elected using a modified version of the [[two-round system]]: to win in the first round, a candidate must receive over 50% of the vote nationally and 25% of the vote in at least 24 of Kenya's [[Counties of Kenya|47 counties]].<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20121216232349/http://www.kenyadiasporavote.com/presidential-candidates/ Presidential Candidates] Kenya Diaspora Vote</ref><ref>Article 138 (4) [[Constitution of Kenya]] 2010</ref> If no candidate achieves this, a second round is held between the top two candidates, in which the candidate with the most votes wins.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.kenyadiasporavote.com/presidential-candidates/ |title=Presidential Candidates – Kenyan Presidential Election, 2012 |work=Kenya Diaspora Vote |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121216232349/http://www.kenyadiasporavote.com/presidential-candidates/ |archive-date=16 December 2012 |access-date=21 March 2022 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.klrc.go.ke/index.php/constitution-of-kenya/130-chapter-nine-the-executive/part-2-the-president-and-deputy-president/306-138-procedure-at-presidential-election |title=Constitution of Kenya – 138. Procedure at presidential election |work=[[Kenya Law Reform Commission|KLRC]] |access-date=21 March 2022 |archive-date=21 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220321050150/https://www.klrc.go.ke/index.php/constitution-of-kenya/130-chapter-nine-the-executive/part-2-the-president-and-deputy-president/306-138-procedure-at-presidential-election |url-status=live }}</ref>

The [[Parliament of Kenya]] consists of two houses: the [[Senate of Kenya|Senate]] ([[upper house]]) and the [[National Assembly (Kenya)|National Assembly]] ([[lower house]]), both of which were fully renewed for five-year terms. Those elected in 2022 formed the [[13th Parliament of Kenya]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-08-12 |title=Kenya elections 2022: Live result updates |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-62444316 |access-date=2022-08-13 |archive-date=12 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220812033216/https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-62444316 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The National Assembly has 350 members, of which 290 are elected in single-member constituencies by [[first-past-the-post voting]]. Of the remaining 60, 47 are [[County woman representative|reserved for women]] and are elected from single-member constituencies based on the 47 [[counties of Kenya|counties]], also using the first-past-the-post system.<ref>[http://www.ipu.org/parline-e/reports/2167_B.htm Electoral system] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170906233716/http://www.ipu.org/parline-e/reports/2167_B.htm |date=6 September 2017 }} IPU</ref> The remaining 13 seats include 12 nominated by political parties based on their number of seats and a [[Speaker of the National Assembly of Kenya|Speaker]], elected by the assembly from outside of it as an ex officio member. The nominated members are reserved for youths, persons with disabilities and workers.<ref>[http://www.parliament.go.ke/index.php/the-national-assembly About the National Assembly] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220708164749/http://www.parliament.go.ke/index.php/the-national-assembly |date=8 July 2022 }} Parliament of Kenya</ref>

The 68 members of the [[Senate of Kenya|Senate]] are elected by four methods; 47 are elected in single-member constituencies based on the counties by first-past-the-post voting. Parties are then assigned a share of 16 seats for women, two for youth and two for persons with disabilities based on their seat share. A speaker is also elected as an ex officio member.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.klrc.go.ke/index.php/constitution-of-kenya/171-chapter-seven-representation-of-the-people/part-2-independent-electoral-and-boundaries-commission-and-delimitation-of-electoral-units/257-90-allocation-of-party-list-seats |title=Constitution of Kenya – 90. Allocation of party list seats |work=[[Kenya Law Reform Commission|KLRC]] |access-date=21 March 2022 |archive-date=16 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220416045855/https://www.klrc.go.ke/index.php/constitution-of-kenya/171-chapter-seven-representation-of-the-people/part-2-independent-electoral-and-boundaries-commission-and-delimitation-of-electoral-units/257-90-allocation-of-party-list-seats |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Campaign==

Leading up to the 2022 election, a new political dynamic based on class politics was emerging in Kenya,<ref name="saferworld.org.uk">{{cite web |title=Why peace remains elusive as Kenya prepares for the 2022 general elections |url=https://www.saferworld.org.uk/long-reads/why-peace-remains-elusive-as-kenya-prepares-for-the-2022-general-elections |work=Saferworld |date=26 August 2021 |access-date=19 March 2022 |archive-date=21 February 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220221152926/https://www.saferworld.org.uk/long-reads/why-peace-remains-elusive-as-kenya-prepares-for-the-2022-general-elections |url-status=live }}</ref> framed as "hustlers" versus "dynasties".<ref name="Al Jazeera news">{{cite web |last=Gathara |first=Patrick |title=Dynasties vs hustlers in Kenya |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2019/9/24/dynasties-vs-hustlers-in-kenya |website=[[Al Jazeera English|Al Jazeera]] |date=24 September 2019 |access-date=19 March 2022 |archive-date=20 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220320063406/https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2019/9/24/dynasties-vs-hustlers-in-kenya |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Global Challenges">{{cite web |last=Pike |first=Isabel |title="Hustlers versus Dynasty": Kenya's New Class Politics |url=https://globalchallenges.ch/issue/9/hustlers-versus-dynasty-kenyas-new-class-politics/ |work=[[Centre for Global Challenges]] |date=March 2021 |access-date=19 March 2022 |archive-date=24 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220324145549/https://globalchallenges.ch/issue/9/hustlers-versus-dynasty-kenyas-new-class-politics/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Nation Media Group">{{cite web |last=Mwazemba |first=John |title='Hustlers' versus 'Dynasties': Ngugi's prophesied apocalypse |url=https://nation.africa/kenya/life-and-style/weekend/-hustlers-versus-dynasties-ngugi-s-prophesied-apocalypse-3289314 |work=[[Nation Media Group]] |date=13 February 2021 |access-date=19 March 2022 |archive-date=15 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220515175310/https://nation.africa/kenya/life-and-style/weekend/-hustlers-versus-dynasties-ngugi-s-prophesied-apocalypse-3289314 |url-status=live }}</ref> The families of incumbent President [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] and opposition leader [[Raila Odinga]] had dominated Kenyan politics since independence in 1963. Moreover, Kenya has traditionally been ruled by presidents who belong to either the [[Kikuyu people|Kikuyu]] people – like Kenyatta – or the [[Kalenjin people|Kalenjin]] people, like [[William Ruto]]. The potential victory of Odinga, a [[Luo people|Luo]], would mark a departure for the country, which has 44 ethnic groups.<ref name="Al Jazeera" />

Ruto initially supported Odinga in the [[2007 Kenyan general election|2007 election]] against [[Mwai Kibaki]]. The announcement of the presidential results led to ethnic clashes among Kenya's tribes.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-08-04 |title=Fated Future: On Ethno-Terrorism, Pungent Politics, Low Information Population, and the Future of Kenya |url=https://geopoliticspress.com/kenya-fatal-future-kikuyu-kalenjin-warriors-luo-violence-cognitive-misery/ |access-date=2022-10-13 |website=Geopolitics Press |language=}}</ref> Police crackdowns on protesters and clashes that turned into ethnic attacks killed more than 1,000 people in [[2007–2008 Kenyan crisis|post-election violence]], eventually prompting a new constitution to devolve power. Ruto aligned himself with Kenyatta in 2013. Both Kenyatta and Ruto had been indicted by the [[International Criminal Court]] (ICC) on crimes against humanity charges for their alleged role in orchestrating the post-election violence in the 2007 election. The cases later collapsed, with former ICC chief prosecutor [[Fatou Bensouda]] saying a relentless campaign of victim and witness intimidation made the trial impossible.<ref name="International Criminal Court">{{cite web |title=Kenyatta case: Trial Chamber V(B) terminates the proceedings |url=https://www.icc-cpi.int/pages/item.aspx?name=pr1099 |work=[[International Criminal Court]] |date=13 March 2015 |access-date=20 March 2022 |archive-date=18 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170818052309/https://www.icc-cpi.int/pages/item.aspx?name=pr1099 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="ICC">{{cite web |title=Ruto and Sang case: ICC Trial Chamber V(A) terminates the case without prejudice to re-prosecution in future |url=https://www.icc-cpi.int/pages/item.aspx?name=pr1205 |work=[[International Criminal Court]] |date=5 April 2016 |access-date=20 March 2022 |archive-date=15 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211015210406/https://www.icc-cpi.int/pages/item.aspx?name=pr1205 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In March 2018, President Kenyatta and his former rival for the presidency, Odinga, stunned the public when they [[2018 Kenya handshake|shook hands]] and declared a truce after post-election violence in 2017 left dozens of people dead. The two leaders also sought to expand the executive through the [[2021 Kenyan constitutional referendum attempt|Building Bridges Initiative (BBI) constitutional changes]], which would have potentially allowed Kenyatta to stay in power as a prime minister. But despite the [[Supreme Court of Kenya]] ruling against the proposed amendments in August, the unexpected alliance has persevered, with Odinga attending official government functions with Kenyatta.<ref name="Citizen Digital">{{cite web |title=Uhuru, Raila tour Kisumu port, Jomo Kenyatta stadium |url=https://www.citizen.digital/news/uhuru-raila-tour-kisumu-port-jomo-kenyatta-stadium-4036530 |website=Citizen Digital |date=11 January 2021 |access-date=20 March 2022 |archive-date=20 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220320134552/https://www.citizen.digital/news/uhuru-raila-tour-kisumu-port-jomo-kenyatta-stadium-4036530 |url-status=live }}</ref> Cracks within the [[Jubilee Party|Jubilee]] government began to appear, leading to an eventual fallout between Kenyatta and his deputy, Ruto.<ref>{{cite web|date=18 August 2019|first=Macharia|last=Gaitho|url=https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2019/8/18/all-you-need-to-know-about-the-clash-between-kenyatta-and-ruto|title=All you need to know about the clash between Kenyatta and Ruto|accessdate=29 July 2022|work=Al Jazeera|archive-date=29 July 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220729215520/https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2019/8/18/all-you-need-to-know-about-the-clash-between-kenyatta-and-ruto|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|date=4 September 2021|first=Otieno|last=Otieno|url=https://www.theeastafrican.co.ke/tea/news/east-africa/uhuru-s-relationship-with-deputy-ruto-getting-grittier-3537466|title=Uhuru's relationship with deputy Ruto getting grittier by the day|accessdate=29 July 2022|work=[[The East African]]|archive-date=29 July 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220729215521/https://www.theeastafrican.co.ke/tea/news/east-africa/uhuru-s-relationship-with-deputy-ruto-getting-grittier-3537466|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Presidential nomination===
In December 2021, the Mount Kenya Foundation, one of the country's most powerful and wealthy Kikuyu lobbies, announced their support for Odinga, while Kenyatta has repeatedly said that the next president will be "neither Kikuyu nor Kalenjin". On 10 December 2021, Odinga declared his intention to run for the presidency for the fifth time.<ref name="Al Jazeera">{{cite web |title=Kenyan opposition leader Odinga announces fifth bid for president |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2021/12/10/kenyan-opposition-leader-odinga-announces-fifth-bid-for-president |work=[[Al Jazeera English|Al Jazeera]] |date=10 December 2021 |access-date=13 March 2022 |archive-date=13 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220313080808/https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2021/12/10/kenyan-opposition-leader-odinga-announces-fifth-bid-for-president |url-status=live }}</ref>

In January 2022, Ruto's [[United Democratic Alliance (Kenya)|United Democratic Alliance]] (UDA) announced a coalition pact with the [[Amani National Congress]], [[Forum for the Restoration of Democracy – Kenya|FORD–Kenya]] and several other political parties. ===Manifestos===
Azimio la Umoja was the first political outfit to launch their manifesto on 6 June 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Azimio Unveils Manifesto |url=https://www.kenyanews.go.ke/azimio-unveils-manifesto/ |access-date=21 September 2022 |website=Kenya news}}</ref> The ten point manifesto voiced key issues such as a [[Corruption in Kenya|corruption-free government]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Otieno|first=Jeff|url=https://www.theafricareport.com/214005/kenya-2022-raila-promises-the-moon-with-azimio-manifesto/|title=Kenya 2022: Raila promises the moon with Azimio manifesto|date=21 June 2022|work=Africa Report|access-date=16 May 2022|archive-date=21 June 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220621120049/https://www.theafricareport.com/214005/kenya-2022-raila-promises-the-moon-with-azimio-manifesto/|url-status=live}}</ref> The manifesto came in the form of a declaration and promised to strengthen devolution; economically empower women; waste no single child; spur the economic pillar; facilitate climate-smart agriculture; revamp the manufacturing sector; enact responsible leadership; preserve sovereignty of the people; increase access to clean water; create "Baba Care",<ref>{{Cite web |title=Baba Care |url=https://azimio.ke/manifesto/babacare/ |access-date=21 September 2021 |website=Azimio la Umoja}}</ref> which would focus on social protection and transformation; and upscale health coverage to [[universal health care]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Muli|first=Francis|url=https://www.pd.co.ke/august-9/azimio-raila-manifesto-explained-130938/|title=Azimio promise: Raila's 10-point manifesto explained|work=Africa Report|access-date=29 July 2022|date=June 7, 2022|archive-date=30 July 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220730012924/https://www.pd.co.ke/august-9/azimio-raila-manifesto-explained-130938/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Nyarangi|first=Edwin|url=https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/national/article/2001447339/azimio-manifesto-raila-odinga-promises-to-grow-the-economy-fight-corruption|title=Azimio Manifesto: Raila Odinga promises to grow the economy, fight corruption|date=6 June 2022|work=[[The Standard (Kenya)|The Standard]]|access-date=29 July 2022|archive-date=29 July 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220729011801/https://standardmedia.co.ke/national/article/2001447339/azimio-manifesto-raila-odinga-promises-to-grow-the-economy-fight-corruption|url-status=live}}</ref>

Ruto's UDA and Wajackoyah's Roots Party launched their manifestos on 30 June 2022. Wajackoyah intended to legalise [[marijuana]] for commercial purposes, introduce snake farming, export dog meat, shut and bring down the [[Mombasa–Nairobi Standard Gauge Railway|standard-gauge railway]], hang the corrupt, suspend the [[Constitution of Kenya|constitution]], introduce four-day work week, move capital city to [[Isiolo]], create eight states, and repatriate idle foreigners.<ref>{{cite web|last=Kagonye|first=Fred|url=https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/politics/article/2001449226/wajackoyahs-manifesto-here-are-his-ten-salient-points|title=Wajackoyah's manifesto: Here are his ten salient points|date=30 June 2022|work=The Standard|access-date=29 July 2022|archive-date=29 July 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220729015928/https://standardmedia.co.ke/politics/article/2001449226/wajackoyahs-manifesto-here-are-his-ten-salient-points|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Electoral candidates clearance===
IEBC registered all aspirants expected to run for the various elective seats between 29 May and 7 June 2022.<ref>{{cite web |last=Makong |first=Bruhan |url=https://www.capitalfm.co.ke/news/2022/05/iebc-to-register-aspirants-between-may-29-and-june-7/ |title=IEBC To Register Aspirants Between May 29 And June 7 |work=Capital FM |date=18 May 2022 |access-date=1 August 2022 |archive-date=1 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220801115038/https://www.capitalfm.co.ke/news/2022/05/iebc-to-register-aspirants-between-may-29-and-june-7/ |url-status=live }}</ref> [[William Ruto]] and [[Raila Odinga]] were cleared on 4 and 5 June respectively, in an event that would see them present their nomination papers.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/2022-05-23-ruto-raila-book-dates-for-submission-of-nomination-papers-to-iebc/ |title=Ruto, Raila book dates for submission of nomination papers to IEBC |work=The Star (Kenya) |date=23 May 2022 |access-date=1 August 2022 |archive-date=1 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220801115038/https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/2022-05-23-ruto-raila-book-dates-for-submission-of-nomination-papers-to-iebc/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In June 2022, reports began to emerge that [[Johnson Sakaja|Sakaja Johnson]] presented a fake certificate to IEBC from a Ugandan university and that he never graduated from the [[University of Nairobi]] (UoN).<ref name="Sakaja" /> Initially, Sakaja had stated in interviews that he was an alumnus of UoN, where he purportedly pursued a bachelor's degree in [[actuarial science]].<ref name="Sakaja" /> It would later emerge that Sakaja was yet to complete his studies at UoN since his enrollment in 2003.<ref name="Sakaja">{{cite web|url=https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/2022-06-12-sakaja-yet-to-graduate-from-uon-since-joining-in-2003/|title=Sakaja yet to graduate from UoN since joining in 2003|work=The Star|date=12 June 2022|access-date=1 August 2022|archive-date=1 August 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220801115039/https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/2022-06-12-sakaja-yet-to-graduate-from-uon-since-joining-in-2003/|url-status=live}}</ref> He admitted in a radio interview that he did not graduate from the city's university, accusing [[Uhuru Kenyatta]] of plotting to destroy his political ambitions.<ref>{{cite web |last=Ayega |first=Davis |url=https://www.capitalfm.co.ke/news/2022/07/sakaja-opens-up-on-why-he-didnt-finish-actuarial-science-degree-at-uon/ |title=Sakaja Opens Up On Why He Didn't Finish Actuarial Science Degree At UoN |work=Capital FM |date=1 July 2022 |access-date=1 August 2022 |archive-date=1 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220801115038/https://www.capitalfm.co.ke/news/2022/07/sakaja-opens-up-on-why-he-didnt-finish-actuarial-science-degree-at-uon/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Oruta |first=Brian |url=https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/2022-06-15-ill-be-on-ballot-sakaja-drags-uhuru-name-into-degree-drama/ |title=I'll be on ballot - Sakaja drags Uhuru name into degree drama |work=The Star |date=15 June 2022 |access-date=1 August 2022 |archive-date=15 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220815181553/https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/2022-06-15-ill-be-on-ballot-sakaja-drags-uhuru-name-into-degree-drama/ |url-status=live }}</ref> At the time of clearance, he had presented a Bachelor of Science in Management certificate from Uganda's [[Team University]], where he alleged he was an external student. On 29 June 2022, the [[Commission for University Education]] revoked his degree, pending investigations.<ref>{{cite web |last=Menya |first=Walter |url=https://nation.africa/kenya/news/education/more-trouble-for-sakaja-as-cue-revokes-recognition-of-degree-3864944 |title=More trouble for Sakaja as CUE shuts door on his degree recognition IEBC declined to revoke Sakaja's clearance, stating it can only disqualify him candidate if issued with a court order.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.citizen.digital/news/relief-for-sakaja-as-iebc-dismisses-cue-decision-to-reject-his-university-degree-n301307 |title=Relief For Sakaja As IEBC Dismisses CUE Decision To Reject His |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220809131408/https://www.citizen.digital/news/relief-for-sakaja-as-iebc-dismisses-cue-decision-to-reject-his-university-degree-n301307 |url-status=live ===IEBC preparation for general election===
By the end of clearance, IBEC gazetted a total of 16,098 candidates contesting 1,882 elective slots.<ref name="First batch">{{cite web |last=Owino |first=Samuel |url=https://nation.africa/kenya/news/politics/the-chaos-at-iebc-3872790 |title=Eyes on IEBC as first batch of ballot papers make surprise arrival |work=[[Daily Nation|Nation Africa]] |date=8 July 2022 |access-date=1 August 2022 |archive-date=29 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220729150302/https://nation.africa/kenya/news/politics/the-chaos-at-iebc-3872790 |url-status=live }}</ref> IEBC received the first batch of ballot papers on 7 July 2022.<ref name="First batch" /><ref>{{cite web |last=Oruta |first=Brian |url=https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/2022-07-07-iebc-to-receive-first-batch-of-ballot-papers-today/ |title=IEBC to receive first batch of ballot papers today |work=The Star |date=7 July 2022 |access-date=1 August 2022 |archive-date=10 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220710195856/https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/2022-07-07-iebc-to-receive-first-batch-of-ballot-papers-today/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The ballot papers were printed by a Greek firm known as Inform P Lykos, situated in [[Athens]], which was awarded the tender worth Ksh 3 billion.<ref>{{cite web |last=Mwende |first=Sharon |url=https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/2022-06-29-greek-firm-to-print-200m-ballot-papers-for-sh3bn-iebc/ |title=Greek firm to print 200m ballot papers for Sh3bn - === Interference ===
An investigation into a company that has reportedly interfered in elections worked on the 2022 Kenyan election. A strategist working on the campaign of William Ruto claims that his Telegram account had been hacked before the elections, including increased activities. It was revealed that this was done by Tal Hanan, an Israeli businessman who has reportedly interfered in several elections around the world. Hanan also hacked the Telegram and Gmail accounts linked to other advisers working with the Ruto campaign.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Kirchgaessner |first1=Stephanie |last2=Burke |first2=Jason |last3=Kimeu |first3=Caroline |date=2023-02-17 |title=Ruto ally says Telegram account was hacked before Kenyan election |language=en-GB |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/feb/17/ruto-ally-says-telegram-account-was-hacked-before-kenyan-election |access-date=2023-02-19 |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

While the client behind the hacks has not been revealed, Odinga has acknowledged that he hired white hat hackers, or ethical hackers, to uncover evidence to uncover electoral fraud that saw him lose the election.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-02-14 |title=Raila: We worked with ethical hackers to know truth about 2022 elections |url=https://www.citizen.digital/news/raila-we-worked-with-ethical-hackers-to-know-truth-about-2022-elections-n314341 |access-date=2023-02-19 |website=Citizen Digital |language=en-KE}}</ref>

==Results and reactions==

The results had been scheduled to be announced at 3 pm on 15 August 2022,<ref>{{cite news |last1=Tongola |first1=Mate |title=All eyes on IEBC as presidential results announcement time moved |url=https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/national/article/2001453303/iebc-to-announce-presidential-election-winner-at-3pm |website=[[The Standard (Kenya)|The Standard]] |access-date=17 August 2022 |date=15 August 2022 |archive-date=5 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220905130745/https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/national/article/2001453303/iebc-to-announce-presidential-election-winner-at-3pm |url-status=live }}</ref> however, by 5 pm no announcement had been made. Four [[Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission|IEBC]] commissioners, led by vice chair [[Juliana Cherera]], held a press conference stating that they do not "take ownership" of the results, citing issues with the final tallying process.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wangari |first1=Stephanie |title=Four IEBC Commissioners distance themselves from final stage of presidential poll tallying |url=https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/national/article/2001453314/four-iebc-commissioners-distance-themselves-from-final-stage-of-presidential-poll-tallying |website=[[Daily Nation|Nation]] |access-date=17 August 2022 |date=15 August 2022 |archive-date=17 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220817025937/https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/national/article/2001453314/four-iebc-commissioners-distance-themselves-from-final-stage-of-presidential-poll-tallying |url-status=live }}</ref> The results were announced at 6 pm by IEBC chairman [[Wafula Chebukati]]. All candidates except [[Raila Odinga]] appeared at the announcement; Odinga's chief agent Saitabao Ole Kanchory announced that Odinga would not appear until his campaign team could verify the results.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Njeru |first1=Betty |title=Kanchory Saitabao explains why Raila Odinga is not at Bomas of Kenya |url=https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/article/2001453312/why-raila-odinga-did-not-go-to-bomas-of-kenya |website=The Standard |access-date=17 August 2022 |date=15 August 2022 |archive-date=17 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220817100228/https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/article/2001453312/why-raila-odinga-did-not-go-to-bomas-of-kenya |url-status=live }}</ref> As Chebukati and other two commissioners made their way into the [[Bomas of Kenya]] auditorium, violence erupted in the venue and the IEBC staff were escorted away.<ref>{{cite web |title=Chaos at Bomas as Ruto makes political history |url=https://www.pd.co.ke/august-9/chaos-at-bomas-as-ruto-makes-political-history-144948/ |website=The Standard |access-date=17 August 2022 |date=15 August 2022 |archive-date=15 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220815220026/https://www.pd.co.ke/august-9/chaos-at-bomas-as-ruto-makes-political-history-144948/ |url-status=live }}</ref> After security personnel resolved the situation, Chebukati made his way to the auditorium and announced the results, naming [[William Ruto]] as the president-elect.<ref name="guardian">{{cite web |title=Kenya's Deputy President William Ruto declared election winner |url=https://english.news.cn/20220816/f5c6938b364e4abf99c40bf55250f344/c.html |website=English News CN |access-date=17 August 2022 |date=16 August 2022 |archive-date=16 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220816002608/https://english.news.cn/20220816/f5c6938b364e4abf99c40bf55250f344/c.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

The following day, 16 August, the dissident IEBC commissioners, Cherera, [[Francis Wanderi]], [[Irene Masit]] and [[Justus Nyang’aya]], gave a more detailed explanation of the division within the commission.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wanjala |first1=Emmanuel |title=Why 4 IEBC commissioners are wrong on vote tally |url=https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/2022-08-16-why-4-iebc-commissioners-are-wrong-on-vote-tally/ |website=The Star |access-date=17 August 2022 |date=16 August 2022 |archive-date=16 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220816160128/https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/2022-08-16-why-4-iebc-commissioners-are-wrong-on-vote-tally/ |url-status=live }}</ref>  The four stated that the total percentage exceeded 100%, the results were not processed and analysed by all the commissioners, and that Chebukati did not provide the total numbers of registered voters, votes cast, or rejected ballots. They accused Chebukati of announcing results prematurely, before votes from some counties had been incorporated,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wangari |first1=Stephanie |title=Why we disputed Chebukati's results – IEBC commissioners |url=https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/national/article/2001453358/why-we-disputed-chebukatis-results-iebc-commissioners |website=The Standard |access-date=17 August 2022 |date=16 August 2022 |archive-date=16 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220816235843/https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/national/article/2001453358/why-we-disputed-chebukatis-results-iebc-commissioners |url-status=live }}</ref> and accused Chebukati of exceeding his legal role.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Ayega |first1=Davis |title=AUGUST ELECTIONSResults Announced By Chebukati A Mathematical Absurdity: 4 Dissenting IEBC Officials |url=https://www.capitalfm.co.ke/news/2022/08/results-announced-by-chebukati-a-mathematical-absurdity-4-dissenting-iebc-officials/ |website=Capital FM |access-date=17 August 2022 |date=16 August 2022 |archive-date=17 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220817065127/https://www.capitalfm.co.ke/news/2022/08/results-announced-by-chebukati-a-mathematical-absurdity-4-dissenting-iebc-officials/ |url-status=live }}</ref> This was disputed by the [[Elections Observations Group]], a Kenyan [[Non-governmental organization|NGO]], who stated "The commission's verification process was credible and every critical player was involved with that process – from observers, political party agents, media, body officials ... The commission made data publicly available".<ref>{{cite news |last1=Kimeu |first1=Caroline |title=Kenya opposition leader rejects election result as 'null and void' |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/aug/16/kenya-opposition-leader-election-result-null-void-raila-odinga |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=16 August 2022 |language=en |access-date=17 August 2022 |archive-date=17 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220817123433/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/aug/16/kenya-opposition-leader-election-result-null-void-raila-odinga |url-status=live }}</ref> Chebukati also defended his announcement by stating that the 100.01% result was attributable to a rounding error,<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-62599219 | title=Kenya elections 2022: Win or lose, why Raila Odinga's election challenge matters | work=BBC News | date=22 August 2022 | accessdate=22 August 2022 | author=Olewe, Dickens | archive-date=22 August 2022 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220822100547/https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-62599219 | url-status=live }}</ref> and accused the four dissenting commissioners of trying to force a re-run of the election.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://nation.africa/kenya/news/politics/chebukati-demand-for-re-run-caused-fallout-3917950 | title=Chebukati: Demand for election re-run caused fallout with four commissioners | work=Daily Nation | date=17 August 2022 | accessdate=22 August 2022 | archive-date=22 August 2022 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220822111831/https://nation.africa/kenya/news/politics/chebukati-demand-for-re-run-caused-fallout-3917950 | url-status=live }}</ref>

{{Wikinews|Kenya's supreme court upholds election result}}
Odinga rejected the outcome of the presidential election and announced he would begin a legal challenge.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Oruta |first1=Brian |title=Raila to move to Supreme Court over presidential results |url=https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/2022-08-16-raila-to-move-to-supreme-court-over-presidential-results/ |website=The Star |access-date=17 August 2022 |date=16 August 2022 |archive-date=17 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220817071724/https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/2022-08-16-raila-to-move-to-supreme-court-over-presidential-results/ |url-status=live }}</ref> He termed the election a "travesty", "unconstitutional", and "null and void".<ref>{{cite web |last1=Owino |first1=Winfrey |title=Raila Odinga: IEBC presidential results are unconstitutional |url=https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/national/article/2001453360/raila-iebc-presidential-results-are-unconstitutional |website=The Standard |access-date=17 August 2022 |date=16 August }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Obulutsa |first1=George |last2=Mersie |first2=Ayenat |title=Kenya's Odinga says presidential election result a 'travesty' |url=https://www.cnbcafrica.com/2022/kenyas-odinga-says-presidential-election-result-a-travesty/ |website=CNBC Africa |access-date=17 August 2022 |date=16 August 2022 |archive-date=18 August 2022 fraudulent activities, his party agents were barred access to several election sites, technology was used for fraud, and the fraud was preplanned. Several others filed complaints too, claiming for instance that the results were not included in the tallying and verification of the IEBC chairman from 28 constituencies with at least 8% of the votes.<ref>By JOSEPH WANGUI: Inside petitions seeking to invalidate Kenya’s presidential election results The East African, News East Africa.

The [[Mount Kenya region]] played a pivotal role in shaping the outcome of Kenya's 2022 presidential election. Comprising 10 ten counties, it had approximately 5.7 million registered voters which is about 27% of Kenya's national registered voters. Ruto won largely in the region with 2,938,802 votes (76.96%), outstripping Odinga’s 847,205 votes (22.19%).<ref name="auto1">{{Cite Web|title=2022 Kenya Presidential Election by County|publisher=Equal Politics|url=https://ke.equalpolitics.com/results/county|accessdate=2025-08-08|lang=en}}</ref> Ruto's strongest performance was in Tharaka-Nithi (89.18 %), and even in traditionally more competitive [[Nakuru County|Nakuru]], he secured 65.90% against Odinga's 32.69%. Turnout ranged from 65% in Laikipia to 70% in [[Tharaka-Nithi County]]. This overwhelming bloc support, delivering nearly 3  million votes, was crucial in tipping the national result in Ruto's favor.<ref>{{Cite Web|title=2022 Kenya general  Election and voter turnout|publisher=Statskenya|url=https://statskenya.co.ke/at-stats-kenya/about/kenya-general-elections-presidential-results-and-voter-turnout-2022/140/|accessdate=2025-08-08|lang=en}}</ref> Ruto won largely in Mount Kenya East region especially in [[Tharaka-Nithi County]] and [[Embu County]], while Odinga secured most of his votes in [[Mount Kenya]] west due to diversity and urbanization.<ref name="auto1"/>

[[Nairobi|Nairobi City]], being both the capital and the largest urban center in Kenya, was a key battleground for presidential candidates. Odinga won with 57% of the votes cast defeating Ruto who garnered 41% of the votes cast.<ref name="auto1"/> [[Raila Odinga]] dominated in constituencies such as [[Kibra Constituency|Kibra]], [[Ruaraka Constituency|Ruaraka]], and [[Dagoretti North Constituency|Dagoretti North]], reflecting strong support in densely populated urban and informal settlement areas. [[William Ruto]] performed better in constituencies such as [[Roysambu Constituency|Roysambu]], [[Kasarani Constituency|Kasarani]], and  [[Dagoretti South Constituency|Dagoretti South]], where peri-urban and mixed-income populations are more significant. Overall, Odinga secured a majority of the votes in Nairobi City, contributing significantly to his nationwide performance in the 2022 presidential election. The county’s results highlighted Nairobi as a major urban stronghold for the Azimio la Umoja coalition.

== Aftermath==
Following William Ruto's victory in the 2022 presidential election, [[Nairobi]] City experienced significant political turbulence. The announcement of Ruto as president-elect on August 15, 2022, led to widespread protests across parts of the capital. Areas such as [[Kibera]], [[Kamukunji]], and [[Mathare]], which had strongly supported [[Raila Odinga]], witnessed demonstrations expressing dissatisfaction with the election results. These protests were marked by clashes with security forces, leading to injuries and heightened tensions in the city.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Drama disappointment in Nairobi as William Ruto wins Kenya Presidential election|publisher=Aljazeera|url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2022/8/15/drama-disappointment-in-nairobi-as-ruto-wins-kenyan-election|accessdate=2025-08-21|language=en}}</ref>

=== Misinformation on various social media ===
There was a fake statement shared on Facebook claiming that two local media houses - Royal Media Services and The Standard Group had called the elections in favour of Raila Odinga. According to this fake statement, Raila Odinga was leading the 2022 Presidential elections with 51.13% while William Samoei Ruto was at 48.22%. These claims were denounced by the media houses' senior editors and PesaCheck also confirmed that the statement was fake.<ref>{{Cite web |work=PesaCheck |title=FAKE: This statement claiming that two Kenyan media houses called the 2022 general election in favour of Raila Odinga is fabricated |date= 21 August 2022|url=https://pesacheck.org/fake-this-statement-claiming-that-two-kenyan-media-houses-called-the-2022-general-election-in-84c260131114}}</ref>
