General elections were held in [[Morocco]] on 8 September 2021 to elect 395 members of the [[House of Representatives (Morocco)|House of Representatives]]. The [[National Rally of Independents]] led by [[Aziz Akhannouch]] won the most seats (102), a gain of 65 seats from [[2016 Moroccan general election|the previous election]]. The liberal [[Authenticity and Modernity Party]] took second place with 87 seats, a net loss of 15 seats compared to their tally in the 2016 elections. The centre-right [[Istiqlal Party]] gained 35 seats and took third place with 81 seats total. The governing [[Justice and Development Party (Morocco)|Justice and Development Party]] suffered an [[electoral wipeout]] and won only 13 seats, a net loss of 112 seats for the party.

==Background==
[[File:King Mohammed VI.jpg|thumb|King Mohammed VI in 2016]]
July 2020 marked the 21st year of [[King Mohammed VI]]'s reign in Morocco.<ref name="missedopportunity"/> The first two decades of the 21st century saw civil and political reforms, as well as "popular disillusionment" with the socioeconomic and political state of the nation.<ref name="missedopportunity"/> In response to the [[2011–2012 Moroccan protests|2011 protests]] that occurred as part of the [[Arab Spring]], King Mohammed VI announced a series of constitutional reforms, passed through [[2011 Moroccan constitutional referendum|a national referendum]] in July 2011.<ref name="nyt">[https://www.nytimes.com/2011/06/18/world/africa/18morocco.html?_r=1&src=me&ref=world Morocco King Proposes Limited Steps to Democracy] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210313165822/https://www.nytimes.com/2011/06/18/world/africa/18morocco.html?_r=1&src=me&ref=world |date=13 March 2021 }}, ''[[The New York Times]]'', 17 June 2011. Retrieved 19 June 2011</ref> The reforms were described by the [[British Broadcasting Corporation|BBC]] as "expanding the powers of parliament and the prime minister but leaving the king with broad authority over the government".<ref name="biebz"/> The [[Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant|Islamic State]]'s presence in the region also posed a threat to Morocco throughout the 2010s.<ref name="missedopportunity"/>

In 2014 <!--the [[Democracy Index]] (a rating published annually for all countries by the [[Economist Intelligence Unit]]) characterized Morocco as an [[authoritarianism|authoritarian regime]], and
This was in another article but it didn't have a ref and I can't find one -->
the Freedom of the Press report gave Morocco a rating of "not free".<ref name="freep2014"/>

After the 2016 elections, protests continued to occur; in 2016 and 2017, a movement known as [[Hirak Rif Movement|Hirak Rif]] demonstrated in the streets of northern Morocco against corruption and unemployment.<ref name="biebz"/> In 2017, the Freedom of the Press report upgraded Morocco's rating to "partly free".<ref name="freep"/> By June 2019, the BBC reported that "almost half of Moroccans [were] considering emigrating" to other countries.<ref name="biebz"/>

2020 saw the beginning of the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Morocco|COVID-19 pandemic]]. In March, a law was passed to outlaw many forms of [[social media|making posts online]].<ref name="ministryoftruth"/> The government claimed the bill was written "without prejudice to the constitutionally guaranteed freedom of digital communications", and shortly began arresting people for posting information it deemed to be false.<ref name="ministryoftruth"/> Morocco's initial response to the pandemic put it "among the world's COVID-19 success stories" in the first months of the pandemic;<ref name="corvids"/> [[COVID-19 lockdowns|lockdown]] measures first implemented on 20 March began to be eased after several months, and a third phase of gradually lifting the lockdown had begun on 19 July. However, the reduction in cases came at a cost: by late July, the government's actions during the pandemic would be described as a "reversal of democratic reforms", with Parliament being "sidelined, its duties increasingly usurped by the [[Makhzen]]".<ref name="snuffsoutflickeringembers"/> The Interior Ministry suspended local council meetings (even remote meetings held online), an action the Constitution reserved exclusively for Parliament.<ref name="snuffsoutflickeringembers"/> While a restriction on visitation from foreign business visitors was lifted on 10 September, a sharp increase in cases (and the possibility of a second wave of infections) prompted the restrictions to be reinstated.<ref name="corvids2"/>

In November 2020 the [[Polisario Front]] ended a 29-year ceasefire agreement with Morocco in [[Western Sahara]], blaming Morocco for breaking the terms of the agreement.<ref name="oppo"/><ref name="royters"/> In December, the [[Israel–Morocco normalization agreement]] established diplomatic relations between the two nations; Morocco became the sixth [[Arab League]] member to do so, and the fourth in the space of four months (along with [[Bahrain]], the [[United Arab Emirates]] and [[Sudan]]).<ref name="israelisreal"/><ref name="zawarudo"/> In exchange, the [[First presidency of Donald Trump|Donald Trump administration]] announced that the United States would recognize [[Political status of Western Sahara|Morocco's claim over Western Sahara]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20201210-morocco-recognizes-israel-and-wins-trump-nod-on-western-sahara|title=Morocco recognizes Israel and wins Trump nod on Western Sahara|website=[[France 24]]|date=10 December 2020}}</ref>

Parties confirmed to be contesting the election included the ruling Justice and Development Party (PJD), the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), and the Istiqlal Party (PI).<ref name="september2"/>

==Electoral system==
Morocco has a [[bicameral legislature]] whose two chambers are the [[House of Councillors (Morocco)|House of Councillors]] and the [[House of Representatives (Morocco)|House of Representatives]]. The House of Representatives has 395 seats, which are elected by proportional representation and consist of two tiers: 305 seats are elected from 92 [[multi-member district|multi-member]] local constituencies (of two to six seats) and the remaining 90 are elected from twelve constituencies based on the [[Regions of Morocco]] (of 3 to 12 seats). Of these 90 seats, a minimum of one third must be women, who must also be the first and second candidates on each list.<ref>[https://leseco.ma/lapolitique/elections-2021-comment-le-quotient-electoral-rebattra-les-cartes.html Élections 2021 : comment le quotient électoral rebattra les cartes]</ref><ref>[https://www.maroc.ma/fr/actualites/elections-du-8-septembre-la-revision-la-hausse-de-la-representativite-feminine-un-des Élections du 8 septembre : La révision à la hausse de la représentativité féminine, un des principaux amendements de la nouvelle loi électorale]</ref>

The election held under a new 2021 law saw the removal of the electoral threshold, which was previously at 6% for local lists and at 3% for the national lists which were replaced by the regional ones.<ref name="alaraby8sep21">{{Cite web |date=8 September 2021 |title=Morocco goes to polls to elect parliament under controversial new law |url=https://english.alaraby.co.uk/news/morocco-goes-polls-elect-parliament-under-new-law |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210909071137/https://english.alaraby.co.uk/news/morocco-goes-polls-elect-parliament-under-new-law |archive-date=9 September 2021 |website=[[The New Arab]]}}</ref> Interior Minister Abdelouafi Laftit said in September 2020 that the political representation of women in Morocco had "not yet reached the required level", but that concerted efforts would ensure a "significant and fair" representation of women in the 2021 elections.<ref name="women"/> The new law calculates the allocations of seats based on the number of registered voters, rather than the number of those who actually cast a ballot.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2021/9/8/elections-kick-off-in-morocco-amid-widespread-apathy|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210908222517/https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2021/9/8/elections-kick-off-in-morocco-amid-widespread-apathy|archive-date = 8 September 2021|title = Ballot counting under way in Morocco vote overshadowed by apathy}}</ref> This means the party that received the largest number of votes in the district will not be able to obtain more than one electoral seat.<ref name="alaraby8sep21" />

All citizens who were at least 18 years old, or have reached the age of 18 by March 2021, were eligible to vote. The period for submitting voter registration requests ended on 31 December 2020.<ref name="deadline"/>

==Campaign==
The electoral calendar was unveiled on 10 May 2021.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.medias24.com/2021/05/10/voici-les-dates-des-elections-2021/|journal={{ill|Médias 24|fr}}|title=Voici les dates des élections 2021|date=10 May 2021|first=Sara|last=Ibriz}}</ref> While the municipal, regional and legislative elections traditionally took place on different days, in 2021, a new electoral law was passed under which all three would be held on the same day, in a bid to increase [[voter turnout]] (the [[2016 Moroccan general election|2016 elections]] had a turnout of less than 50%).<ref name="youts"/><ref name="september"/><ref name="september2"/><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.jeuneafrique.com/1170416/politique/elections-legislatives-au-maroc-les-enjeux-du-scrutin/|journal=[[Jeune Afrique]]|title=Élections législatives au Maroc : les enjeux du scrutin|date=11 May 2021|first=Nina|last=Kozlowski}}</ref> However, a high level of abstention was expected due to a loss of confidence in the institutions, with the government's sidelining of parliament leading to a lack of real issues at stake in the elections.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.medias24.com/2021/01/13/des-experts-craignent-un-record-dabstentionnisme-lors-des-elections-de-2021/|journal=Médias 24|title=Des experts craignent un record d'abstentionnisme lors des élections de 2021|date=13 January 2021|first=M.|last=M.}}</ref>

On 15 August 2021, the Ministry of Religious Endowments and Islamic Affairs issued a communiqué signed by Minister [[Ahmed Toufiq]] calling on all imams and preachers in the country to remain neutral, and warning that religious rectors who do so would be removed from their administrative duties. This request was also addressed to the delegates and representatives of the ministry.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.moroccoworldnews.com/2021/08/343917/morocco-calls-on-imams-preachers-to-remain-neutral-during-elections|journal=[[Morocco World News]]|title=Morocco Calls on Imams, Preachers To Remain Neutral During Elections|first=Safaa|last=Kasraoui|date=15 August 2021}}</ref>

The election campaign began on 26 August.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.lemonde.fr/afrique/article/2021/08/27/au-maroc-debut-de-campagne-pour-les-elections-de-septembre_6092502_3212.html|journal=[[Le Monde]]|title=Au Maroc, début de campagne pour les élections de septembre|date=27 August 2021}}</ref>

The Justice and Development Party (PJD) of Prime Minister [[Saadeddine Othmani]] hoped to repeat for the third time in a row the lead in the vote that brought it to power in 2011. In particular, the moderate Islamists of the party hoped to gain control of key ministries, which they had traditionally lacked. The PJD trailed by two-thirds in the polls,<ref name="LPFR">{{Cite journal |date=28 August 2021 |title=Maroc – Élections générales : les partis dans les starting-blocks |url=https://www.lepoint.fr/afrique/maroc-elections-generales-les-partis-dans-les-starting-blocks-28-08-2021-2440514_3826.php |journal=Le Point |language=fr}}</ref> behind the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), led by [[Abdellatif Ouahbi]], and known for its royalist stance in a country where public attachment to the monarch is already strong.<ref name="LPFR" />

The Istiqlal party (PI), led by [[Nizar Baraka]], had come third in 2016 and proposed an economic development program that focuses on reducing inequalities while tackling environmental issues such as water resource management, biodiversity, and pollution.<ref name=LPFR />

The National Rally of Independents (RNI) of minister [[Aziz Akhannouch]] presented a program focused on five commitments and 25 actions whose total cost was estimated at 275 billion dirhams, or more than 25 billion euros.<ref name=LPFR />

===COVID-19 measures===
The election was organized in the context of the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Morocco|COVID-19 pandemic]]. By July 2020, rumors had started to circulate that the elections would be postponed due to the virus. While Interior Minister Abdelouafi Laftit launched political consultations for the 2021 elections on 8 July,<ref name="initiald"/> on 8 August it was reported that the government was considering postponing the elections due to the ongoing pandemic. The difficulty of carrying out election activities while limiting transmission of the virus, as well as the economic challenges of carrying out an election during the [[COVID-19 recession|concurrent economic recession]], were cited as motivating factors.<ref name="corvids"/> Meanwhile, some parties voiced opposition to the proposal, claiming it was a ploy by the incumbent government to prolong its control over the nation.<ref name="corvids"/><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.medias24.com/2020/09/16/la-majorite-des-partis-nexcluent-plus-un-report-des-elections-de-2021/|journal=Medias24|title=La majorité des partis n'excluent plus un report des élections de 2021|date=16 September 2020|first=Samir|last=El Ouardighi}}</ref>

However, on 9 November it was announced that general elections had been scheduled to take place in September 2021.<ref name="september"/><ref name="september2"/> The organization of the electoral campaign was under significant health restrictions, including a nighttime curfew and a ban on gatherings of more than 25 people and large political rallies.<ref name=LPFR /><ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-08-03 |title=Covid-19 : les Marocains soumis à une extension du couvre-feu |url=https://www.lepoint.fr/sante/covid-19-les-marocains-soumis-a-une-extension-du-couvre-feu-03-08-2021-2437771_40.php |access-date=2023-12-14 |website=Le Point |language=fr}}</ref>

==Results==
Turnout rose sharply from 43% in 2016 to 50% in 2021, the highest since the [[2002 Moroccan general election|2002 elections]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.hespress.com/%D9%88%D8%B2%D8%A7%D8%B1%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AF%D8%A7%D8%AE%D9%84%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D9%86%D8%B3%D8%A8%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B4%D8%A7%D8%B1%D9%83%D8%A9-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%AA%D8%AE%D8%A7-872736.html|title=وزارة الداخلية: نسبة المشاركة في "انتخابات 8 شتنبر" تتجاوز 50 بالمائة|date=8 September 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/moroccans-vote-parliament-election-under-new-voting-rules-2021-09-08/|journal=[[Reuters]]|title=Half of Morocco's electorate voted in parliamentary elections|date=8 September 2021|first=Ahmed|last=Eljechtimi}}</ref> 

The elections were won by the National Rally of Independents (RNI), led by Aziz Akhannouch, which won 102 seats, gaining 65. It was followed by the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), which won 87 seats, losing 15. In third place, the Istiqlal Party won 81, gaining 35 seats. The [[Socialist Union of Popular Forces]] (USFP) won 34; the [[Popular Movement (Morocco)|Popular Movement]] (MP), 28; the [[Party of Progress and Socialism]] (PPS), 22; the [[Constitutional Union (Morocco)|Constitutional Union]] (UC), 18; the [[Democratic and Social Movement (Morocco)|Democratic and Social Movement]] (MDS), 5; the [[Front of Democratic Forces]] (FFD), 3 and the [[Federation of the Democratic Left|Alliance of the Left Federation]] (FGD), 1. The historic defeat of the Justice and Development Party (PJD) led the ruling party to win only 13 seats, thus losing 112, more than 90% of its seats and placing it in eighth place after winning the three previous elections. Saadeddine Othmani also failed to win re-election in his constituency of Rabat.<ref name="Monde">{{Cite journal|url=https://www.lemonde.fr/afrique/article/2021/09/09/elections-au-maroc-les-islamistes-au-pouvoir-severement-battus-au-profit-de-partis-liberaux_6093973_3212.html|journal=Le Monde|title=Elections législatives au Maroc : sévère défaite des islamistes au pouvoir|date=8 September 2021}}</ref> Two new parties entered: FFD with 3 deputies and PSU with one. The PUD and the PSGV lost one seat each, thus remaining outside the House of Representatives.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.lepoint.fr/monde/les-marocains-se-prononcent-sur-l-avenir-du-parti-islamiste-au-pouvoir-08-09-2021-2442100_24.php|journal=[[Le Point]]|title=Maroc: spectaculaire déroute électorale des islamistes au pouvoir|date=9 September 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/09/08/world/africa/morocco-elections.html|journal=[[The New York Times]]|title=Islamists See Big Losses in Moroccan Parliamentary Elections|date=8 September 2021|first1=Aida|last1=Alami|first2=Nicholas|last2=Casey}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.yabiladi.com/articles/details/114413/resultats-definitifs-elections-septembre-sieges.html|website=Yabiladi.com|title=Résultats définitifs des élections du 8 septembre : 102 sièges pour le RNI, 13 pour|date=9 September 2021}}</ref>

At the request of the Moroccan authorities, the [[Congress of Local and Regional Authorities]] of the [[Council of Europe]] deployed four groups of congress observers in and around [[Rabat]] and [[Casablanca]] to make an electoral assessment between 7 and 9 September.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.coe.int/en/web/congress/news-2021/-/asset_publisher/XLGtwSgAs7nz/content/congress-to-observe-regional-and-municipal-elections-in-morocco?|website=[[Council of Europe]]|title=Congress observed regional and municipal elections in Morocco|date=2 September 2021|first=Ahmed|last=Eljechtimi}}</ref> A total of 4,500 observers were accredited, 70 of which were international and 14 of which were NGOs.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.moroccoworldnews.com/2021/09/344340/moroccan-national-elections-2021-polls-close-without-incidents|journal=Morocco World News|title=Moroccan National Elections 2021: Polls Close Without Incidents|date=8 September 2021|first=Jasper|last=Hamann}}</ref>

==Reactions==
===National===
*In the afternoon of 9 September the PJD announced the resignation of the incumbent prime minister Saadeddine El Othmani as its secretary-general.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=9 September 2021 |title=PJD: Othmani démissionne du secrétariat général |url=https://www.leconomiste.com/flash-infos/pjd-othmani-demission-du-secretariat-general |journal=[[L'Économiste]]}}</ref> The party also described the election results as "incomprehensible, illogical and not reflecting the party's position on the political scene".<ref name="Monde" /> Former prime minister and former secretary-general of the PJD [[Abdelilah Benkirane]] had previously called on Othmani to resign as leader of the party arguing that "after noting the painful defeat suffered in the elections ... I consider it imperative in these difficult circumstances that the Secretary General assumes his responsibility and resigns from the leadership of the party".<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.moroccoworldnews.com/2021/09/344348/elections-benkirane-calls-on-el-othmani-to-resign-after-painful-results|journal=Morocco World News|title=Elections: Benkirane Calls on El Othmani to Resign After 'Painful' Results|date=9 September 2021|first=Safaa|last=Kasraoui}}</ref> On 30 October, Benkirane was re-elected as the PJD secretary-general.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Benkirane Elected Morocco's PJD Party Secretary General |url=https://www.assahifa.com/english/?p=7344 |access-date=2021-10-31 |website=Assahifa}}</ref>
*The leader of the RNI, Aziz Akhannouch, characterized the election results as "a victory for democracy" and a "victory for all Moroccans".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-09-09 |title=Morocco: RNI party wins most seats in legislative election |url=https://www.africanews.com/2021/09/09/morocco-rni-party-wins-most-seats-in-legislative-election/ |access-date=2022-12-30 |website=Africanews}}</ref> PAM leader Abdellatif Ouahbi described the results as "very positive despite the period that the PAM has gone through which was marked by problems and disputes of an organic nature", while also noting the election as a "victory of democracy in the kingdom".<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Return of Liberals to Power in the Moroccan General Elections |url=https://www.washingtoninstitute.org/policy-analysis/return-liberals-power-moroccan-general-elections |access-date=2022-12-30 |website=The Washington Institute |language=en}}</ref>
*In the morning of 9 September Minister of the Interior Abdelouafi Laftit expressed satisfaction with the elections, noting that they were held in the "best conditions" as the country "experienced an atmosphere of global mobilization to turn the elections into a step that condenses the broad hopes of the Moroccan people as a whole in the strengthening of the development dynamic and the consecration of the democratic choice".<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.moroccoworldnews.com/2021/09/344347/best-conditions-minister-highlights-transparency-of-moroccos-elections|journal=Morocco World News|title=E'Best Conditions': Minister Highlights Transparency of Morocco's Elections|date=9 September 2021|first=Safaa|last=Kasraoui}}</ref>

===International===
*{{Flag|United States}}: The U.S. Embassy in Rabat congratulated Morocco "on successfully holding" its elections. Noting the [[Morocco–United States relations|US-Morocco ties]], the embassy added, "Our shared commitment to democratic processes strengthens our 200-year partnership."<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.moroccoworldnews.com/2021/09/344341/the-us-congratulates-morocco-on-successful-general-elections|journal=Morocco World News|title=The US Congratulates Morocco on 'Successful' General Elections|date=8 September 2021|first=Shaquille|last=Goff}}</ref>
*{{Flag|Council of Europe}}: The Council of Europe said four of their Congress teams were able to observe an Election Day in two Moroccan regions which was "calm, orderly and transparent overall except some procedural inconsistencies, in particular during the closing of the polling stations and the counting." It further added that the increased representation of women in elected bodies, both at regional and municipal level and at all tiers of government, was welcomed by the Congress delegation. At the same time, it regretted a slightly lower turnout compared to the last local elections in 2015.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Congress concludes electoral observation mission in Morocco|url=https://www.coe.int/en/web/congress/news-2021/-/asset_publisher/XLGtwSgAs7nz/content/congress-concludes-electoral-observation-mission-in-morocco|access-date=2021-09-09|website=Congress of Local and Regional Authorities|language=en-GB}}</ref>
==Aftermath==
On 10 September 2021, [[Aziz Akhannouch]] was nominated as [[Prime Minister of Morocco|Prime Minister]] by [[Mohammed VI of Morocco|King Mohammed VI]] and was tasked by the King to form a new government.<ref>{{Cite news|date=10 September 2021|title=Le Roi Mohammed VI nomme Aziz Akhannouch chef du gouvernement|language=fr-FR|website=Medias24|url=https://medias24.com/2021/09/10/le-roi-mohammed-vi-nomme-aziz-akhannouch-chef-du-gouvernement/|access-date=10 September 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title=Mohammed VI nomme Aziz Akhannouch Chef de gouvernement|language=fr|website=[[Telquel]]|url=https://telquel.ma/2021/09/10/mohammed-vi-nomme-aziz-akhannouch-chef-de-gouvernement_1736449?fbrefresh=8|access-date=10 September 2021}}</ref> On 22 September, it was announced that Akhannouch's National Rally of Independents, the Istiqlal Party, and the Authenticity and Modernity Party had reached a coalition agreement.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-09-22|title=Morocco: 3 parties agree to form new coalition government|url=https://apnews.com/article/africa-elections-morocco-cc475bda28b05d74c6d578f2c5a55e2f|access-date=2021-09-29|website=AP NEWS|language=en}}</ref> The new government took office on 7 October.<ref>{{cite web|title=SM le Roi préside la cérémonie de nomination des membres du nouveau gouvernement|date=|url=http://www.mapexpress.ma/actualite/activites-royales/sm-roi-preside-ceremonie-nomination-membres-du-nouveau-gouvernement/|website=MAP Express|accessdate= 7 October 2021}}</ref>

[[Ethnic Affairs Minister]]s were also elected by their designated electorates on the same day, although only select ethnic minorities in particular states and regions were entitled to vote for them. A total of 1,171 national, state, and regional seats were contested in the election, with polling having taken place in all townships, including areas considered conflict zones and [[Self-administered zone|self-administered regions]].{{Cite web|title=Myanmar sets November 8 date for general election|url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2020/07/myanmar-sets-november-8-date-general-election-200702033020917.html|website=Al Jazeera|date=2 July 2020|access-date=28 July 2020|archive-date=28 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200728014018/https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2020/07/myanmar-sets-november-8-date-general-election-200702033020917.html|url-status=live}} On 1 February 2021, the [[Tatmadaw]] (Myanmar Armed Forces) baselessly{{cite news |last1=Goodman |first1=Jack |title=Myanmar coup: Does the army have evidence of voter fraud? |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/55918746 |access-date=7 February 2023 |work=[[BBC News]] |date=5 February 2021}} claimed the results of the election were illegitimate and [[2021 Myanmar coup d'état|launched a coup d'état]] that deposed [[State Counsellor of Myanmar|State Counsellor]] [[Aung San Suu Kyi]] and [[President of Myanmar|President]] [[Win Myint]], causing military-affiliated Vice President [[Myint Swe]] to become Acting President. |date=1 February 2023 |location=[[Yangon]]}} ==Background== The [[2015 Myanmar general election|prior elections in 2015]] were only the second to be considered at least semi-democratic in the country since 1960 (the first being in [[1990 Myanmar general election|1990]], which the military invalidated), as for a majority of its independent history, it was either controlled by a [[Burmese Way to Socialism|totalitarian dictatorship]] or a [[State Peace and Development Council|military junta]]. The [[National League for Democracy]], led by [[Aung San Suu Kyi]], won a majority of seats and votes, taking 86 percent of the seats in the Assembly of the Union (235 in the House of Representatives and 135 in the House of Nationalities), well more than the 67 percent supermajority needed to ensure that its preferred candidates would be elected president and second vice president in the Presidential Electoral College. The party technically also needed at least 67 percent to outvote the combined pro-military bloc in the Presidential Electoral College (the [[Union Solidarity and Development Party]] and the appointed legislators representing the military). Although NLD leader Aung San Suu Kyi is constitutionally barred from the presidency (as both her late husband and her children are foreign citizens), she was the de facto head of government, after being appointed to a newly created office, the [[State Counsellor of Myanmar]], a position akin to a Prime Minister.{{cite news|date=13 November 2015|title=Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy Wins Majority in Myanmar|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-34805806|access-date=13 November 2015|archive-date=13 November 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151113070516/http://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-34805806|url-status=live}} Most political parties in the country are ethnically-based, with only two (the NLD and the USDP) having large sway at the national level, although both are dominated by the ethnic [[Bamar people|Bamar]] majority. Parties also tend to be based more on personality (based on the attitudes and personality of their leaders) rather than a stable ideological platform. Statistics for share of the popular vote appear not to be available. The election took place during the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Myanmar|COVID-19 pandemic]], as well as both the [[Rohingya conflict]] and the [[Rohingya genocide]] (alongside international condemnation for these events). Retrieved 28 August 2018{{Cite news|last=Beech|first=Hannah|date=25 August 2018|title=Year After Rohingya Massacres, Top Generals Unrepentant and Unpunished|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/08/25/world/asia/rohingya-myanmar-ethnic-cleansing-anniversary.html|url-status=live|access-date=27 August 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180902110118/https://www.nytimes.com/2018/08/25/world/asia/rohingya-myanmar-ethnic-cleansing-anniversary.html|archive-date=2 September 2018}} Over 25,000 people have been killed in the conflicts, with tens of thousands more being injured or subjected to sexual violence,{{Cite web|last=Khan|first=Ahmed|title=Prevalence of violence against children: Evidence from 2017 Rohingya Refugee crises|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/333118905|access-date=14 August 2019|website=ResearchGate|archive-date=18 October 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191018141408/https://www.researchgate.net/publication/333118905|url-status=live}} in addition to over 725,000 people having fled the country, mostly to neighboring [[Bangladesh]]. Media activity in the province is heavily restricted by the government. The Rohingya are currently classed as [[stateless people]], as Myanmar refuses to give them citizenship, claiming they are illegal immigrants from Bangladesh, despite evidence suggesting they have been present in the area for centuries. In the rare cases that Rohingya individuals do possess citizenship, the government routinely refuses to acknowledge the validity of documents they provide.{{Cite news|last=Naing|first=Shoon|date=25 August 2020|title=Rohingya politicians excluded from Myanmar election|language=en|work=Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-myanmar-election-rohingya-idUSKBN25L02T|access-date=25 August 2020|archive-date=25 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200825102451/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-myanmar-election-rohingya-idUSKBN25L02T|url-status=live}} === Economic issues === According to the [[International Monetary Fund|IMF]]:{{Cite web|last1=De|first1=Jayendu|last2=Nadeem|first2=Sanaa|date=7 July 2020|title=Six Charts on Myanmar's Economy in the Time of COVID-19|url=https://www.imf.org/en/News/Articles/2020/07/07/na70720-myanmars-economy-in-the-time-of-covid19-six-charts|access-date=29 July 2020|website=International Monetary Fund|language=en|archive-date=1 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200801190913/https://www.imf.org/en/News/Articles/2020/07/07/na70720-myanmars-economy-in-the-time-of-covid19-six-charts|url-status=live}} * Myanmar has seen a sharp decline in exports, remittances, and tourist arrivals due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Domestic economic activity has also been constrained by measures taken to control the spread of the virus. Additionally, nearly four out of five workers in Myanmar are employed in the informal sector, with limited access to social safety nets to help cope with any economic fallout. * Natural gas comprised 40 percent of exports and 20 percent of government revenues in fiscal year 2018/19, and due to a drop in prices in 2020, the current account and fiscal position of the country became even more strained. * The [[Burmese kyat]], in contrast to trends elsewhere in the region, has appreciated in value. "The country's trade deficit had narrowed for about a year, leading to exchange rate appreciation pressures. This trend has now started to unwind. This may continue as imports pick up and the economy is projected to recover. At the same time, Myanmar’s foreign exchange intervention rule, adopted late last year, has facilitated accumulation of foreign exchange reserves, which remain inadequate." In addition, some construction and infrastructure projects have been either delayed or cancelled due to supply and demand shocks as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic, including the US$1 billion Yangon Elevated Expressway and the development of the US$8–10 billion [[Dawei Port Project|Dawei Special Economic Zone]] and accompanying US$137.1 million Dawei-Htee Kee Road linking the zone to [[Ratchaburi]] in [[Thailand]]. The government has also not been able to muster up enough funds to put together a stimulus package, only allocating the equivalent of around US$72 million to assist small- and medium-sized enterprises compared to the tens of billions allocated in nearby countries like Thailand.{{Cite web|last=Bharat|first=Shah Suraj|date=17 April 2020|title=COVID-19 Threatens Myanmar's Economy|url=https://thediplomat.com/2020/04/covid-19-could-leave-myanmars-economy-in-ruins/|access-date=29 July 2020|website=The Diplomat|language=en-US|archive-date=5 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200805052109/https://thediplomat.com/2020/04/covid-19-could-leave-myanmars-economy-in-ruins/|url-status=live}} Prior to the pandemic, some areas of the country's economy had been highlighted as trouble spots, including bank lending and tourism.{{Cite web|last=Sainsbury|first=Michael|date=26 February 2019|title=The gloom about Myanmar's economy|url=https://www.lowyinstitute.org/the-interpreter/the-gloom-about-myanmar-economy|access-date=29 July 2020|website=The Lowy Institute|language=en|archive-date=2 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200702104416/https://www.lowyinstitute.org/the-interpreter/the-gloom-about-myanmar-economy|url-status=live}} GDP growth is expected to decline nearly 7% from the prior year, with overall GDP expected to about break even with the prior year due to the pandemic.{{Cite web|date=25 June 2020|title=Myanmar's Economy Severely Impacted by COVID-19: Report - Myanmar|url=https://reliefweb.int/report/myanmar/myanmar-s-economy-severely-impacted-covid-19-report|access-date=29 July 2020|website=ReliefWeb|language=en|via=The World Bank|archive-date=27 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200627210943/https://reliefweb.int/report/myanmar/myanmar-s-economy-severely-impacted-covid-19-report|url-status=live}} === COVID-19 pandemic === {{main|COVID-19 pandemic in Myanmar}} Despite only reporting around 300 confirmed cases of [[COVID-19]] nationwide as of early July 2020, Myanmar has limited testing capacity, so the true extent of the spread of the virus is still unknown. Regardless, authorities implemented strict containment measures early on, including travel restrictions, closure of land borders, and bans on mass public gatherings. Nevertheless, the number of confirmed cases has ballooned to more than 50,000 by November 2020. === Constitutional reform === In January 2019, the National League for Democracy pushed for constitutional reform, but was unsuccessful because any changes required 75% approval in the legislature, and 25% of seats are reserved for the military. Outside of these seats, the pro-military USDP was also unlikely to go along (as well as other minor parties potentially being unwilling), meaning any proposals were dead on arrival. ==Electoral system== All offices elected by popular vote are contested under a [[first-past-the-post]] system, in which a candidate needs only a [[Plurality (voting)|plurality]] of votes in a constituency to be elected. All candidates must be citizens of Myanmar. One-quarter of seats in both houses of the [[Assembly of the Union]] and one-third of seats in state and regional legislatures are reserved for the military under the [[Constitution of Myanmar|2008 Constitution]], and three ministries (Home Affairs, Border Affairs, and Defense) of the national government formed following the election must be headed by a military appointee. After the new legislators take office, the [[President of Myanmar|President]] and the two [[Vice-President of Myanmar|Vice Presidents]] of Myanmar are elected by the [[Presidential Electoral College]], made up of MPs from three committees: one of elected members from each house of the Assembly of the Union, and one from the military-appointed members. Each committee recommends one candidate, and the Assembly then holds a vote. The position the candidates are elected to depends on their overall vote total (the highest vote-getter becomes President, while the second-highest becomes First Vice President, and the remaining candidate becomes Second Vice President). People married to a non-Burmese citizen and/or who have children without Burmese citizenship are barred from being elected to any presidential position. Elected officials will take office in March 2021. For a majority, a party or coalition(s) require 221 seats in the House of Representatives and 113 seats in the House of Nationalities. On 29 June 2020, the Union Election Commission (UEC) announced the constituency reapportionment for the 168 non-appointed seats of the House of Nationalities (Amyotha Hluttaw), 330 non-appointed seats of the House of Representatives (Pyithu Hluttaw), 644 non-appointed seats of the State and Regional Hluttaws and 29 Ethnic Affair Ministers. The UEC also announced in which constituencies elections would be fully or partially cancelled on 16 October 2020 and 27 October 2020. Elections were fully cancelled in 15 townships and partially in 41. Of the opposition campaign materials that were broadcast on state media, some had portions censored by the election commission, which was controlled by the NLD government. Residents without citizenship documents were barred from voting in the election, which disproportionately affected the [[Rohingya]], [[Burmese Indians]] and [[Chinese people in Myanmar|Sino-Burmese]] communities. Townships in conflict areas faced denial of internet access for months before the election. The report additionally took issue with 25% of the seats in parliament being reserved for the military. The 2020 election was observed by domestic and international election observers. In total, the Union Election Commission accredited 7,232 observers from 13 domestic groups at the union-level, an additional 985 observers from 23 groups at the state and region levels.{{Cite web|work=ANFREL|date=10 November 2020|title=ANFREL IEOM to the 2020 Myanmar General Elections Interim Report|url=https://anfrel.org/anfrel-ieom-to-the-2020-myanmar-general-elections-interim-report/|access-date=6 February 2021|language=en-US|archive-date=5 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210205160940/https://anfrel.org/anfrel-ieom-to-the-2020-myanmar-general-elections-interim-report/|url-status=live}} International observers included the [[Asian Network for Free Elections]] (ANFREL), the Carter Center, the European Union, and the government of Japan, totaling 61 international observers, 182 diplomatic observers, and 53 staff from [[International Foundation for Electoral Systems|IFES]] and [[International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance|International IDEA]]. A coalition of 12 domestic election observer groups found the election results credible, reflecting the will of the majority of voters.{{Cite web|date=29 January 2021|title=Joint Statement: Domestic election observer groups say 2020 Myanmar polls results credible, call support for peaceful power transition|url=https://anfrel.org/joint-statement-domestic-election-observer-groups-say-2020-myanmar-polls-results-credible-call-support-for-peaceful-power-transition/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210223120542/https://anfrel.org/joint-statement-domestic-election-observer-groups-say-2020-myanmar-polls-results-credible-call-support-for-peaceful-power-transition/ |archive-date=23 February 2021 |access-date=6 February 2021|website=Asian Network for Free Elections|language=en-US}} The coalition also noted weaknesses in Myanmar's electoral legal framework, including the [[2008 Constitution of Myanmar|2008 Constitution]], and found some inconsistencies in electoral administration and election administration amid the ongoing pandemic. The [[Carter Center]] assessment did not find any major irregularities with conduct at polling stations.{{Cite web|date=11 November 2020|title=Election 2020 {{!}} No Major Irregularities in Myanmar Election: Carter Center|url=https://www.irrawaddy.com/elections/no-major-irregularities-myanmar-election-carter-center.html|access-date=6 February 2021|website=The Irrawaddy|language=en-US|archive-date=6 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210206022902/https://www.irrawaddy.com/elections/no-major-irregularities-myanmar-election-carter-center.html|url-status=live}} A team of 43 observers had visited 234 polling stations across 10 of Myanmar's 14 states and regions.{{Cite web|title=Carter Center Preliminary Statement on the 2020 Myanmar General Elections|url=https://www.cartercenter.org/news/pr/2020/myanmar-111020.html|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201111071153/https://www.cartercenter.org/news/pr/2020/myanmar-111020.html |archive-date=11 November 2020 |access-date=6 February 2021|website=Carter Center}} The Carter Center praised the Union Election Commission's efforts to update the voter roll, train election officials, and adapt procedures for older voters during the COVID-19 pandemic. It also noted the UEC's failure to provide timely access to election data, and that election postponements and cancellations stopped voting for 1.4 million citizens, leaving 24 seats vacant. == | party3 = Labour Party (Nigeria) | last_election3 = 1 | seats_before3 = 10 | seats_after3 = 35 | seat_change3 = {{increase}}34 }} The '''2023 Nigerian House of Representatives elections''' were held on 25 February 2023 where voters elected members of the House of Representatives using [[first-past-the-post voting]] in all 360 federal constituencies.{{cite web |last1=Oyekanmi |first1=Rotimi |title=It's Official: 2023 Presidential, National Assembly Elections to Hold Feb 25 |url=https://inecnews.com/its-official-2023-presidential-national-assembly-elections-to-hold-feb-25-%EF%BF%BC/ |website=[[Independent National Electoral Commission (Nigeria)|INEC]] News |access-date=27 February 2022 |date=26 February 2022 |archive-date=26 February 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220226233141/https://inecnews.com/its-official-2023-presidential-national-assembly-elections-to-hold-feb-25-%EF%BF%BC/ |url-status=live }}{{Cite news |last1=Jimoh |first1=Abbas |title=INEC Sets New Dates For 2023 General Elections |url=https://dailytrust.com/just-in-inec-sets-new-dates-for-2023-general-elections |newspaper=[[Daily Trust]] |access-date=26 February 2022 |date=26 February 2022 |archive-date=25 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220725032251/https://dailytrust.com/just-in-inec-sets-new-dates-for-2023-general-elections |url-status=live }} The last regular House elections for all districts were in 2019. [[2023 Nigerian elections#Federal elections|Other federal elections]], including the [[2023 Nigerian Senate election|Senate elections]] and the [[2023 Nigerian presidential election|presidential election]], held on the same date while [[2023 Nigerian elections#State elections|state elections]] were held two weeks afterwards on 18 March. The winners of these House elections will serve beginning in the [[10th Nigerian National Assembly]]. The APC have held a majority in the [[Nigerian House of Representatives|House of Representatives]] since the [[2015 Nigerian general election#House of Representatives|2015 elections]] and solidified that majority in [[2019 Nigerian House of Representatives election|2019]]. {{Horizontal TOC}} ==Background== After the 2015–2019 House of Representatives term led by [[Speaker of the House of Representatives of Nigeria|Speaker]] [[Yakubu Dogara]] ([[Peoples Democratic Party (Nigeria)|Peoples Democratic Party]]) and with a slight [[All Progressives Congress]] majority, the [[2019 Nigerian Senate election|2019 elections]] were categorized by a large shift back towards the APC. As in the [[2019 Nigerian Senate election|Senate]], the APC solidified its majority after nearly losing it due to defections in 2018. At the opening of the [[9th Nigeria National Assembly]], [[Femi Gbajabiamila]] (APC-Surulere I) was elected as [[Speaker of the House of Representatives of Nigeria|Speaker]] and [[Ahmed Idris Wase]] (APC-Wase) became [[Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives|Deputy Speaker]] as the party avoided the internal struggles that led Dogara and [[Yusuf Sulaimon Lasun]] to take those offices in 2015.{{Cite news |title=Femi Gbajabiamila, Ahmed Idris emerge Speaker, Deputy |url=https://www.vanguardngr.com/2019/06/femi-gbajabiamila-ahmed-idris-emerge-speaker-deputy/ |location=Lagos, Nigeria|newspaper=[[Vanguard (Nigeria)|Vanguard]] |date=11 June 2019 |access-date=16 October 2021 |archive-date=16 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211016201433/https://www.vanguardngr.com/2019/06/femi-gbajabiamila-ahmed-idris-emerge-speaker-deputy/ |url-status=live }} On the other hand, the emergence of PDP leadership was immensely contentious as the party nominated [[Kingsley Chinda]] (PDP-Obio/Akpor) to become the House Minority Leader but Gbajabiamila named [[Ndudi Elumelu]] (PDP-Aniocha/Oshimili) to the position; the dispute over Elumelu's leadership lasted nearly two years.{{Cite news |last1=Ayitogo |first1=Nasir |title=Why Gbajabiamila ignored PDP, named Elumelu House Minority Leader |url=https://www.premiumtimesng.com/news/headlines/338694-updated-how-gbajabiamila-named-elumelu-house-minority-leader-amidst-protests.html |newspaper=[[Premium Times]] |access-date=16 October 2021 |archive-date=16 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211016201434/https://www.premiumtimesng.com/news/headlines/338694-updated-how-gbajabiamila-named-elumelu-house-minority-leader-amidst-protests.html |url-status=live }}{{Cite news |last1=Matazu |first1=Hamisu Kabir |last2=Alkassim |first2=Balarabe |title=House: PDP Lifts Suspension On Minority Leader, 6 Others |url=https://dailytrust.com/house-pdp-lifts-suspension-on-minority-leader-6-others |newspaper=[[Daily Trust]] |date=19 February 2021 |access-date=16 October 2021 |archive-date=16 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211016201431/https://dailytrust.com/house-pdp-lifts-suspension-on-minority-leader-6-others |url-status=live }} During the first half of the 2019–2023 term, the APC expanded its majority through the defections of over a dozen MHRs but in the second half of the term, both major parties were hit by several defections to the other side and to minor parties as party primaries for 2023 neared. The defections to minor parties even lead to speculation on the possibility of no party gaining a majority in 2023.{{cite web |last1=Chirkpi |first1=Lizzy |title=Does the rise of NNPP signal the possibility of a coalition-led NASS? |url=https://orderpaper.ng/opinion-does-the-rise-of-nnpp-signal-the-possibility-of-a-coalition-led-nass/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220520095307/https://orderpaper.ng/opinion-does-the-rise-of-nnpp-signal-the-possibility-of-a-coalition-led-nass/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=May 20, 2022 |website=OrderPaper Nigeria |access-date=30 May 2022 }} From the perspective of the APC, analysts viewed the 9th House as a stark change from the legislature versus executive disputes that were commonplace during the 8th House but critics mocked the body as a [[Rubber stamp (politics)|rubber stamp]] that practically acted as an arm of the executive branch. ({{New}}) | map_image = [[File:2022 Nepalese general election results by constituency.svg|400px]] | map_caption = Results by constituency | title = [[Prime Minister of Nepal|Prime Minister]] | posttitle = Prime Minister after election | before_election = [[Sher Bahadur Deuba]] | before_party = Nepali Congress | after_election = [[Pushpa Kamal Dahal]] | after_party = Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre) }} General elections were held in [[Nepal]] on 20 November 2022 to elect the 275 members of the [[House of Representatives (Nepal)|House of Representatives]].{{Cite web |title=Federal and provincial polls to be held on November 20 |url=https://kathmandupost.com/politics/2022/08/04/federal-and-provincial-polls-to-be-held-on-november-20 |access-date=2022-08-08 |website=kathmandupost.com |language=English}} There were two ballots in the election; one to elect 165 members from single-member constituencies via [[First-past-the-post voting|FPTP]], and the other to elect the remaining 110 members from a single nation-wide constituency via [[party-list proportional representation]]. The election was held alongside [[2022 Nepalese provincial elections|provincial elections]] for the seven [[Provincial Assembly (Nepal)|provincial assemblies]]. After power sharing talks between the outgoing Democratic Left Alliance broke down on 25 December 2022, [[CPN (Maoist Centre)]] chairman [[Pushpa Kamal Dahal]] became [[Prime Minister of Nepal|prime minister]], its eight-member [[Cabinet of Nepal|cabinet]] consisting of MPs from his party, CPN (UML), Rastriya Swatantra Party and Janamat Party, with the [[confidence and supply]] of RPP, JSP, NUP and three independents. ==Background== The [[5th House of Representatives (Nepal)|5th House of Representatives]] [[2017 Nepalese general election|elected in 2017]] had a five-year term ending in March 2023. In May 2018, the [[CPN (Unified Marxist-Leninist)|CPN (Unified Marxist–Leninist)]] and [[CPN (Maoist Centre)]] parties merged to form the [[Nepal Communist Party]]. The merger between the two coalition partners took their total strength in the [[House of Representatives (Nepal)|House of Representatives]] to 174. The leaders of the two parties had an agreement to share the post of [[Prime Minister of Nepal|Prime Minister]] with the CPN (Unified Marxist–Leninist) chairman [[K. P. Sharma Oli]] handing over the post to Maoist Centre chairman [[Pushpa Kamal Dahal]] after two and a half years. On 20 November 2019, the two leaders agreed to let Oli complete his full term as prime minister.{{cite web |last1=Subedi |first1=Binu |title=नेकपा विवाद : घुमीफिरी मंसिर ४ |url=https://ekantipur.com/news/2020/08/24/159823166942739789.html |website=Ekantipur |publisher=Kailash Sirohiya |access-date=31 December 2020}} In a secretariat meeting of the [[Nepal Communist Party]] on 14 November 2020, Dahal presented a political document which accused Oli not following party orders and being individualistic.{{Cite web|title=At Secretariat meet, Dahal asks Oli to 'sacrifice' for saving party and republic|url=https://kathmandupost.com/politics/2020/11/14/at-secretariat-meet-dahal-asks-oli-to-sacrifice-for-saving-party-and-republic|access-date=2020-12-30|website=kathmandupost.com|language=English}} In response to Dahal, Oli rejected Dahal's accusations and presented his own political document which accused Dahal of not letting Oli run the government.{{Cite web|title=Oli goes on the offensive as he responds to Dahal's allegations|url=https://kathmandupost.com/politics/2020/11/29/oli-goes-on-the-offensive-as-he-responds-to-dahal-s-allegations|access-date=2020-12-30|website=kathmandupost.com|language=English}} As the strife within the party continued, Oli requested [[President of Nepal|President]] [[Bidya Devi Bhandari]] to dissolve the House of Representatives on 20 December 2020 as a [[No confidence motion|no-confidence motion]] was being prepared against him.{{cite web |title=Oli sacrifices the constitution to save his skin |url=https://www.recordnepal.com/wire/features/oli-sacrifices-the-constitution-to-save-his-skin/ |website=Recordnepal |publisher=Gyanu Adhikari |access-date=21 December 2020}}{{Cite web|title=Parliament Secretariat says no-confidence motion against Oli was registered after House dissolution decision|url=https://kathmandupost.com/national/2020/12/23/parliament-secretariat-says-no-confidence-motion-against-oli-was-registered-after-house-dissolution-decision|access-date=2020-12-30|website=kathmandupost.com|language=English}}{{Cite web |title=Preparations were on to register no confidence motion against me: PM Oli|url=https://en.setopati.com/political/154669/|access-date=2020-12-30|website=Setopati}} In protest of the decision by Oli, seven ministers of [[Oli cabinet, 2018|the cabinet]] resigned.{{Cite web|title=Seven ministers, all from the Dahal-Nepal faction in ruling party, resign|url=https://kathmandupost.com/politics/2020/12/20/seven-ministers-all-from-the-dahal-nepal-faction-in-ruling-party-resign-1608463576|access-date=2020-12-30|website=kathmandupost.com|language=English}}{{Cite web|title=7 Nepali ministers resign over dissolution of parliament – Xinhua {{!}} English.news.cn|url=http://www.xinhuanet.com/english/2020-12/20/c_139604926.htm|access-date=2020-12-30|website=www.xinhuanet.com}} The House of Representatives was reinstated on 23 February 2021 but on 7 March 2021, deciding on a separate writ, the [[Supreme Court of Nepal|Supreme Court]] annulled the decision of the [[Election Commission, Nepal|Election Commission]] to grant the name Nepal Communist Party to the party created by merger of the CPN (Unified Marxist–Leninist) and CPN (Maoist Centre), and positioned them to their pre merger status.{{Cite web|title=Supreme Court awards Nepal Communist Party to Rishiram Kattel|url=https://kathmandupost.com/national/2021/03/07/supreme-court-awards-nepal-communist-party-to-rishiram-kattel|access-date=2021-03-07|website=kathmandupost.com|language=English}} The CPN (Maoist Centre) withdrew its support from the government on 5 May 2021 and Oli failed to obtain a vote of confidence while a faction of his own party boycotted the vote.{{Cite web|last=Pradhan|first=Tika R.|title=Nepal Prime Minister Oli fails trust vote in Parliament|url=https://kathmandupost.com/politics/2021/05/10/nepal-prime-minister-oli-fails-trust-vote-in-parliament|url-status=live|access-date=2021-05-11|website=kathmandupost.com|language=English|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210510121939/https://kathmandupost.com/politics/2021/05/10/nepal-prime-minister-oli-fails-trust-vote-in-parliament |archive-date=2021-05-10 }} On 13 May 2021, Oli was appointed minority prime minister as the leader of the party in parliament with the highest seats.{{Cite web|title=केपी ओली प्रधानमन्त्री नियुक्त, शपथ शुक्रबार|url=https://www.onlinekhabar.com/2021/05/953625|access-date=2021-05-14|website=Online Khabar|language=en-US}} Rather than retake a vote of confidence, Oli started the process of formation of government through provision of Article 76(5), which was challenged in the Supreme Court. [[Sher Bahadur Deuba]] claimed signed support of 149 MPs, including 26 from the CPN (Unified Marxist–Leninist) and 13 from the [[People's Socialist Party, Nepal (2020)|People's Socialist Party, Nepal]].{{Cite web|title=Opposition parties meeting to chart out strategy to counter Oli's House dissolution Times|language=en}} Oli claimed support of all MPs of the CPN (UML) and the People's Socialist Party, Nepal.{{Cite web |date=2021-05-21|title=Opposition alliance to stake claim to form govt under Deuba's leadership|url=https://thehimalayantimes.com/kathmandu/opposition-alliance-to-stake-claim-to-form-govt-under-deubas-leadership|access-date=2021-05-23|website=The Himalayan Times|language=en}} aftermath== {{See also|6th House of Representatives (Nepal)|Third Dahal cabinet}} There were 12 political parties that were represented at the House of Representatives following the election. Only seven parties met the three percent threshold set in proportional voting to become national parties.{{Cite web |title=प्रतिनिधिसभामा १२ दल, राष्ट्रिय पार्टी ७ मात्रै |url=https://ekantipur.com/news/2022/12/06/167034242099737230.html |access-date=2022-12-07 |website=ekantipur.com |language=ne}} [[Nepali Congress]] emerged as the largest party after the elections winning 89 seats. The Democratic Left Alliance won 136 seats at the election but failed to get a majority by two seats. The alliance were in talks with [[Janamat Party]] and [[Nagrik Unmukti Party]] in order to gain a majority in the House of Representatives.{{Cite web |title=Congress reaches out to Janamat Party chief Raut to discuss new government |url=https://kathmandupost.com/politics/2022/12/01/congress-reaches-out-to-janamat-party-chief-raut-to-discuss-new-government |access-date=2022-12-07 |website=kathmandupost.com |language=English}}{{Cite web |title=अन्तर्वार्ता: 'टीकापुर घटनाका राजबन्दीलाई रिहाइ गर्नेसँग सहकार्य हुन्छ' |url=https://ekantipur.com/Interview/2022/12/06/167032541917868014.html |access-date=2022-12-07 |website=ekantipur.com |language=ne}} [[CPN (UML)]] won 78 seats at the election and was the second largest party in the House of Representatives. The party however got the most votes in the party list proportional system.{{Cite web |title=समानुपातिकतर्फको मतगणना सकियो : कसले कति सिट पाए ? |url=https://ekantipur.com/news/2022/12/06/167033811765474170.html |access-date=2022-12-07 |website=ekantipur.com |language=ne}} President [[Bidya Devi Bhandari]] called on the parties to form a government on 19 December 2022, after the final results of the election were presented to her by the [[Election Commission (Nepal)|Election Commission]].{{Cite news |last=Sharma |first=Gopal |date=2022-12-18 |title=Nepal president gives parties a week to form new government |language=en |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/nepal-president-gives-parties-week-form-new-government-2022-12-18/ |access-date=2022-12-27}} [[Pashupati Shumsher Jung Bahadur Rana]] from the [[Rastriya Prajatantra Party]], as the senior-most member of the new House of Representatives, was sworn in on 21 December 2022 by the president.{{Cite web |title=Pashupati Shamsher Rana takes oath of office and secrecy |url=https://kathmandupost.com/national/2022/12/21/pashupati-shamsher-rana-takes-oath-of-office-and-secrecy |access-date=2022-12-27 |website=kathmandupost.com |language=English}} He administered the oath of office to the newly elected members of the [[House of Representatives (Nepal)|House of Representatives]] on 22 December 2022.{{Cite web |title=MPs-elect taking oath at 1:00 pm today |url=https://risingnepaldaily.com/news/20393 |access-date=2022-12-27 |website=GorakhaPatra}} After power sharing talks between the Democratic Alliance broke down on 25 December 2022, [[CPN (Maoist Centre)]] chairman [[Pushpa Kamal Dahal]] presented his claim for the post of [[Prime Minister of Nepal|prime minister]] with the support of [[CPN (UML)]], [[Rastriya Swatantra Party]], [[Rastriya Prajatantra Party]], [[People's Socialist Party, Nepal (2020)|People's Socialist Party]], [[Janamat Party]], [[Nagrik Unmukti Party]] and three [[Independent politician|independents]].{{Cite web |title=President appoints Pushpa Kamal Dahal prime minister |url=https://kathmandupost.com/national/2022/12/25/president-appoints-pushpa-kamal-dahal-prime-minister |access-date=2022-12-27 |website=kathmandupost.com |language=English}} Dahal was sworn in as prime minister for the third time the next day with an eight-member [[Cabinet of Nepal|cabinet]] consisting of MPs from his party, CPN (UML), Rastriya Swatantra Party and Janamat Party, with the [[confidence and supply]] of RPP, PSP, NUP and three independents.{{Cite web |title=Dahal sworn in as prime minister |url=https://kathmandupost.com/national/2022/12/26/dahal-sworn-in-as-prime-minister |access-date=2022-12-27 |website=kathmandupost.com |language=English}} The inaugural session was scheduled for 9 January 2023.{{Cite web |title=Diverse Parliament’s first sitting stresses a range of issues |url=https://kathmandupost.com/national/2023/01/09/diverse-parliament-s-first-sitting-stresses-a-range-of-issues |access-date=2023-01-09 |website=kathmandupost.com |language=English}} Dahal secured a [[vote of confidence]] on 10 January 2023 with 268 votes in his favor and only two MPs from [[Nepal Majdoor Kisan Party]] and [[Rastriya Janamorcha]] voting against him.{{Cite web |title=Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal secures vote of confidence |url=https://kathmandupost.com/national/2023/01/10/prime-minister-pushpa-kamal-dahal-secures-vote-of-confidence |access-date=2023-01-10 |website=kathmandupost.com |language=English}} The CPN (UML) withdrew from the coalition on 27 February 2023, citing Dahal's decision to back an opposition candidate supported by the Nepali Congress in the [[2023 Nepalese presidential election|upcoming presidential election]].{{Cite web |title=Key party withdraws from Nepal fragile coalition government |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/nation-world/key-party-withdraws-from-nepal-fragile-coalition-government/ |access-date=2023-03-01 |website=The Seattle Times |language=en}} Dahal had announced this in order to gain the support of NC in the legislature. A vote of confidence is due within 30 days of the loss of a legislative majority.{{Cite web |title=Key left party quits Nepal’s fragile ruling coalition: Reports |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2023/2/27/key-left-party-quits-nepals-fragile-ruling-coalition-reports |access-date=2023-03-01 |website=Al Jazeera |language=en}} The Rastriya Prajatantra Party had withdrawn support days prior due to the same issue.{{Cite news |last=Sharma |first=Gopal |date=2023-02-25 |title=Nepal's ruling coalition in turmoil as deputy PM and 3 other ministers quit |language=en |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/nepals-ruling-coalition-turmoil-deputy-pm-3-other-ministers-quit-2023-02-25/ |access-date=2023-03-01}} The Rastriya Swatantra Party had also previously withdrawn its ministers from the government,{{Cite web |last=Poudel |first=Santosh Sharma |date=2023-02-08 |title=Key Ally Quits Government in Nepal |url=https://thediplomat.com/2023/02/key-ally-quits-government-in-nepal/ |access-date=2023-03-01 |website=The Diplomat |language=en-US}} although remained supportive under a confidence-and-supply General elections, originally scheduled to be held in 2023,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hussain |first1=Abid |title=Pakistan parliament dissolved to hold election without ex-PM Imran Khan |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2023/8/9/pakistan-national-assembly-to-dissolve-for-polls-without-ex-pm-imran-khan |website=Al Jazeera |language=en |access-date=4 March 2024 |archive-date=14 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240214153227/https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2023/8/9/pakistan-national-assembly-to-dissolve-for-polls-without-ex-pm-imran-khan |url-status=live }}</ref> were held in [[Pakistan]] on 8 February 2024 to elect the members of the [[List of members of the 16th National Assembly of Pakistan|16th]] [[National Assembly of Pakistan|National Assembly]]. The [[Election Commission of Pakistan]] announced the detailed schedule on 15 December 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://ecp.gov.pk/election-schedule-general-elections-2024 |title=Election Commission of Pakistan |access-date=16 February 2024 |archive-date=6 January 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240106074409/https://ecp.gov.pk/election-schedule-general-elections-2024 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The elections were held following [[2022–2023 Pakistan political unrest|two years of political unrest]] after Prime Minister [[Imran Khan]] of the [[Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf]] (PTI) was [[No-confidence motion against Imran Khan|removed from office by a no-confidence motion]]. Subsequently, Khan was arrested and convicted for corruption and barred from politics for five years. In the run-up to the elections, [[PTI intra-party elections case|a Supreme Court ruling]] stripped the PTI of their [[electoral symbol]] for failing to hold intra-party elections for years.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2023/8/8/former-pakistan-pm-imran-khan-barred-from-politics-for-5-years|title=Former Pakistan PM Imran Khan barred from politics for 5 years|publisher=Al Jazeera|date=8 August 2023|access-date=10 February 2024|archive-date=8 February 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240208230518/https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2023/8/8/former-pakistan-pm-imran-khan-barred-from-politics-for-5-years|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/imran-khans-appeal-against-conviction-rejected-by-pakistan-court-lawyer-says-2023-12-21/|title=Pakistan's Imran Khan still barred from vote after conviction appeal fails -lawyer|publisher=Reuters|date=21 December 2023|access-date=10 February 2024}}</ref><ref name="theguardian/10feb24" /><ref name="theguardian/11feb24">{{cite news |last1=Ellis-Petersen |first1=Hannah |last2=Baloch |first2=Shah Meer |title=Protests take place across Pakistan amid election vote-rigging allegations |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2024/feb/11/protests-pakistan-election-vote-rigging-allegations-imran-khan?CMP=share_btn_tw |access-date=11 February 2024 |work=The Guardian |date=11 February 2024 |archive-date=11 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240211192259/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2024/feb/11/protests-pakistan-election-vote-rigging-allegations-imran-khan?CMP=share_btn_tw |url-status=live }}</ref>

In the final election results, independent candidates ended up winning 103 general seats including 93 backed by the PTI, followed by 75 from the [[Pakistan Muslim League (N)]] (PML-N) and 54 from the [[Pakistan People's Party]] (PPP). In [[Punjab, Pakistan|Punjab]] and [[Sindh]] provinces, the PML-N and the PPP respectively emerged as the largest parties. Independent candidates backed by the PTI won the most number of seats in [[Khyber Pakhtunkhwa]] while [[Balochistan, Pakistan|Balochistan]] voted for the PPP and the PML-N as the largest parties. Later all parties except the PTI were given reserved seats for women and minorities.

==Background==
===2018 elections===
{{further|2018 Pakistani general election}}
General elections were held in [[Pakistan]] on 25 July 2018 after the completion of a five-year term by the outgoing government. At the national level, elections were held in [[List of constituencies of Pakistan|272 constituencies]], each electing one member to the [[National Assembly of Pakistan|National Assembly]]. At the provincial level, elections were held in each of the four provinces to elect Members of the Provincial Assemblies (MPA).<ref>{{cite news |last1=Chaudhry |first1=Fahad |title=PTI largest party with 115 NA seats as ECP releases final tally two days after polls |url=https://www.dawn.com/news/1423442 |access-date=15 February 2024 |work=dawn.com |date=28 July 2018 |language=en |archive-date=30 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230930162808/https://www.dawn.com/news/1423442 |url-status=live }}</ref>

As a result of the elections, the [[Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf]] (PTI) became the single largest party at the national level in terms of both popular vote and seats. At the provincial level, the PTI remained the largest party in [[2018 Khyber Pakhtunkhwa provincial election|Khyber Pakhtunkhwa]] (KP); the [[Pakistan People's Party]] (PPP) remained the largest party in [[2018 Sindh provincial election|Sindh]] and the newly-formed [[Balochistan Awami Party]] (BAP) became the largest party in [[2018 Balochistan provincial election|Balochistan]]. In [[2018 Punjab provincial election|Punjab]], a hung parliament prevailed with [[Pakistan Muslim League (N)]] (PML-N) emerging as the largest party in terms of directly elected seats by a narrow margin.<ref>{{cite news |title=Election vote count: PTI poised to form government with 115 seats so far |url=https://www.dawn.com/news/1423240 |access-date=15 February 2024 |work=dawn.com |date=27 July 2018 |language=en |archive-date=5 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220705103358/https://www.dawn.com/news/1423240 |url-status=live }}</ref> However, following the support of the [[Pakistan Muslim League (Q)]] and the joining of [[Independent (politician)|independent]] MPAs into the PTI, the latter became the largest party and was able to form the government.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Malik |first1=Mansoor |title=Buzdar wins race against Hamza for Punjab CM |url=https://www.dawn.com/news/1428059 |access-date=15 February 2024 |work=dawn.com |date=20 August 2018 |language=en |archive-date=13 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220713212634/https://www.dawn.com/news/1428059 |url-status=live }}</ref>

===PDM government===
After the success of the no-confidence motion, on 11 April 2022 [[Shehbaz Sharif]] became the Prime Minister after receiving 174 votes out of a total of 342, two more than the required majority with the support of the Pakistan People's Party, Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam and various smaller parties under the coalition of the PDM. Dissident members of PTI also supported his candidature. Meanwhile, the remaining PTI members, who were now in the opposition, boycotted the session terming it a continuation of a "foreign conspiracy".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-04-11 |title=Shehbaz Sharif elected prime minister of Pakistan |url=https://www.dawn.com/news/1684500 |access-date=2024-02-06 |website=dawn.com |language=en |archive-date=29 June 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230629004957/https://www.dawn.com/news/1684500 |url-status=dead }}</ref> A day later, over 100 PTI members tendered resignations from their National Assembly seats.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-04-12 |title=Pakistan: 100 PTI members resign from Parliament |url=https://www.hindustantimes.com/world-news/pakistan-100-pti-members-resign-from-parliament-101649722258735.html |access-date=2024-02-06 |website=Hindustan Times |language=en |archive-date=6 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240206004907/https://www.hindustantimes.com/world-news/pakistan-100-pti-members-resign-from-parliament-101649722258735.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

The PDM government remained in power until 10 August 2023. [[Premiership of Shehbaz Sharif|Sharif's tenure]] was marked by historically [[Pakistani economic crisis (2022-present)|high inflation, contraction of the national economy]], and a record devaluation of the [[Pakistani rupee]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-08-10 |title=PDM govt leaves behind massive inflation |url=https://tribune.com.pk/story/2430074/pdm-govt-leaves-behind-massive-inflation |access-date=2024-02-06 |website=The Express Tribune |language=en |archive-date=7 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240207084914/https://tribune.com.pk/story/2430074/pdm-govt-leaves-behind-massive-inflation |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Kiani |first=Khaleeq |date=2023-11-29 |title=GDP figure under PDM rule 'turns negative' |url=https://www.dawn.com/news/1793415 |access-date=2024-02-06 |website=dawn.com |language=en |archive-date=6 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240206004907/https://www.dawn.com/news/1793415 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-08-24 |title=Rupee plunges to all-time low against US dollar |url=https://tribune.com.pk/story/2432233/rupee-plunges-to-all-time-low-against-us-dollar |access-date=2024-02-06 |website=The Express Tribune |language=en |archive-date=10 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240210120226/https://tribune.com.pk/story/2432233/rupee-plunges-to-all-time-low-against-us-dollar |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Assassination attempt on Imran Khan and his subsequent arrest===
{{Main|Attempted assassination of Imran Khan|2023 Zaman Park raid|Arrest of Imran Khan|May 9 riots}}

During [[2022 Pakistani by-elections|October 2022 by-elections]] conducted for the National Assembly, the party won 7 out of 9 seats with Khan winning 6 of the 7 seats he was contesting for.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-10-16 |title=Oct 16 by-polls: PTI wins majority of seats in all three provinces |url=https://www.brecorder.com/news/40203351 |access-date=2024-02-07 |website=Business |date=2022-11-03 |url=https://www.isas.nus.edu.sg/papers/interpreting-imran-khans-long-march-economy-establishment-and-the-politics-of-neutrality-in-pakistan/ |title=Interpreting Imran Khan's Long As Khan was recovering from the gunshot wounds to his leg, the government registered several cases against him and [[2023 Zaman Park raid|attempted to arrest]] him from his home in [[Zaman Park]] on two different occasions during March 2023. === Return of Nawaz Sharif to electoral politics ===
At the start of May 2023, the PDM government adopted a law allowing for filing review petitions against prior Supreme Court verdicts.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-05-29 |title=New review law stuns top court |url=https://tribune.com.pk/story/2419137/new-review-law-stuns-top-court |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=The Express Tribune |language=en |archive-date=11 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230811083013/https://tribune.com.pk/story/2419137/new-review-law-stuns-top-court |url-status=live }}</ref> At the end of June, another law, limiting disqualification to five years, was adopted. It also allows the electoral commission to announce the date of an election without consulting the President of the country.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sadozai |first=Irfan |date=2023-06-25 |title=NA passes bill limiting disqualification of lawmakers to five years |url=https://www.dawn.com/news/1761671 |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=dawn.com |language=en |archive-date=28 December 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231228194257/https://www.dawn.com/news/1761671 |url-status=live }}</ref>

After serving 12 months of his 7-year sentence on corruption charges, former prime minister [[Nawaz Sharif]] left the country on 19 November 2019 to receive medical treatment in [[London]], promising to return in 4 weeks.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2019-11-19 |title=Nawaz Sharif: Ex-PM leaves Pakistan for medical treatment |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-50462154 |access-date=2024-01-26
