== Background ==
=== Early polling, pension reform, and 2018 protests ===
{{unreferenced section|date=September 2021}}
After the [[2016 Russian legislative election]], [[United Russia]] was the most popular party, with its polling rates ranging from 40% to 55%, while the ratings of the main opposition parties were much lower; the [[Communist Party of the Russian Federation]] (CPRF) and the [[Liberal Democratic Party of Russia]] (LDPR) each had just over 10%, while [[A Just Russia]] (JR) was around the 5% threshold required to enter the State Duma.

In June 2018, after Prime Minister [[Dmitry Medvedev]] announced a reform to raise the retirement age, the rating of ruling party United Russia fell sharply and since then has fluctuated from around 35% to 25% sparking the [[2018 Russian pension protests]] during summer. At the same time, the CPRF's rating has grown and currently ranges from 11% to 17%, while the rating of JR had also increased but still remained relatively low and varied in between 5% and 8%, and the rating of the LDPR has remained consistent at around 10% to 13%. Polling results differ on whether the CPRF or the LDPRF are ranked as the second most popular party. The ratings of all non-parliamentary parties combined ranges from around 6% to 17%, with exact numbers for each party unknown. When the share of people who answered they would not vote and who are unsure are equally distributed among the parties, voter share for United Russia fluctuates around 41%, the CPRF around 20%, the LDPR around 15%, JR around 8%, and other parties around 14%.

=== 2020 constitutional reform and speculations about a snap election ===
{{main|2020 Russian constitutional referendum}}
[[File:PS862_Ryazan,_Russia_-_Parliamentary_Election_September_2021.jpg|thumb|Two [[voting machine]]s of the polling place on the last day of the election in [[Ryazan]], Russia]]
During his [[2020 Presidential Address to the Federal Assembly]] on 15 January, President [[Vladimir Putin]] proposed a [[referendum]] to be held on the number of amendments arguing that a national vote would be necessary to make the changes to the [[Constitution of Russia]] "legitimate".<ref>{{cite web|date=15 January 2020|title=Russian government quits as Putin plans to stay in power past 2024|url=http://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/jan/15/putin-calls-for-constitution-changes-that-would-weaken-successor|access-date=30 March 2021|website=the Guardian|language=en}}</ref> The amendments proposed to weaken the executive power and expand the powers of the [[Federal Assembly (Russia)|Federal Assembly]]. In particular, it is supposed to transfer the power to form a government to the [[State Duma]]; this means that if the amendments were adopted, the next Cabinet would be formed by the State Duma.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://regnum.ru/news/polit/2829995.html|title=Путин: Госдума готова к формированию правительства РФ|website=regnum.ru|access-date=18 January 2020}}</ref> Immediately after Putin's speech, Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev [[Dmitry Medvedev's Second Cabinet#Resignation|resigned]] along with the entire government. On 16 January, [[Mikhail Mishustin]] was appointed as the new Prime Minister. After that, there were suggestions about the dissolution of the State Duma and holding a snap election after the constitutional reform; the State Duma can only be dissolved if it refuses the President's appointment of a Prime Minister three times in a row or passes a no-confidence motion against the government. According to sources from the [[Presidential Administration of Russia]], the constitution may be amended to allow self-dissolution of the State Duma. Some political scientists and MPs also have said that the dissolution of the State Duma and holding of a snap election is likely;<ref>{{cite web|url=https://wek.ru/vsled-za-pravitelstvom-medvedeva-mogut-raspustit-gosudarstvennuyu-dumu|title=Вслед за правительством Медведева могут распустить Государственную думу|website=wek.ru|language=ru|access-date=18 January 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.kommersant.ru/doc/4221443|title=Конституции отвели срок|work=Коммерсантъ|access-date=18 January 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://fedpress.ru/article/2409934|title=Государственная дума готовится к самороспуску {{!}} Москва|website=ФедералПресс|date=16 January 2020 |language=ru-RU|access-date=18 January 2020}}</ref> however, this opinion is not shared by [[Andrey Klishas]], head of the Legal Committee of the [[Federation Council (Russia)|Federation Council]], who is part of the working group on preparing amendments to the constitution.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.interfax.ru/russia/691574|title=Клишас опроверг планы внести в Конституцию положение о самороспуске Думы|website=Interfax.ru|language=ru|access-date=18 January 2020}}</ref>

During the second reading of the draft law on amendments to the constitution on 10 March, Member of Parliament (MP) [[Alexander Karelin]] introduced an amendment on holding a snap election.<ref>[https://rg.ru/2020/03/10/deputat-karelin-predlozhil-provesti-dosrochnye-vybory-v-gosdumu.html Депутат Карелин предложил провести досрочные выборы в Госдуму]</ref> The amendment gave the State Duma the opportunity to decide once to dissolve itself after the amendments were adopted. At first, the proposal was supported by a majority of deputies; however, because there was no consensus on this issue, with the CPRF in particular against it, President Putin urged not to dissolve the State Duma, and Karelin then withdrew the amendment.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.znak.com/2020-03-10/edinaya_rossiya_podderzhit_iniciativu_o_rospuske_gosdumy |title=Депутат: "Единая Россия" поддержит инициативу о роспуске Госдумы |access-date=2 March 2021 |archive-date=6 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210206101842/https://www.znak.com/2020-03-10/edinaya_rossiya_podderzhit_iniciativu_o_rospuske_gosdumy |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>[https://www.rbc.ru/politics/11/03/2020/5e6807139a7947ab213b93a6 Досрочные выборы в Госдуму сорвались в последний момент из-за коммунистов]</ref> If the amendment had been passed, a snap election would have been held on 13 or 20 September 2020.<ref>[https://www.interfax.ru/russia/698398 В Думе назвали возможную дату досрочных парламентских выборов в случае их проведения]</ref> MP [[Valentina Tereshkova]] proposed a reset on Putin's presidential terms, which would allow him to stay in office past his second term until 2036, as it was originally set to end in 2024. [[United Russia]] supported Tereshkova's proposal, and in Putin's response, "I believe and am deeply convinced that a strong presidential power is absolutely necessary for our country [and] for stability", citing examples of countries without presidential term limits and referencing former United States president [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]], who served four consecutive terms.<ref>{{cite news|last=McLaughlin|first=Daniel|date=10 March 2020|title=Russia opens path for Putin to retain power until 2036|url=https://www.irishtimes.com/news/world/europe/russia-opens-path-for-putin-to-retain-power-until-2036-1.4199009|url-status=live|access-date=30 March 2021|newspaper=The Irish Times|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200517204022/https://www.irishtimes.com/news/world/europe/russia-opens-path-for-putin-to-retain-power-until-2036-1.4199009 |archive-date=17 May 2020 }}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite web|title=Vladimir Putin Was 47 When He Came To Power. A New Law Could Let Him Rule Until He's 83.|url=https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/christopherm51/vladimir-putin-president-of-russia-2036|access-date=30 March 2021|website=BuzzFeed News|language=en}}</ref> The decision received backlash among the opposition and political groups, accusing Putin of trying to serve as [[president for life]].<ref name=":0"/>

The 2020 constitutional referendum was held from 25 June to 1 July; 78% of Russian voters approved on the new amendments including extension of Putin's term to 2036.<ref>{{cite web|date=1 July 2020|title=Referendum In Russia Passes, Allowing Putin To Remain President Until 2036|url=https://www.npr.org/2020/07/01/886440694/referendum-in-russia-passes-allowing-putin-to-remain-president-until-2036|url-status=live|access-date=30 March 2021|website=NPR.org|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200702030142/https://www.npr.org/2020/07/01/886440694/referendum-in-russia-passes-allowing-putin-to-remain-president-until-2036 |archive-date=2 July 2020 }}</ref> Despite the outcome, the referendum was criticized as being flawed with cases of [[electoral fraud]].<ref>{{cite web|date=1 July 2020|title=Preliminary statement on the early vote on the amendment of the Russian Constitution|url=https://www.golosinfo.org/en/articles/144476|url-status=live|access-date=30 March 2021|website=Голос — за честные выборы|language=ru|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200702145758/https://www.golosinfo.org/en/articles/144476 |archive-date=2 July 2020 }}</ref> Unsanctioned protests over the result of the vote occurred to with 140 people being detained in [[Moscow]].<ref>{{cite web|date=16 July 2020|title=Russian police detain over 140 anti-Putin protesters in Moscow|url=https://www.france24.com/en/20200716-russia-vladimir-putin-mosow-protests-constitution-2036|access-date=30 March 2021|website=France 24|language=en}}</ref> In spite of the rejection of the self-dissolution amendment, the legal possibility of holding a snap election remained in the case of a triple refusal of the State Duma to confirm the Prime Minister or Ministers, or a double vote of no confidence in the government. Immediately after the amendments to the constitution came into force, speculation about possible early elections resumed. In particular, [[Sergey Mironov]], the leader of JR, assumed that early elections could be held, referring to the desire of the country's senior leadership.<ref>[https://tass.ru/politika/9128983 Миронов допустил досрочные выборы в Госдуму в конце декабря]</ref> According to analysts, a snap election could have been held in December 2020 or early 2021.<ref>[https://www.mk.ru/politics/2020/07/03/shulman-nazvala-vozmozhnyy-srok-dosrochnykh-vyborov-gosdumy.html Политологи назвали возможный срок досрочных выборов Госдумы]</ref>

=== COVID-19 pandemic ===
{{see also|COVID-19 pandemic in Russia|Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on politics}}
[[File:Сейфы на избирательном участке в школе 1034 в Москве, 19 сентября 2021 года 20210919 122644-.jpg|thumb|Because of the pandemic the elections lasted for 3 days. In between of election days already cast ballots were stored in packages that in turn were put into safes like these. Reportedly, little was done to make them [[tamper-proof]] (note a broken seal on the right door).<ref>{{Cite news|title=Mop up: Ballot-stuffing videos taint Russian election|language=en-US|newspaper=Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/mop-up-ballot-stuffing-videos-taint-russian-election/2021/09/20/c650a4f0-1a46-11ec-bea8-308ea134594f_story.html|access-date=2021-09-23|issn=0190-8286}}{{Dead link|date=June 2022 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>]]
Owing to the COVID-19 pandemic, the format of individual electoral events can be changed for health reasons. In 2020, a law was passed that allows early voting at polling stations two days before the official voting day. In addition, the polling stations themselves can be organized outside the premises, but this decision is not mandatory and may be made by the CEC within ten days after the election is scheduled.<ref>[http://duma.gov.ru/news/49147/ Трехдневное голосование: как будет работать новый закон]</ref><ref>[https://rg.ru/2020/07/21/priniat-zakon-o-trehdnevnom-golosovanii-na-vyborah-i-referendumah.html В удобный день. Принят закон о трехдневном голосовании на выборах]</ref>

=== Barring of opposition candidates ===
{{see also|Media freedom in Russia|Russian foreign agent law}}

A number of opposition candidates were barred from running in the elections,<ref name=":7" /> including allies of imprisoned opposition leader [[Alexei Navalny]] and other candidates affiliated with him following the designation of his networks, including the [[Anti-Corruption Foundation]], as "extremist" earlier in the year,<ref name=":7" /> effectively banning anyone associated with Navalny or his groups from running for office.<ref name="grudinin-rferl" /> Navalny allies barred from running include [[Lyubov Sobol]], [[Ilya Yashin]], Oleg Stepanov, Irina Fatyanova, and Alexandra Semenova.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{cite web|date=2019-07-16|title=Russia bars opposition candidates from Moscow city ballot|url=https://www.france24.com/en/20190716-russia-bars-opposition-candidates-moscow-city-ballot|access-date=2021-09-14|website=France 24|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Troianovski2" /> Other allies of Navalny were exiled prior to the election and tried to coordinate opposition votes from abroad.<ref name="Troianovski2" />

[[Pavel Grudinin]], a high-profile candidate of the CPRF who run in the [[2018 Russian presidential election]], was excluded from the ballot by the election commission for allegedly owning foreign assets. The CPRF linked the barring of Grudinin to the waning support of the ruling United Russia party and likelihood of opposition parties securing strong results. Party leader [[Gennady Zyuganov]] said he would appeal the decision.<ref name="grudinin-rferl">{{cite web|title=Russia Bars Leading Communist Politician From Upcoming Elections|url=https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-communist-election-ban/31375410.html|access-date=2021-09-14|website=RadioFreeEurope/RadioLiberty|date=24 July 2021 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":12">{{Cite web|last=Galeotti|first=Mark|date=2021-08-03|title=Real Politics Is Being Forced on Russia's Communist Party|url=https://www.themoscowtimes.com/2021/08/03/real-politics-is-being-forced-on-russias-communist-party-a74681|access-date=2021-09-29|website=The Moscow Times|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Russia Bars Leading Communist Politician From Upcoming Elections|url=https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-communist-election-ban/31375410.html|access-date=2021-09-29|website=RadioFreeEurope/RadioLiberty|date=24 July 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

[[Yabloko]] party candidates who were barred from the legislative elections included [[Yulia Galyamina]], [[Lev Schlossberg]], Viktor Rau, Natalia Rezontova, Yelena Izotova, Ruslan Zinatullin, and Anatoly Nogovitsin. Six [[Party of Growth]] candidates (Rafail Gibadullin, Magomed Magomedaliev, Elena Motova, Evgenia Orlova, Alexei Uryvaev, and Zaur Shakhbanov) were eliminated in a single court ruling over alleged foreign funding. Anton Furgal and Roman Yuneman, two [[independent candidate]]s, were removed from the candidate lists using other legal pretexts.<ref name=":7">{{cite web|date=2021-09-10|title=Who Has Been Banned From Russia's Parliamentary Elections?|url=https://www.themoscowtimes.com/2021/09/10/who-has-been-banned-from-russias-parliamentary-elections-a74848|access-date=2021-09-11|website=The Moscow Times|language=en}}</ref>

=== Smart Voting ===
{{main|Smart Voting}}

[[Smart Voting]], a [[tactical voting]] strategy created by Navalny and his team aimed at electing candidates with the best chance of defeating those backed by the Kremlin and the ruling United Russia party, faced a crackdown by authorities before the election.<ref name="ap-smart-voting">{{cite web|url=https://apnews.com/article/europe-russia-elections-media-voting-cec43110142e7ce362b2d4f9acd9b1f0|title=EXPLAINER: How Navalny election tool challenges the Kremlin|website=apnews.com|date=14 September 2021}}</ref><ref name=":5"/><ref name="SmartVotingStrategy">{{Cite news|last1=Troianovski|first1=Anton|author-link=Anton Troianovski|last2=Nechepurenko|first2=Ivan|author-link2=Ivan Nechepurenko|date=2021-09-15|title=Could Navalny's 'Smart Voting' Strategy Shake Up Russia's Election?|language=en|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/09/15/world/europe/navalny-smart-voting-russia-election.html|access-date=2022-01-28|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Navalny urged voters to use the Smart Voting website to vote against pro-Kremlin candidates.<ref name=":2"/> Smart Voting was previously used twice in regional elections, helping opposition candidates win 20 of 45 seats in the [[2019 Moscow City Duma election]] and United Russia lose its majorities in the legislatures of the cities of Novosibirsk, Tambov, and Tomsk.<ref name="ap-smart-voting"/> Navalny ally [[Leonid Volkov (politician)|Leonid Volkov]] stated that "15%-20% of candidates endorsed by Smart Voting have won seats in legislatures".<ref name="ap-smart-voting"/><ref name=":2"/>

On 3 September, the Moscow Arbitration Court ordered [[Google]] and [[Yandex]] to stop displaying the search term "smart voting" (in Russian) from its search results, after a wool company called Woolintertrade, which registered a trademark with the phrase during the summer, demanded that the phrase be removed from search results.<ref name="dw-5-sept">{{cite web|url=https://www.dw.com/en/russia-google-told-to-clamp-down-on-navalnys-smart-voting/a-59092740|title=Russia: Google told to clamp down on Navalny's 'Smart Voting'|website=dw.com|date=5 September 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://meduza.io/en/feature/2021/09/07/the-men-behind-a-patent-dispute-with-navalny-s-smart-vote-initiative-have-apparent-ties-to-russia-s-police|title=The men behind a patent dispute with Navalny's 'Smart Vote' initiative have apparent ties to Russia's police|website=Meduza|date=7 September 2021}}</ref><ref name="bbc-6-sept">{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.com/russian/news-58466687|title="Умное голосование" теперь принадлежит продавцу шерсти из Дагестана. Связан ли он с силовиками?|website=BBC Russian|date=6 September 2021}}</ref> According to a report by [[BBC Russian]], the company, founded in Dagestan, may have ties with Russian police.<ref name="bbc-6-sept"/> Navalny ally [[Ivan Zhdanov]] called the decision "illegal" and also said: "It's naive to think that some company can register a trademark in a month, and then quickly file a lawsuit in the Moscow court and immediately get interim measures".<ref name="dw-5-sept"/>

On 6 September, access to the Smart Voting website in Russia was cut off, with Volkov stating that authorities had used a TSPU (technical tools to counter threats) system as part of the [[Sovereign Internet Law]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-smart-voting-app-blocked/31447576.html|title=Russian Authorities Block Final Access Point To Navalny's 'Smart Voting' Website|website=rferl.org|date=7 September 2021}}</ref> [[Roskomnadzor]] said the website was blocked because it was being used to "continue the activities and holding events of an extremist organisation". The previous week, Roskomnadzor warned [[Apple, Inc.|Apple]] and [[Google]] that it could face fines if the Smart Voting mobile app was not removed from their stores.<ref name=":2">{{cite web|date=2021-09-06|title=Russia blocks access to 'Smart Voting' website linked to Navalny|url=https://www.euronews.com/2021/09/06/russia-blocks-access-to-smart-voting-website-linked-to-alexei-navalny|access-date=2021-09-09|website=euronews|language=en}}</ref>

On 15 September, Roskomnadzor reportedly began temporarily blocking [[Google Docs]] after the lists of Smart Voting endorsements had been released, later restoring access to the service by the next day. Roskomnadzor denied it ordered any blocking of the site.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rferl.org/a/google-docs-blocked-russia/31463371.html|title=Watchdogs Say Google Docs Temporarily Blocked In Russia After Navalny Releases Smart Voting List|website=rferl.org|date=16 September 2021}}</ref> Navalny's team subsequently published the list on [[GitHub]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Russia Starts Blocking Google Docs After Navalny Shares Anti-Kremlin Vote Strategy – Monitor |url=https://www.themoscowtimes.com/2021/09/16/russia-starts-blocking-google-docs-after-navalny-shares-anti-kremlin-vote-strategy-monitor-a75059 |website=The Moscow Times |date=September 16, 2021 |access-date=September 21, 2021}}</ref> On 18 September, Navalny's team shared a letter by Google ordering the deletion of the endorsements on Google Docs otherwise it may block access to them. According to the document, Google states that the content is illegal in Russia as the URLs to the documents appear on the government's registry of banned resources.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://meduza.io/en/news/2021/09/18/google-orders-team-navalny-to-delete-smart-vote-s-endorsements-from-google-docs|title=Google orders Team Navalny to delete Smart Vote's endorsements from Google Docs|website=Meduza|date=18 September 2018}}</ref>

On 17 September, as elections began, Google and Apple removed the app from their stores.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.themoscowtimes.com/2021/09/17/apple-google-delete-navalny-app-on-day-of-russian-parliamentary-vote-a75069|title=Apple, Google Delete Navalny App on Day of Russian Parliamentary Vote|website=The Moscow Times|date=17 September 2021}}</ref> According to [[Agence France-Presse]], the decision was made after significant pressure from authorities which included threats of criminal charges and arrest of staff in Russia.<ref>{{cite web|title=Navalny's 'Smart Voting' App Disappears From Apple, Google Stores In Russia|url=https://www.rferl.org/a/navalny-smart-voting-google-apple/31464646.html|access-date=2021-09-17|website=RadioFreeEurope/RadioLiberty|language=en}}</ref> Later that day, [[Telegram (software)|Telegram]] blocked the Smart Voting [[chat bot]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Telegram Messenger Blocks Navalny's Bot During Vote |url=https://www.rferl.org/a/telegram-navalny-smart-voting/31466263.html |website=RadioFreeEurope/RadioLiberty |date=September 18, 2021 |access-date=September 21, 2021}}</ref> Telegram founder and CEO [[Pavel Durov]] said that Telegram would "limit the functioning of bots associated with election campaigns" and abide by Russia's "[[election silence]]", where campaigning during voting is banned. Durov also stated that he was following Apple and Google, which "dictate the rules of the game to developers like us", while adding that "the blocking of applications by Apple and Google creates a dangerous precedent that will affect freedom of speech in Russia and around the world."<ref>{{Cite web|title=Telegram Messenger Blocks Navalny's Bot During Vote|url=https://www.rferl.org/a/telegram-navalny-smart-voting/31466263.html|access-date=2021-09-29|website=RadioFreeEurope/RadioLiberty|date=18 September 2021 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.themoscowtimes.com/2021/09/18/telegram-messenger-blocks-navalny-bot-during-russian-election-a75079|title=Telegram Messenger Blocks Navalny Bot During Russian Election|website=The Moscow Times|date=18 September 2021}}</ref> Google also complied with Russian government requests to remove [[YouTube]] videos by Navalny where users attempting to access the videos were met with a message that read: "This content is not available on this country domain due to a legal complaint from the government."<ref name="TroianovskiNechepurenko2"/>

2021}}</ref> On 31 August, Putin approved one-off cash payments of 15,000 rubles ($200) for law enforcement, servicemen, firefighters and others, with the move seen by critics as bolstering support {{main|Elections in Russia}}

As of 2021, under Article 96 of [[Constitution of Russia]] the service term of the [[State Duma]] is limited to five years and each seat is allocated through a [[parallel voting]]: one ballot for party-lists and one ballot for a single candidate (both are counted by [[first-past-the-post voting]] method).<ref>{{Cite web|title=Chapter 5. The Federal Assembly|website=The Constitution of the Russian Federation|url=http://www.constitution.ru/en/10003000-06.htm|access-date=2021-09-21}}</ref>

=== Political parties and candidates ===
{{See also|Constituencies of Russia}}
According to the law enacted since 2014 half of the seats (225) are elected by [[party-list proportional representation]] (PLPR) with a minimum of 5% [[electoral threshold]] of number of votes that enable the party to get seats. The other half elected in 225 [[single-member constituencies]] ([[Constituencies of Russia|circuits, SMC]]) by [[first-past-the-post voting]] (plurality voting).<ref name=":8">{{Cite web|date=June 4, 2021|title=О выборах депутатов Государственной Думы Федерального Собрания Российской Федерации|trans-title=Federal Law "On election of deputies of the State Duma of the Federal Assembly of Russian Federation"|url=http://pravo.gov.ru/proxy/ips/?docbody=&nd=102171479#:~:text=%D0%97%D0%B0%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BD%D0%BE%D0%B4%D0%B0%D1%82%D0%B5%D0%BB%D1%8C%D1%81%D1%82%D0%B2%D0%BE%20%D0%BE%20%D0%B2%D1%8B%D0%B1%D0%BE%D1%80%D0%B0%D1%85%20%D0%B4%D0%B5%D0%BF%D1%83%D1%82%D0%B0%D1%82%D0%BE%D0%B2%20%D0%93%D0%BE%D1%81%D1%83%D0%B4%D0%B0%D1%80%D1%81%D1%82%D0%B2%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%BD%D0%BE%D0%B9%20%D0%94%D1%83%D0%BC%D1%8B%20%D0%BE%D1%81%D0%BD%D0%BE%D0%B2%D1%8B%D0%B2%D0%B0%D0%B5%D1%82%D1%81%D1%8F%20%D0%BD%D0%B0%20%D0%9A%D0%BE%D0%BD%D1%81%D1%82%D0%B8%D1%82%D1%83%D1%86%D0%B8%D0%B8%20%D0%A0%D0%BE%D1%81%D1%81%D0%B8%D0%B9%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%B9,%D0%B4%D0%B0%D0%BB%D0%B5%D0%B5%20-%20%D0%A4%D0%B5%D0%B4%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%BB%D1%8C%D0%BD%D1%8B%D0%B9%20%D0%B7%D0%B0%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BD%20%22%D0%9E%D0%B1%20%D0%BE%D1%81%D0%BD%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%BD%D1%8B%D1%85|url-status=live|access-date=2021-09-21|website=pravo.gov.ru|language=ru|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160306084704/http://pravo.gov.ru/proxy/ips/?docbody=&nd=102171479 |archive-date=6 March 2016 }}</ref><ref name=":9">{{Cite web|date=February 14, 2014|title=Federal Law On Elections of Deputies to the State Duma of the Federal Assembly of the Russian Federation|url=https://www.legislationline.org/download/id/6192/file/Law%20on%20Parliamentary%20Elections%20of%20the%20Russian%20Federation%20as%20of%20February%202014.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201023170830/https://www.legislationline.org/download/id/6192/file/Law%20on%20Parliamentary%20Elections%20of%20the%20Russian%20Federation%20as%20of%20February%202014.pdf |archive-date=23 October 2020 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-09-16|title=LONG READ: Russia's hybrid Duma elections|url=https://www.intellinews.com/long-read-russia-s-hybrid-duma-elections-220922/|access-date=2021-09-28|website=www.intellinews.com|language=en}}</ref>

In the proportional part, candidates can be nominated only by political parties, and the lists of parties must include at least 200 and no more than 400 candidates; the list may also include candidates who are not members of the party, but their number should not exceed 50% of the number of candidates on the list. The party list of candidates should be divided into federal and regional parts, which include regional groups of candidates corresponding to the group of bordering [[federal subjects of Russia]]. The number of regional groups must be at least 35, and no more than fifteen candidates may be included in the federal part of the list of candidates. The regional parts of the party list should cover the entire territory of Russia.<ref>[http://www.consultant.ru/document/cons_doc_LAW_159349/e9d53f8a920c8149b8738592414a10d304ea10f0/ Статья 39. Выдвижение федерального списка кандидатов]</ref>

In the majoritarian part, candidates can be nominated both by political parties and in the order of self-nomination. The political party must provide a list of candidates to the CEC, and the list must contain the name and number of the constituencies in which each candidate would run. Documents of candidates-self-nominees, unlike candidates from political parties, have to submit applications to District Election Commissions.<ref>[http://www.consultant.ru/document/cons_doc_LAW_159349/ceb0b0966a1751b6d3a69b7fc33d984fab94f8c1/ Статья 40. Выдвижение политической партией кандидатов по одномандатным избирательным округам]</ref> For registration on the ballot list, the self-nominated candidate must collect at least 3% of the signatures of voters residing in the constituency, or at least 3,000 signatures if the constituency has less than 100,000 voters.<ref>[http://www.consultant.ru/document/cons_doc_LAW_159349/5d7c96689425a8bf766e76131e9204e49caa5338/ Статья 45. Сбор подписей избирателей]</ref>

One and the same candidate can be nominated both in the party list and in the single-member constituency; however, in the case of their passage to the State Duma and the party list and in the single-member constituency, they would need to give up one of the places. They usually refuse the seat received on the party list, as in this case the party does not lose this seat and simply would pass it on to another candidate.{{citation needed|date=September 2021}}

=== Seats distribution ===
Article 89 of the State Duma deputies election law stipulates the proportional algorithm (i.e. [[Hare quota]]) should be used to distribute 225 seats among parties who clear 5% [[electoral threshold]] in number of votes cast per given party.<ref name=":9"/><ref name=":8"/> The rest of seats (225) are distributed according to the [[plurality voting]], as it was stipulated by law at the time of the election.{{efn|This is only true relative to the 2021 legislative election. Due to amendments done to the federal law, the election system may differ in the future.}}

=== Changes in the electoral system ===
Owing to allegedly falling ratings of the ruling party, it was assumed that the party would try to reform the electoral system in order to maintain a majority in the new State Duma. In particular, it was assumed that the share of MPs elected by party lists could be reduced from 50% (225 seats) to 25% (112 or 113), and the rest would be elected in single-member constituencies by first-past-the-post voting,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.forbes.ru/obshchestvo/379933-bloomberg-uznal-ob-obsuzhdenii-reformy-kotoraya-pozvolit-putinu-ostatsya-u-vlasti|title=Bloomberg узнал о готовящейся реформе, которая позволит Путину остаться у власти после 2024 года {{!}} Общество|date=12 July 2019|website=Forbes.ru|language=en-US|access-date=10 September 2019}}</ref> or elections on the party lists could be canceled altogether and all 450 seats would be elected in single-member constituencies;<ref>[https://www.rbc.ru/politics/23/04/2019/5cbdf32d9a79475dccdd6c6b Политологи предложили четыре сценария думских выборов-2021]</ref> however, such assumptions were not justified, and the electoral system remained the same. In April 2021, an amendment was made to the Federal Law on Elections to the State Duma, increasing the federal part of the party list from 10 to 15 candidates.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://tass.ru/politika/11196699|title=Путин подписал закон о расширении федеральной части партийных списков до 15 кандидатов|date=20 April 2021|website=ТАСС|language=ru|access-date=19 May 2021}}</ref>

== Observers ==
=== International ===
Putin's government restricted [[Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] (OSCE) representatives from carrying out [[election monitoring]] activity;<ref name=":5"/> the Russian government cited [[COVID-19]] concerns but did not elaborate on details.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|last1=Scollon |first1=Michael |title=Elections In A Vacuum: Russians Prepare For Duma Vote With Dearth Of Independent Information|url=https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-elections-dearth-information/31456424.html|access-date=2021-09-17|website=[[Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty]]|date=15 September 2021 |language=en}}</ref> The OSCE reported that Russian authorities insisted on limiting a number of OSCE [[Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights]] observers to 50, and limiting the number of the [[OSCE Parliamentary Assembly]] observers to ten, even though the [[Russian government response to the COVID-19 pandemic]] had no restrictions that "would seem to prevent the deployment of a full election observation mission" at that time.<ref name=":4"/> It was the first time since 1993 that the OSCE would not participate in observing elections in Russia.<ref>{{Cite web|title=U.S. OSCE Mission Decries 'Repressive' Conditions For Russian Duma Vote|url=https://www.rferl.org/a/us-osce-russian-duma-vote/31475220.html|access-date=2021-09-24|website=RadioFreeEurope/RadioLiberty|date=23 September 2021 |language=en}}</ref> The OSCE had earlier determined that 420 short-term and 80 long-term observers would be needed in order to reliably assess the process.<ref name=":4"/> Faced with major limitations on its freedom to observe, OSCE decided not to send a monitoring team at all.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":5">{{Cite web|author=Jim Heintz|title=Russia votes in parliament election without main opposition|url=https://apnews.com/article/europe-russia-elections-voting-vladimir-putin-0f42660b4b4475e08a0d922a0abc6c93|date=September 16, 2021|work=Associated Press News}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite web|title=No OSCE observers for Russian parliamentary elections following major limitations|date=4 August 2021 |url=https://www.osce.org/odihr/elections/russia/494488|access-date=2021-09-17|publisher= [[Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights]], [[Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]]|language=en}}</ref> Only a symbolic delegation would be present.

In August 2021, the Russian government designated [[Golos (election monitor)|Golos]] (funded in part by [[United States Agency for International Development|USAID]], [[National Endowment for Democracy|NED]], the US Government & [[Embassy of the United States, Moscow|Embassy]]) as a "foreign agent" under the [[Russian foreign agent law]]; the move hindered the group's ability to observe the election.<ref name=":3"/><ref name=":5"/> According to [[TASS]], 55 unnamed countries would send up to 249 delegates to observe the election.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Foreign observers to get access to video surveillance of Russian elections, official says|url=https://tass.com/politics/1337929|access-date=2021-09-17|website=TASS}}</ref> The [[Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe]] announced that it would send a five-member mission to Moscow for the three days of the election.<ref>{{Cite web|date=September 6, 2021|title=Parliamentary elections in the Russian Federation: PACE Election Assessment Mission|url=https://pace.coe.int/en/news/8415/parliamentary-elections-in-the-russian-federation-pace-election-assessment-mission|url-status=live|publisher=PACE|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210906160913/https://pace.coe.int/en/news/8415/parliamentary-elections-in-the-russian-federation-pace-election-assessment-mission |archive-date=6 September 2021 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Viacheslav Volodin: PACE President agreed to send representatives to observe elections to the State Duma|url=http://duma.gov.ru/en/news/51290/|access-date=2021-09-17|website=The State Duma|date=20 April 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Belarus ===
The [[National Assembly of Belarus]] has reportedly sent a delegation to Russia to observe the voting process. The group consisted of the same parliament members who are part to the [[Union State]].<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-09-17|title=Belarus MPs start monitoring elections to Russia's State Duma|url=https://eng.belta.by/society/view/belarus-mps-start-monitoring-elections-to-russias-state-duma-143371-2021/|access-date=2021-09-17|website=eng.belta.by|language=en-EN}}</ref>

== Political parties ==
{{see also|List of political parties in Russia}}
As of August 2021, there are 32 registered political parties in Russia.<ref>{{cite web |title=Политические партии |url=https://minjust.gov.ru/ru/pages/politicheskie-partii/ |access-date=2021-08-30 |website=Министерство юстиции Российской Федерации |language=ru |archive-date=13 September 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200913094341/https://minjust.gov.ru/ru/pages/politicheskie-partii/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> Parties represented in the State Duma, in which case seats must be obtained in the vote on the party list, parties that received more than 3% of the vote by party list in the previous elections, or parties that are represented at least in one of the [[Regional parliaments of Russia|regional parliaments]], or also by party list, are allowed to contest in the elections without collecting signatures. Other parties need to collect 200,000 signatures if they have also held conventions and nominated candidates to participate in the elections. The official list of parties entitled to participate in the elections without collection of signatures was announced before the election. After the [[2020 Russian regional elections]], there are only 14 such parties.<ref name="TASS2"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.consultant.ru/document/cons_doc_LAW_159349/6ddf587240f921d7fd7d0c0ed83d0ceafb99b687/ |script-title=ru:Федеральный закон от 22.02.2014 N 20-ФЗ (ред. от 28.12.2016, с изм. от 13.04.2017) "О выборах депутатов Государственной Думы Федерального Собрания Российской Федерации" Статья 44. Поддержка выдвижения федеральных списков кандидатов, кандидатов |trans-title=Federal Law of 22.02.2014 N 20-FZ (as amended on 04.06.2021) "On the elections of deputies of the State Duma of the Federal Assembly of the Russian Federation" |website=consultant.ru |language=ru |access-date=13 September 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cikrf.ru/politparty/spisok/ |script-title=ru:Сведения о политических партиях, выдвижение которыми кандидатов, списков кандидатов не требует сбора подписей избирателей |trans-title=Information about political parties whose nomination of candidates, lists of candidates does not require the collection of signatures of voters |website=cikrf.ru |language=ru |access-date=13 September 2021 |archive-date=23 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190323190626/http://www.cikrf.ru/politparty/spisok/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Campaign ==
=== Party of Growth ===
On 19 December 2018, the [[Party of Growth]] became the first party to launch a campaign when its leader [[Boris Titov]] opened the party's "Election 2021" federal headquarters in [[Miass]], [[Chelyabinsk Oblast]]. According to Titov, the party would focus on elections in single-mandate constituencies, not party lists. He said: "Today, no slogans, no 'locomotives',{{efn|name=locomotives|Political technology aimed at increasing the number of voters who vote for the list by attracting a candidate with a high political rating (most often governors and mayors of large cities). After winning, the candidate immediately refuses the position that they have been elected to. The "locomotive" then passes their mandate on to a party member who is usually less known to voters.}} we can't win ... we can't cover the whole of Russia, so it's easier for us to focus on specific constituencies. We need real candidates who will be known on the ground. And the electorate who will know first of all the person, and not even the Party of Growth." The party would nominate about 40 candidates in single-member constituencies. According to the plan, deputies elected in the course of elections to municipal and regional legislative bodies prior to 2021 should form the election headquarters of the main candidates.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ridus.ru/news/289709|title=Партия Роста начала подготовку к выборам в Госдуму 2021|website=Ридус|language=ru|access-date=10 September 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.kommersant.ru/doc/3835834|title=Партия роста начала путь в Госдуму из Челябинска|work=Коммерсантъ|access-date=10 September 2019}}</ref>

On 7 July 2020 a party convention was held in Moscow, at which the party program was approved, and governing bodies were elected. Boris Titov retained the post of party leader, while the posts of co-chairmen of the party were established.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.mk.ru/politics/2020/07/07/titova-pereizbrali-glavoy-partii-rosta.html|title=Титова переизбрали главой Партии роста|website=МК.ru|access-date=8 July 2020}}</ref> In addition to Titov, nine people became co-chairs: musician [[Sergey Shnurov]], actor [[Nikolai Fomenko]], former Minister of Labor and MP [[Oksana Dmitriyeva]], former MP [[Sergey Stankevich]], economist [[Yevgeny Kogan]], journalist [[Alexander Lyubimov]], businessman [[Ilya Sachkov]], social entrepreneur [[Ksenia Bezuglova]], and human rights activist [[Alexander Huruji]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://rost.ru/presscenter/posts/v-moskve-prokhodit-ocherednoy-sezd-partii-rosta/|title=В Москве проходит очередной съезд Партии Роста|website=rost.ru|access-date=8 July 2020}}</ref>

On 30 September 2020, Titov said that the party list would be headed by Sergey Shnurov if he takes up the offer and the party approves.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://echo.msk.ru/news/2717467-echo.html|title=Глава "Партии Роста" Титов готов доверить Шнурову возглавить список кандидатов на выборах в Госдуму|website=echo.msk.ru|access-date=30 September 2020}}</ref>

=== United Russia ===
[[United Russia]] launched its campaign at the party convention on 23 November 2019. The convention identified priorities and key areas of work that should allow the party to maintain its position as the leading political force in Russia and win the 2021 election.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://tass.ru/mezhdunarodnaya-panorama/7183549|title="Единая Россия" на съезде даст старт подготовке к выборам в Госдуму 2021 года|work=ТАСС|access-date=23 November 2019}}</ref> Party leader [[Dmitry Medvedev]] said that he would head a commission to prepare a new election program for the party.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://ria.ru/20191123/1561510242.html?in=t|title=Медведев возглавит комиссию по подготовке программы "Единой России"|work=РИА Новости|access-date=24 November 2019}}</ref> In addition, a project office was established to prepare for the election.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://ria.ru/20191123/1561515997.html?in=t|title="Единая Россия" создала структуру для подготовки к выборам-2021|work=РИА Новости|access-date=24 November 2019}}</ref> According to the party's General Council Secretary [[Andrey Turchak]], United Russia would fight to preserve its constitutional majority, and intends to win at least 301 seats.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.znak.com/2019-11-22/turchak_zayavil_chto_er_pod_silu_sohranit_konstitucionnoe_bolshinstvo_v_parlamente|title=Турчак заявил, что "ЕР" под силу сохранить конституционное большинство в парламенте|work=ZNAK|access-date=23 November 2019|archive-date=22 December 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191222220539/https://www.znak.com/2019-11-22/turchak_zayavil_chto_er_pod_silu_sohranit_konstitucionnoe_bolshinstvo_v_parlamente|url-status=dead}}</ref> According to sources from the party leadership, United Russia has assessed the work of its deputies in the State Duma. Based on this assessment, not all of them would be able to run in the upcoming election, and is assumed that about half of the faction would be made up of new deputies.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.kommersant.ru/doc/4197026|title=Госдума обновится не полностью. "Единая Россия" оценила полезность своих депутатов|work=Коммерсанъ|access-date=17 December 2019}}</ref>

On 15 January 2020, Medvedev resigned from office of the [[Prime Minister of Russia]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ria.ru/20200115/1563456719.html|title=Правительство России уходит в отставку|date=15 January 2020|website=РИА Новости|language=ru|access-date=15 January 2020}}</ref> Current Prime Minister [[Mikhail Mishustin]] is not a member of United Russia or any other party; at the same time, Medvedev remains the party's leader.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.vedomosti.ru/politics/articles/2020/01/16/820726-medvedev-ostalsya-liderom|title=Медведев остался лидером партии "Единая Россия"|date=15 January 2020|website=ТАСС|language=ru|access-date=16 January 2020}}</ref> In July 2020, Turchak announced the start of preparations for the party's election program.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://ria.ru/20200706/1573951646.html|title="Единая Россия" приступит к формированию программы для выборов в Госдуму|work=РИА Новости|access-date=8 July 2020}}</ref> Medvedev said the new version of the [[Constitution of Russia]] should be used as the basis for the election program.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://news-ru.turbopages.org/s/news.ru/politics/er-idyot-na-shturm-gosdumy-pod-prikrytiem-konstitucii/?platform=desktop|title="ЕР" идёт на выборы под прикрытием Конституции|work=news.ru|access-date=8 July 2020}}</ref> On 22 October 2020, it became known that the party leadership had identified the first group of candidates for single-member constituencies. This group includes 71 incumbent MPs, whom the party intends to nominate again in their constituencies. Among these MPs is the party's parliamentary leader [[Sergey Neverov]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://iz.ru/1077348/2020-10-22/edinaia-rossiia-otobrala-bolee-70-kandidatov-na-vybory-v-gosdumu|title="Единая Россия" отобрала более 70 кандидатов на выборы в Госдуму|date=22 October 2020|website=Известия|language=ru|access-date=22 October 2020}}</ref>

On 19 June 2021, the party's pre-election congress was held in Moscow, at which the candidates and the party's program were approved. At the congress, President [[Vladimir Putin]] proposed the following five individuals for the party's federal list for the elections, among them [[Sergei Shoigu]] ([[Ministry of Defence (Russia)|Defence Minister]]), [[Sergey Lavrov]] ([[Minister of Foreign Affairs (Russia)|Foreign Minister]]), [[Denis Protsenko]] (head doctor of Russia's main coronavirus hospital), [[Yelena Shmelyova]] (co-chair of the [[All-Russia People's Front]]), and [[Anna Kuznetsova]] ([[Children's Ombudsman#Russia|Children's Rights Commissioner for the President of the Russian Federation]]).<ref name="meduza.io">{{cite web|title=Путин назвал кандидатов в первую пятерку списка "Единой России" на предстоящих выборах. Среди них не оказалось Медведева|url=https://meduza.io/news/2021/06/19/putin-nazval-kandidatov-v-pervuyu-pyaterku-spiska-edinoy-rossii-na-predstoyaschih-vyborah-sredi-nih-ne-okazalos-medvedeva|access-date=19 June 2021|website=Meduza|language=ru}}</ref> To the surprise of many analysts, Medvedev did not top the list.<ref name="meduza.io"/> The party also campaigned in the self-proclaimed [[Donetsk People's Republic]] and [[Luhansk People's Republic]] in [[eastern Ukraine]], where half a million Russian passports had been received by local residents.<ref name="2524257300690UnitedRussia">{{in lang|uk}} [https://www.pravda.com.ua/news/2021/07/15/7300690/ The leader of fighters Pushilin gathered in "United Russia"], [[Ukrayinska Pravda]] (15 July 2021)<br>{{in lang|uk}} [https://tyzhden.ua/Politics/252425 "United Russia" went on the offensive in the Donbass], [[The Ukrainian Week]] (15 July 2021)</ref>

==== United Russia primaries ====
From 24 to 30 May 2021, United Russia held primaries to select candidates for the election. These were the third legislative primaries held by the party since 2011 and the second [[open primaries]] in which all Russian citizens could participate. Electronic voting was used in the primaries due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Russia]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Предварительное голосование|url=https://er.ru/pages/predvaritelnoe-golosovanie|access-date=24 May 2021|website=er.ru|language=ru}}</ref><ref>[https://pg.er.ru/ official website of the primaries]</ref> A total of 7,624 candidates participated in the primaries, of which almost half were not party members. Of the 336 incumbent deputies from the party, only 237 applied to participate in the primaries.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rbc.ru/politics/17/05/2021/60a12b139a79470c6352727a|title=Кто собрался в Госдуму от "Единой России". Главное|date=17 May 2021|website=РБК|language=ru|access-date=19 May 2021}}</ref>

=== Yabloko ===
On 14 and 15 December 2019, [[Yabloko]] held its party convention in Moscow. Elections of the party leadership, including its leader, were held during the convention. [[Nikolay Rybakov]] was elected the new leader of the party for the next four years. He said his main goal will be to transform the party for the 2021 election. Rybakov said: "We'll see Yabloko, where the candidates will be requested to prepare for the election campaign starting from Monday in practice. If you enter an election campaign late people do not have time to learn that there are candidates from Yabloko."<ref>{{Cite news|title=Новый глава "Яблока" заявил о преобразовании партии к выборам в Госдуму|url=https://www.dp.ru/a/2019/12/15/Novij_glava_JAbloka_zajav|website=dp.ru|date=15 December 2019}}</ref> Rybakov has stated that he expects to win approximately 10% of the electorate. When asked by a journalist if he is open to working with supporters of [[Alexei Navalny]] and in fact nominating some of his supporters as candidates, Rybakov replied: "We are open to conversation. We are discussing all this." On 3 July, [[Grigory Yavlinsky]], the founder of the party, decided to not run for parliament, instead endorsing younger candidates. Yabloko was expected to nominate other famous opposition candidates such as [[Dmitry Gudkov]] and [[Andrei Pivovarov]], along with many Navalny supporters.<ref>{{cite web|title=Лидер "Яблока" подтвердил в Иванове, что обсуждается вопрос о выдвижении партией команды Навального на выборах|url=https://www.ivanovonews.ru/news/1081255/|access-date=2021-08-18|website=www.ivanovonews.ru}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Лидер "Яблока" - о Навальном, коррупции, протестах и выборах-2021|url=https://www.ivanovonews.ru/news/1081587/|access-date=2021-08-18|website=www.ivanovonews.ru}}</ref>

In an early August interview with [[TV Rain]], [[Grigory Yavlinsky]] denounced "Navalny's Politics" and his [[Smart Voting]] strategy. Yavlinsky also called on Navalny supporters to not vote for Yabloko.<ref>{{cite web|title=Телеканал Дождь|url=https://tvrain.tv/|access-date=2021-08-18|website=tvrain.ru}}</ref> As a consequence, experts from [[Carnegie Moscow Center]] have stated that Yabloko has lost all chances at overcoming the 5% [[electoral threshold]].<ref>{{cite web|author1=Борис Макаренко|author2=Андрей Колесников |title=Дума-2021: четыре интриги выборов|url=https://carnegie.ru/2021/05/31/ru-pub-84618|access-date=2021-08-18|website=Carnegie Moscow Center|language=ru}}</ref>

=== A Just Russia — For Truth ===
On 20 January 2021, [[Sergey Mironov]] announced the merger of [[A Just Russia]], [[Patriots of Russia]], and [[For Truth]].<ref name="merger">{{cite web|url=https://polit74.ru/politics/kto_vozglavit_partiyu_spravedlivaya_rossiya_posle_sozdaniya_koalitsii/|title= Кто возглавит партию "Справедливая Россия" после создания коалиции}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title="Справедливая Россия" объединится с партиями "За правду" и "Патриоты России"|url=https://www.vedomosti.ru/politics/news/2021/01/20/854727-spravedlivoi-rossii|website=Ведомости|date=20 January 2021}}</ref> A congress was held on 22 February, at which the three parties officially united into one and its leadership was elected. Mironov became the leader of the new party, while [[Zakhar Prilepin]] and [[Gennady Semigin]] (the leaders of the other two parties) were appointed co-chairmen. The new party is called the Socialist Party "A Just Russia — Patriots — For Truth", or simply A Just Russia — For Truth.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Новая партия Миронова и Прилепина определила трех лидеров|url=https://ura-news.turbopages.org/ura.news/s/news/1052468100|website=URA.ru|date=21 January 2021}}</ref>

==== A Just Russia ====
On 24 September 2020, A Just Russia launched its election campaign at a meeting of the presidium of the central council of the party. According to party leader Sergey Mironov, he will carry out general management of the campaign, and the head of the election headquarters will be MP [[Valery Gartung]].<ref>{{Cite news|title=Заседание Президиума Центрального совета Партии СПРАВЕДЛИВАЯ РОССИЯ|url=https://spravedlivo.ru/10568110|website=spravedlivo.ru|date=24 September 2020}}</ref>

==== For Truth ====
On 22 October 2020, at a meeting of the party's central committee, it was decided that party leader [[Zakhar Prilepin]] would head the party list of candidates for the election. Prilepin rejected speculation about his intention to run from a single-member constituency in the [[Nizhny Novgorod Oblast]] and said that he would run only as part of the federal list. Prilepin also said that [[Nikolai Starikov]] and [[Sergey Mikheev]] would also run only on the party list.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Захар Прилепин возглавит список партии ЗА ПРАВДУ на выборах в Государственную Думу РФ|url=https://zapravdu.org/2020/10/23/zaxar-prilepin-vozglavit-spisok-partii-za-pravdu-na-vyborax-v-gosudarstvennuyu-dumu-rf/|website=zapravdu.org|date=23 October 2020}}</ref> Mikheev explained this decision by saying that it is more reasonable to nominate the most famous candidates on the party list, since candidates in single-member constituencies do not participate in debates.{{citation needed|date=September 2021}}

=== New People ===
On 21 October 2020, party leader [[Alexey Nechaev]] announced that he would head the [[New People (political party)|New People]] party list in the election. According to him, the party intends to nominate more than 200 candidates in single-member constituencies. According to Nechaev, the party expects to get 15–20% of the vote.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Нечаев возглавит список партии "Новые люди" на выборах в Госдуму в 2021 году|url=https://www.interfax.ru/russia/732552|website=Интерфакс|date=21 October 2020}}</ref> According to the results of the 2020 regional elections, New People was named the most promising party of the so-called new parties which were registered in 2020<ref>{{Cite news|title="Новые люди" стали наиболее перспективной новой партией|url=https://www.vedomosti.ru/politics/articles/2020/09/13/839724-novie-lyudi|website=Ведомости|date=14 September 2020}}</ref> as well as one of the two non-parliamentary parties that has a chance to overcome the 5% barrier.<ref name=NP_RPPSJ_1>{{Cite news|title=Непарламентская оппозиция: чьи шансы на попадание в ГД-2021 выше остальных|url=https://fedpress.ru/article/2611504|website=ФдералПресс|date=2 November 2020}}</ref><ref name=NP_RPPSJ_2>{{Cite news|title=Запрос на перемены, низкая явка и трехдневное голосование. Общие итоги электоральных результатов избирательной кампании 2020 года|url=http://liberal.ru/reports/7668|website=Фонд "Либеральная миссия"|date=30 September 2020}}</ref>

On 30 November 2020, it became known that political strategist [[Yevgeny Minchenko]] had been chosen as the head of the party's election headquarters. According to political commentators, Minchenko as the head of campaign significantly increases the party's chances of being elected to the State Duma, since he previously conducted successful election campaigns in some [[Post-Soviet states|post-Soviet countries]].<ref>{{Cite news|title=Новая партия резко повысила шансы на проход в Госдуму-2021|url=https://ura-news.turbopages.org/ura.news/s/news/1052460906|website=URA.RU|date=30 November 2020}}</ref> On 21 December 2020, it was announced that the party intends to spend about 500 million rubles on its election campaign for the party list; for comparison, only the Liberal Democratic Party spent more than 500 million rubles in the previous election.<ref>{{Cite news|title=200 кандидатов на 500 миллионов. "Новые люди" хотят потратиться на выборы в Госдуму|url=https://www.kommersant.ru/doc/4625934|website=Коммерсантъ|date=22 December 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title=Как партии тратили деньги на выборах|url=https://www.rline.tv/news/2016-09-20-kak-partii-tratili-dengi-na-vyborakh/|website=Красная линия|date=20 September 2016}}</ref>

=== Communist Party of the Russian Federation ===
The [[Communist Party of the Russian Federation]] launched its campaign during the plenum of the central committee of the party on 24 October 2020. Party leader [[Gennady Zyuganov]] instructed to start developing an electoral program. According to the party's representative, the program would be less [[populist]] than in the 2016 election and more detailed for specific groups of voters.<ref>{{Cite news|title=КПРФ готовится по всему фронту|url=https://www.vedomosti.ru/politics/articles/2020/10/25/844495-kprf-gotovitsya|website=Ведомости|date=25 October 2020}}</ref> During the plenum, Zyuganov also proposed creating a new coalition, the Popular Front of the Left and Patriots.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Зюганов предложил создать правительство народного доверия|url=https://ria.ru/20201024/zyuganov-1581324945.html?nw=1603706619000|website=ria.ru|date=24 October 2020}}</ref>

On 14 December 2020, Deputy Chairman of the Central Committee of the party [[Yury Afonin]] said that the party intends to hold the next (non-election) convention in spring 2021. It is planned to elect the party leadership at the convention. Initially, it was planned that the convention would be held after the election in the fall of 2021. According to Afonin, it was decided to hold this convention earlier because "the campaign will be tense, and attempts will be made to beat the candidates".<ref>{{Cite news|title=КПРФ намерена переизбрать руководство весной 2021 года|url=https://www.kommersant.ru/doc/4614203|website=Коммерсантъ|date=14 December 2020}}</ref>

=== Green Alternative ===
[[Green Alternative (Russia)|Green Alternative]] launched its campaign on 22 November 2020 at a party board meeting. According to party leader [[Ruslan Khvostov]], the party would focus on social issues, health care, science, and protection of minority rights, alongside environmental issues.<ref>{{Cite news|title="Зелёная Альтернатива" идёт покорять Госдуму|url=https://zaecology.ru/sobytija/zeljonaja-alternativa-budet-pokorjat-gosdumu/|website=zaecology.ru|date=22 November 2020}}</ref>

=== Russian Party of Pensioners for Social Justice ===
The [[Russian Party of Pensioners for Social Justice]] launched its campaign on 7 December 2020 at a meeting of the party's presidium of the central council.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Партия пенсионеров приняла решение об участии в выборах в ГД|url=https://regnum.ru/news/polit/3134682.html|website=Regnum|date=7 December 2020}}</ref> According to some experts, the Party of Pensioners is one of two non-parliamentary parties that have a chance to overcome the 5% barrier.<ref name="NP_RPPSJ_1" /><ref name="NP_RPPSJ_2" />

=== Liberal Democratic Party of Russia ===
The [[Liberal Democratic Party of Russia]] launched its campaign during the party's convention on 14 December 2020. The party leadership was elected at the convention, and [[Vladimir Zhirinovsky]] was re-elected as its leader. Owing to the COVID-19 pandemic, the convention was held in a truncated format. Nevertheless, it became one of the few Russian political parties and the only parliamentary political party to hold a convention despite the pandemic.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Один за всех, все за одного|url=https://rg.ru/2020/12/14/zhirinovskogo-pereizbrali-predsedatelem-ldpr-na-chetyre-goda.html|website=RG.RU|date=14 December 2020}}</ref>

=== Russian Party of Freedom and Justice ===
On 28 March 2021, the convention of the [[Communist Party of Social Justice]] was held, at which political strategist [[Konstantin Rykov]] was elected as the new chairman of the central committee of the party. At the same congress, it was decided to rename the party to the Russian Party of Freedom and Justice.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Выборы-2021: Медпомощь для «пенсионеров» и реформа КПСС|url=https://vz.ru/news/2021/3/29/1091737.html|website=Взгляд|date=21 April 2021}}</ref> On 31 March, it was announced that the party list would be headed by journalist [[Maksim Shevchenko (journalist)|Maxim Shevchenko]].<ref>{{Cite news|title=Максим Шевченко положил партбилет на другой стол|url=https://www.kommersant.ru/doc/4752609|website=Коммерсантъ|date=21 April 2021}}</ref>

=== Russian Ecological Party "The Greens" ===
The [[Russian Ecological Party "The Greens"]] launched its campaign on 15 May 2021 during the party's convention. At the convention, a decision was made to start preparing for the election. The congress also included elections to the party's governing bodies, and Andrey Nagibin was elected its new leader.<ref>{{Cite news|title="Зеленые" начали подготовку к выборам в Госдуму|url=https://regnum.ru/news/3270173.html|website=Regnum|date=15 May 2021}}</ref>

== Controversy ==
=== Irregularities ===
The election was marred by multiple episodes of systemic fraud.<ref name=Litvinova/><ref name=WagnerThiele>Hannah Wagner and Christian Thiele, [https://www.detroitnews.com/story/news/world/2021/09/25/putin-praises-russia-election-protest/118949116/ Putin praises elections as hundreds in Moscow protest against results], ''Detroit News'' (September 25, 2021).</ref> Multiple episodes of [[ballot-stuffing|ballot-box stuffing]] and other forms of fraud were recorded in photographs and video recordings, many of which circulated widely on Russian social media.<ref name=Litvinova/><ref name=":10">{{Cite web|author=Robert Coalson|title=Russian Social Media Swamped With Video Evidence Of Ballot-Box Stuffing|url=https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-election-fraud/31466758.html|date=September 18, 2021|publisher=Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty|language=en}}</ref> In some regions, episodes of [[carousel voting]] (groups of voters casting multiple ballots at different polling stations) were reported.<ref name=HeintzLitvinova>Jim Heintz & Daria Litvinova, [https://apnews.com/article/europe-russia-elections-voting-presidential-elections-b765d71003b5e81ab347edd9144b0c2e Early results in Russia show pro-Kremlin party leads], Associated Press (September 19, 2021).</ref> There were also reports of clashes between poll workers and election monitors.<ref name=HeintzLitvinova/>

[[Ella Pamfilova]], head of the CEC, said that the government's commission had invalidated some 25,830 ballots but insisted at a press conference with Putin that the complaints of fraud were "minimal as ever";<ref name=Litvinova/><ref>[https://tass.com/politics/1340163 25,830 voting ballots in 35 regions of Russia deemed invalid — CEC head], TASS (September 20, 2021).</ref> outside analysts identified fraud on a much broader scale.<ref name=Litvinova/><ref name=Massive>{{Citation|title=Researcher Says Raw Voting Data Points To Massive Fraud In United Russia's Duma Victory|url=https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-election-fraud-shpilkin/31472787.html|publisher=Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty|language=en|date=September 22, 2021}}</ref> After the election, the independent Russian election-monitoring organization [[Golos (election monitor)|Golos]] said that there were violations during the voting procedure which led to "significantly distorted" results that cast doubt on the "veracity of the results" officially reported by the CEC.<ref name=Litvinova/> Golos said it had received about 5,000 reports of possible voter violations.<ref>{{cite news|date=20 September 2021|title=Russia election: Putin's party wins election marred by fraud claims|agency=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-58614227|access-date=21 September 2021}}</ref>

Physicist and independent Russian election analyst Sergei Shpilkin conducted a statistical analysis of anomalies in the voting data, concluding that massive fraud was a major factor in United Russia's victory<ref name=Massive/> and over 14 million votes were added artificially.<ref name=":11">{{Cite web|title=A crackdown before the storm. Vladimir Milov explains why fake votes cannot hide the weakening of Putin's power|url=https://theins.ru/en/opinion/vladimir-milov/245350|access-date=2021-09-29|website=The Insider|language=ru}}</ref> Shpilkin estimated that United Russia would have likely received around 31–33% of votes, rather than nearly half of the vote as officially reported,<ref name=Massive/> and United Russia would have lost its majority in the State Duma without voting fraud. Electronic vote accounted for 4% of overall votes and was decisive for a number of Duma seats, especially in Moscow.<ref name=":11"/> Shpilikin also estimated that nationwide [[voter turnout]] was probably around 38%, rather than 52% as officially reported.<ref name=Massive/> Statistical analysis by the [[Complexity Science Hub Vienna]] also indicate massive fraud, with clear statistical signs for voter rigging and ballot-stuffing; voter turnout was rather around 30%.<ref>{{Cite web|date=12 October 2021|title=Election forensics of the Russia 2021 elections statistically indicate massive election fraud|url=https://www.csh.ac.at/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/CSH-Policy-Brief-5-2021-Russian-Elections.pdf|url-status=live|publisher=Complexity Science Hub Vienna|access-date=13 October 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211013080722/https://www.csh.ac.at/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/CSH-Policy-Brief-5-2021-Russian-Elections.pdf |archive-date=13 October 2021 }}</ref> A machine learning model applied to electoral data also indicates the mediocre quality of election results registration.<ref>{{Cite web|date=24 January 2022|title=An attempt to find out real results of 2021 Russia parliamentary elections using machine learning.|url=https://pub.towardsai.net/an-attempt-to-find-out-real-results-of-2021-russia-parliamentary-elections-using-machine-learning-9ec4cbe7b869|url-status=live|publisher=Towards AI|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220125123102/https://pub.towardsai.net/an-attempt-to-find-out-real-results-of-2021-russia-parliamentary-elections-using-machine-learning-9ec4cbe7b869 |archive-date=25 January 2022 }}</ref>

There were reports on members of election committees casting ballots for voters,<ref>{{Citation|title=НЕИЗВЕСТНЫЕ ПРОГОЛОСОВАЛИ ЗА ЦЕЛУЮ СЕМЬЮ!/ЕДИНОРОССКА УМОЛЯЕТ НЕ РАЗДУВАТЬ СКАНДАЛ| date=20 September 2021 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-EYkehU4xnM|language=en|access-date=2021-09-24}}</ref> and removal of observers by police during counting.<ref>{{Citation|title=СРОЧНО! Силами полиции удаляют наблюдателей и членов УИК от КПРФ!| date=19 September 2021 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vSc37e-2s7c|language=en|access-date=2021-09-24}}</ref> With the election taking three days, there were numerous reports of members of election committees returning to polling stations at late hours,<ref>{{Citation|title=Вбросы, вбросы, вбросы| date=18 September 2021 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zd9uZt78mAI&t=2s|language=en|access-date=2021-09-26}}</ref> although the polling stations were supposed to be closed.<ref>{{Citation|title=ЦИК утвердил порядок голосования 17-19 сентября|date=July 2021 |url=https://rg.ru/2021/07/01/cik-utverdil-poriadok-golosovaniia-17-19-sentiabria.html|language=en|access-date=2021-09-26}}</ref>

==== Remote voting ====
===== Absentee ballots =====
According to Article 83 of Federal Law 20, individuals unable to come to the polling stations are allowed to vote remotely outside polling station. Such individuals are required to make a request for a remote voting, then members of election committees would come to locations specified by such individuals, typically to their home addresses, in order to collect the vote. There were multiple reports on members of election committees compiling such requests themselves.<ref>{{Citation|title=Нарушения на выборах 19.09.2021 #2|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9pcDfAhNodU|language=en|access-date=2021-09-24}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|title=УИК 97. Где реестр надомного голосования?| date=18 September 2021 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7DTh-VcafSg|language=en|access-date=2021-09-24}}</ref><ref name="youtube.com">{{Citation|title=Бондаренко: выборы сфальсифицированы|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7wwQreBqlwg|language=en|access-date=2021-09-26}}</ref> The overall number of requests for remote voting became inflated. There were reports for a single district in Saratov of 5,200 votes collected remotely for 3,700 votes collected at polling stations.<ref>{{Citation|title=Саратовские кандидаты от КПРФ не признают итоги выборов в Госдуму, но это их личная позиция, точка зрения партии пока неизвестна|url=https://www.business-vector.info/saratovskie-kandidaty-ot-kprf-128455|language=en|access-date=2021-09-26}}</ref>

A remote voting procedure takes from 5 to 10 minutes, because voter's ID must be verified and due to some paperwork, and some extra time is needed for reaching the next location. One mobile group of members of election committee usually collects about 20 votes in a single trip.<ref name="youtube.com"/> A number of observers per polling station is limited by law. In order to get rid of observers, a few mobile groups of members of election committee would depart almost simultaneously. The last mobile groups would often depart without observers and would return in just two hours with over 100 ballots, which is a clear indication of fraud. Тhis violation took place on multiple polling stations.<ref name="youtube.com"/> Golos has reported over 700 possible violations related to this type of fraud.<ref>{{Citation|title=Карта нарушений на выборах 19.09.2021 #2|url=https://www.kartanarusheniy.org/2021-09-19/stat/2502966789|language=en|access-date=2021-09-25}}</ref>

===== Electronic voting =====
For the first time, the highly-controversial<ref name="DGAP2"/> remote [[electronic voting]], or E-voting, was introduced in [[2019 Moscow City Duma election]]. On 17 March 2021, the CEC has announced that at least six E-voting elections, both federal and municipal, would be held in regions, including Moscow.<ref name="DGAP2"/> E-voting was heavily used on the election days in Moscow. Even though initially considered convenient for casting votes after the election, E-voting was met with severe public criticism that followed by accusations of rigging election results,<ref name="MTY">{{cite news|date=20 September 2021|title=Russian Communist Party Says Won't Recognize Moscow E-Voting Results|work=The Moscow Times|url=https://www.themoscowtimes.com/2021/09/20/russian-communist-party-says-wont-recognize-moscow-e-voting-results-a75087|accessdate=23 September 2021}}</ref><ref name="The Economist">{{cite news|date=25 September 2021|title=How Russia's election was fixed|newspaper=The Economist|url=https://www.economist.com/europe/2021/09/25/how-russias-election-was-fixed|issn=0013-0613|accessdate=25 September 2021|archive-date=25 September 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210925005345/https://www.economist.com/europe/2021/09/25/how-russias-election-was-fixed|url-status=dead}}</ref> and the opposition parties demanding to abandon it and amend the outcome.<ref name="Meduza">{{cite news|last=Litvinovich|first=Marina|author-link=Marina Litvinovich|date=23 September 2021|title=Russian State Duma candidates form coalition for the abolition of electronic voting|website=Meduza|url=https://meduza.io/en/news/2021/09/23/russian-state-duma-candidates-form-coalition-for-the-abolition-of-electronic-voting|accessdate=23 September 2021}}</ref>

=== Candidate duplicates ===
While non-systemic opposition was largely eliminated from the elections, those candidates (mostly of [[systemic opposition]]) who were allowed to participate were targeted by various semi-legal intimidation or confusion techniques. The one includes "doppelganger candidates",{{Citation needed|date=November 2021}} where a person of similar look and surname was put on the same ballot in order to confuse voters.<ref name=":14">{{Cite news|last=Kramer|first=Andrew E.|date=2021-09-17|title=Fake Parties and Cloned Candidates: How the Kremlin 'Manages' Democracy|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/09/17/world/europe/russia-elections-interference.html|access-date=2021-09-29|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> More than 20 doppelgangers were reported.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kovalev |first=Alexey |author-link=Alexey Kovalev (journalist) |date=2021-09-16 |title=Russia's Crazy Sham Election |url=https://foreignpolicy.com/2021/09/16/russia-election-duma-putin/ |access-date=2021-11-03 |website=[[Foreign Policy]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Spoiled elections The BBC dissects the dirty tactics used to demoralize voters on both wings of Russia's 'systemic' opposition|url=https://meduza.io/en/feature/2021/09/09/spoiled-elections|access-date=2021-11-03|website=Meduza|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-07-23|title=Раздвоение пройденного|trans-title=Dichotomy of the past|url=https://www.kommersant.ru/doc/4910820|url-status=live|access-date=2021-11-03|website=www.kommersant.ru|language=ru|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210722222324/https://www.kommersant.ru/doc/4910820 |archive-date=22 July 2021 }}</ref>

=== Spoiler and fake parties ===
Putin's administrations has engineered an approach to draw away votes from seemingly genuine systemic-opposition parties and spread them among many less-known but politically crippled spoilers in order to secure the ruling party dominance.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Rise of the spoiler parties The Putin administration is building political parties to split the opposition vote. Say hello to new groups from a nationalist novelist and the product director for World of Tanks.|url=https://meduza.io/en/feature/2020/01/15/rise-of-the-spoiler-parties|access-date=2021-09-29|website=Meduza|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":16">{{Cite web|last=Light|first=Felix|date=2021-09-17|title=In Russia's Parliamentary Vote, Spoiler Parties and Dirty Tricks Abound|url=https://www.themoscowtimes.com/2021/09/17/in-russias-parliamentary-vote-spoiler-parties-and-dirty-tricks-abound-a75071|access-date=2021-09-29|website=The Moscow Times|language=en}}</ref> [[Communists of Russia]], a party created in 2009 that took part in both the [[2016 Russian legislative election|2016]] and 2021 legislative elections, was described as a spoiler whose purpose is to split votes from the [[CPRF]].<ref name=":15"/><ref>{{Cite news|title=In Time-Tested Spoiler Tactic, Russian Opposition Candidates Face Rivals With The Same Names|language=en|work=RadioFreeEurope/RadioLiberty|url=https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-elections-spoiler-tactics/31387966.html|access-date=2021-09-30}}</ref>
