==Reactions==
===Domestic===
[[Nikolai Bondarenko]], [[Saratov City Duma]] MP from the CPRF, vocal critic of the ruling party, and [[YouTube]] blogger, stated that the outcome was simply "rewritten" to the benefit of the candidate of the United Russia he ran against. He also said that his fellow allies were jailed and police has otherwise harassed them.<ref name=":12"/><ref>{{Cite web|title=Саратовский коммунист Николай Бондаренко: "Власть даже не стеснялась переписывать итоги выборов"|trans-title=Saratov communist Nikolay Bondarenko: "Authorities shamelessly rigged outcome of the elections"|url=https://saratov.mk.ru/politics/2021/09/20/saratovskiy-kommunist-nikolay-bondarenko-vlast-dazhe-ne-stesnyalas-perepisyvat-itogi-vyborov.html|url-status=live|access-date=2021-09-29|website=saratov.mk.ru|language=ru|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210929222335/https://saratov.mk.ru/politics/2021/09/20/saratovskiy-kommunist-nikolay-bondarenko-vlast-dazhe-ne-stesnyalas-perepisyvat-itogi-vyborov.html |archive-date=29 September 2021 }}</ref>

In a [[Levada Center]] poll in October 2021, 23.7% respondents described the elections as "certainly not honest", and 21.4% as "likely not honest".<ref>{{cite news|title=Опрос: рекордное число россиян считает выборы определенно нечестными|language=ru|agency=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/russian/news-58815414|access-date=6 October 2021}}</ref>

==== Protests ====
{{see also|2021 Russian election protests}}
Protests against alleged large-scale [[electoral fraud]] began in September 2021.<ref>{{Cite web|language=ru|url=https://echo.msk.ru/news/2909664-echo.html|title=После митинга КПРФ на Пушкинской площади десятки протестующих пошли к Госдуме|website=Эхо Москвы|access-date=2021-09-28}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|language=ru|url=https://kprf.ru/activity/elections/205709.html|title="За честные и чистые выборы!". Репортаж в газете "Правда"|website=kprf.ru|access-date=2021-09-28}}</ref> The [[CPRF]] stated that it did not recognize the results of electronic voting in Moscow after several of its candidates were suddenly beaten by pro-government candidates. Party leader Zyuganov called on supporters "to defend the election results like the [[Podolsk cadets]] defended Moscow." The Moscow mayoral office denied the party's requests to hold protests from the 20th, citing COVID-19 restrictions.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://tvrain.tv/news/kprf_otkazalas_priznat_rezultaty_elektronnogo_golosovanija_v_moskve-538237/|title=КПРФ отказалась признать результаты электронного голосования в Москве|agency=TV Rain|date=20 September 2021|access-date=21 September 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://tvrain.tv/news/merija_moskvy_otkazalas_soglasovat_tri_mitinga_kprf-538250/|title=Мэрия Москвы отказалась согласовать три митинга КПРФ|agency=TV Rain|date=20 September 2021|access-date=21 September 2021}}</ref> [[Sergei Udaltsov]] (the coordinator of the [[Left Front (Russia)|Left Front]] Sergei Udaltsov) and Nikolai Zubrilin (head of the CPRF fraction in the [[Moscow City Duma]]) were detained by the police.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Координатора "Левого фронта" Удальцова арестовали на десять суток|url=https://www.rbc.ru/rbcfreenews/614f0d6a9a7947156a5e5ec0|website=[[РБК]]|date=2021-09-25}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=На главу фракции КПРФ в Мосгордуме составили протокол за призывы и участие в несанкционированной акции |url=https://www.kommersant.ru/doc/5016388 |access-date=3 October 2021 |publisher=Коммерсант |date=1 October 2021 |language=ru}}</ref>

===International===
The [[Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Georgia]] condemned Russia for conducting elections in [[Abkhazia]] and [[South Ossetia|Tskhinvali]], which are occupied by Russia and referred to as the [[occupied territories of Georgia]] but internationally recognized as part of Georgia.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Ministry of Foreign Affairs releases statement on holding Russian Duma elections in occupied territories of Georgia|url=https://www.interpressnews.ge/en/article/115735-ministry-of-foreign-affairs-releases-statement-on-holding-russian-duma-elections-in-occupied-territories-of-georgia/|access-date=2021-09-23|website=www.interpressnews.ge|date=21 September 2021 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Tbilisi condemns occupied Tskhinvali's involvement in Russian parliamentary elections|url=http://www.messenger.com.ge/issues/4988_september_22_2021/4988_natalia.html|access-date=2021-09-23|website=The Messenger}}</ref>

The [[United States Department of State]] has stated<ref>{{cite web|date=21 September 2021|title=The Russian Federation's Duma Elections|url=https://www.state.gov/the-russian-federations-duma-elections/|accessdate=21 September 2021|publisher=United States Department of State}}</ref> that the election proceedings were neither free nor fair, and does not recognize results of the election that took place in the [[Crimean problem|disputed territory]] of [[Crimea]].<ref>{{cite web|date=21 September 2021|title=U.S. does not recognize Russian Duma elections on Ukraine territory -State Dept|url=https://www.euronews.com/2021/09/21/us-russia-election-usa|accessdate=21 September 2021|website=Euronews}}</ref>

The [[British foreign ministry]] stated that the elections "represent a serious step back for democratic freedoms in Russia" and that measures by Russian authorities "to marginalise civil society, silence independent media and exclude genuine opposition candidates from participating" undermined political plurality and Russia's international commitments.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-response-to-russian-state-duma-elections-20-september|title=UK response to Russian State Duma elections (20 September 2021)|website=gov.uk|date=20 September 2021}}</ref>

General elections were held in [[Sudan]] on 13–16 April 2015 to elect the [[List of heads of state of Sudan|President]] and the [[National Assembly of Sudan|National Assembly]]. They were originally scheduled for 2 April, but were delayed by eleven days.<ref>[https://www.reuters.com/article/us-sudan-election-idUSKBN0JY0J420141220 Sudan postpones April elections by 11 days: elections committee] Reuters, 20 December 2014</ref> These were the first elections to be held following the [[2011 South Sudanese independence referendum|secession]] of [[South Sudan]].<ref name ="embassy"/>

Incumbent President [[Omar al-Bashir]] won the presidential election by a [[Landslide victory|landslide]],<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-africa-32481013 |title=Omar al-Bashir wins Sudan elections by a landslide |date=27 April 2015 |publisher=BBC News |access-date=30 April 2015}}</ref> amid a boycott from the majority of the opposition. The ruling [[National Congress Party (Sudan)|National Congress Party]] of [[Sudan]] also won a majority in the 426 seats of the National Assembly.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://nec.org.sd/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/%D9%86%D8%AA%D8%A7%D8%A6%D8%AC-%D9%88-%D8%A7%D8%AD%D8%B5%D8%A7%D8%A6%D9%8A%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%AA%D8%AE%D8%A7%D8%A8%D8%A7%D8%AA-2015.pdf |title=Election results |date=27 April 2015 |language=ar |publisher=NEC |access-date=28 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518072336/http://nec.org.sd/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/%D9%86%D8%AA%D8%A7%D8%A6%D8%AC-%D9%88-%D8%A7%D8%AD%D8%B5%D8%A7%D8%A6%D9%8A%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%AA%D8%AE%D8%A7%D8%A8%D8%A7%D8%AA-2015.pdf |archive-date=2015-05-18 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Electoral system==
The President was elected using the [[two-round system]]; if no candidate gained a majority of the vote in the first round, a run-off would have been held.<ref>[http://www.electionguide.org/elections/id/2145/ Election for President] IFES</ref>

The 426 seats of the [[National Assembly of Sudan|National Assembly]] were elected by three methods:<ref name=IPU>[http://www.ipu.org/parline-e/reports/2297_B.htm Electoral system] IPU</ref>
*Half seats (50%) were elected by [[majority voting]] in multi-member constituencies based on the 18 [[States of Sudan|states]] and containing between 4 and 36 seats.
*128 seats (30%) reserved for women were elected by [[closed list]] [[proportional representation]] in a single national constituency.
*85 seats (20%) unreserved were elected by the same system.

==Conduct==
===Campaign===
Incumbent President [[Omar al-Bashir]] was re-selected as the presidential candidate of the [[National Congress Party (Sudan)|National Congress Party]] (NCP) in October 2014.<ref>[http://www.aljazeera.com/news/middleeast/2014/10/sudan-bashir-seek-re-election-2015-201410211230386761.html Sudan's Bashir to seek re-election in 2015] Al Jazeera, 21 October 2014</ref> Fifteen other candidates registered to contest the elections, although they are relatively unknown.<ref name=BBC/>

The majority of opposition parties were boycotting the elections, although a total of 44 parties put forward candidates. However, the ruling NCP opted not to field candidates in 30% of constituencies in order to allow other parties to win seats.<ref name=BBC>[https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-africa-32249860 Sudan election: Will Bashir be snubbed by his people?] BBC News, 13 April 2015</ref>

===Observers===
[[Election observer]] missions (EOM) were deployed from the [[African Union]] (AU), [[Arab League]], [[Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa]] (COMESA), [[Intergovernmental Authority on Development]] (IGAD), [[Organisation of Islamic Cooperation]] (OIC);<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.oic-oci.org/oicv2/topic/?t_id=9996&ref=3961&lan=en|title=OIC observes Presidential and Legislative Elections in the Sudan|date=21 April 2015|publisher=OIC|access-date=28 April 2015}}{{Dead link|date=June 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=no }}</ref> as well as from [[China]], [[Russia]] and [[Turkey]].<ref name="summon"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://sudanow.info.sd/west-unhappy-about-the-elections-what-do-others-say/ |title=West Unhappy About the Elections: What Do Others Say? |last1=al-Haj Hassan |first1=Abdullah |date=25 April 2015 |publisher=Sudan News Agency |access-date=28 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190213115444/http://sudanow.info.sd/west-unhappy-about-the-elections-what-do-others-say/ |archive-date=13 February 2019 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The African Union's EOM was led by former Nigerian President [[Olusegun Obasanjo]]. The AUEOM was "satisfied that voting went on peacefully" and noted that the country "still faces serious challenges to democracy building and national reconciliation". It concluded that the "results.. would reflect the expression of the will of the voters of Sudan".<ref>{{cite press release|date=16 April 2015|title=AUEOM to Sudan|url=http://pa.au.int/en/sites/default/files/Press%20Statement%20of%20the%20AUEOM%20in%20Sudan_0.pdf|publisher=African Union|access-date=2015-04-28}}{{Dead link|date=June 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=no }}</ref>

COMESA EOM noted that the "general environment within which the general elections were organized ha[d] remarkably been peaceful" and commended the Sudanese people. It also noted with concern that the "general elections were boycotted by several opposition political parties".<ref>{{cite press release |date=April 2015 |title=COMESA Election Observer Mission to the General Elections in the Republic of the Sudan|url=http://www.comesa.int/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=1480:comesa-election-observer-mission-to-the-general-elections-in-the-republic-of-the-sudan-april-2015&catid=5:latest-news&Itemid=41 |publisher=COMESA |access-date=2015-04-28}}</ref>

==Reactions==
On 9 April 2015, the [[European Union]] said that there was a "lack of a conducive environment for the upcoming elections" and that it was  disappointed that the Sudanese government missed an opportunity "by not responding to the efforts by the African Union to bring all stakeholders together."<ref>{{cite press release |date=9 April 2015 |title=Declaration by the High Representative on behalf of the European Union on the lack of a conducive environment for the upcoming elections in Sudan |url=http://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2015/04/04-declaration-hr-upcoming-elections-sudan/ |publisher=European Union |access-date=2015-04-29}}</ref>

On 20 April 2015; [[Norway]], the [[United Kingdom]] and the [[United States]] issued a joint statement saying that the Sudanese Government failed "to create a free, fair, and conducive elections environment" and that the "outcome of these elections cannot be considered a credible expression of the will of the Sudanese people".<ref>{{cite press release |date=20 April 2015 |title=Joint Statement on Elections in Sudan |url=https://www.regjeringen.no/en/aktuelt/troika_elections_Sudan/id2407289/ |publisher=[[Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Norway)]] |access-date=2015-04-29}}</ref><ref>{{cite press release |date=20 April 2015 |title=Troika statement on elections in Sudan |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/news/troika-statement-on-elections-in-sudan |publisher=[[Foreign and Commonwealth Office]] |access-date=2015-04-29}}</ref><ref>{{cite press release|date=20 April 2015|title=Joint Statement on Elections in Sudan|url=https://2009-2017.state.gov/r/pa/prs/ps/2015/04/240887.htm|publisher=[[United States Department of State]]|access-date=2015-04-28|df=dmy-all}}</ref> Following this statement, the [[Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Sudan)|Sudanese Foreign Ministry]] summoned the ambassadors from these countries and condemned the statement as "erroneous information and prejudgment of the elections"; and also deemed it as "[[wikt:flagrant|flagrant]] intervention in Sudan's internal affairs."<ref name="summon">{{cite web |url=http://news.xinhuanet.com/english/2015-04/22/c_134171501.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518140229/http://news.xinhuanet.com/english/2015-04/22/c_134171501.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=May 18, 2015 |title=Sudan summons ambassadors of Britain, Norway, U.S. over elections criticism |date=22 April 2015 |publisher= Xinhuanet|access-date=28 April 2015}}</ref> President Bashir labeled the critics as "[[Colonialism|colonialist]] parties".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://english.alarabiya.net/en/News/africa/2015/04/24/Sudan-s-Bashir-says-foreign-criticism-will-not-affect-polls-.html |title=Sudan's Bashir says foreign criticism will not affect polls |date=24 April 2015 |publisher=al Arabiya |access-date=28 April 2015}}</ref>

On 21 April 2015, the [[Embassy of Sudan, London|Sudanese Embassy]] in [[London]] issued a statement saying that other international bodies were clearly [[wikt:biased|biased]] as they refused to even send their observers and "the claim that unrest in some isolated peripheries reduces the validity of elections does not hold water; because [[Northern Ireland]] suffered serious “[[The Troubles|troubles]]” for decades and that didn't stop UK [[Elections in Northern Ireland|elections]]."<ref name ="embassy">{{cite web |url=http://www.sudantribune.com/spip.php?article54696 |title=Sudan's 2015 Elections: A huge step in democratic consolidation |date=21 April 2015 |website=sudantribune.com |publisher=[[Embassy of Sudan, London]] |access-date=28 April 2015 |archive-date=29 August 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190829002818/http://www.sudantribune.com/spip.php?article54696 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

On 28 April 2015, the [[China|Chinese]] Foreign Ministry spokesperson [[Hong Lei (politician)|Hong Lei]] said that they respect "the choice made by the Sudanese people" and congratulated President Bashir on his re-election.<ref>{{cite web |date=28 April 2015 |title= Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Hong Lei's Regular Press Conference on April 28, 2015|url=http://www.fmprc.gov.cn/mfa_eng/xwfw_665399/s2510_665401/t1258874.shtml |publisher=Ministry of Foreign Affairs |access-date=2015-04-28}}</ref>

Parliamentary elections were held in [[Senegal]] on 31 July 2022 to elect the 165 members of the [[National Assembly (Senegal)|National Assembly]]. President [[Macky Sall]]'s [[Benno Bokk Yakaar|United in Hope coalition]] remained the largest bloc in the National Assembly but lost its majority it had held since [[2012 Senegalese parliamentary election|2012]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-05-11 |title=Main Senegalese opposition coalitions unite ahead of parliamentary elections |url=https://www.africanews.com/2022/05/11/main-senegalese-opposition-coalitions-unite-ahead-of-parliamentary-elections/ |access-date=2022-05-13 |website=Africanews |language=en}}</ref>

== Electoral system ==
The 165 members of the [[National Assembly (Senegal)|National Assembly]] are elected by two methods; 112 are elected by either [[First-past-the-post voting|first-past-the-post]] or [[General ticket|party bloc vote]] in single- or multi-member constituencies based on the 46 [[Departments of Senegal|departments]], with an additional 15 elected by overseas voters.<ref name="JA">[http://www.jeuneafrique.com/462131/politique/senegal-les-electeurs-dans-lattente-des-resultats-des-legislatives/ "Sénégal : les électeurs dans l’attente des résultats des législatives"], ''Jeune Afrique'', 31 July 2017 (in French)</ref> The other 53 seats are elected from a nationwide constituency by proportional representation, with seats allocated initially using the simple quotient, with remaining seats allocated using the [[largest remainder method]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Senegal Assemblée nationale (National Assembly)|url=http://www.ipu.org/parline-e/reports/2277_B.htm|publisher=Inter-Parliamentary Union|accessdate=17 June 2017}}</ref>

==Campaign==
[[Ousmane Sonko]] was disqualified as a candidate by the Constitutional Council as a result of his arrest due to rape charges, leading to violent protests. Alongside Sonko, [[Khalifa Sall]] and [[Karim Wade]] were disqualified as candidates.<ref name="ajaz" />

Aminata Touré of the APR called on Senegalese youth to vote for her party, citing Macky Sall's work for the country.<ref name="ajaz" />

==Results==
Polls opened at 8:00 GMT and closed at 18:00 GMT on 31 July 2022. Partial results were expected to be announced on 31 July, with the provisional overall results to be announced on 5 August 2022.<ref name="ajaz">{{cite news |title=Senegal elects parliament in test for ruling party's influence |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2022/7/31/senegal-elects-parliament-in-test-for-ruling-partys-influence |access-date=1 August 2022 |work=Al Jazeera |language=en}}</ref> Women won 64 of the 165 seats, in line with the requirement of the 2010 [[gender parity]] law on [[elections in Senegal|Senegalese elections]].<ref name="BBC_SN_highest_fraction_women">{{cite Q|Q125176756|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Aftermath==
Both the [[Alliance for the Republic (Senegal)|Alliance for the Republic]] and the opposition [[Wallu Sénégal]] alongside [[Yewwi Askan Wi]] claimed victory on election night. [[Aminata Touré (Senegalese politician)|Aminata Touré]] declared that the APR had won 30 of the country's 46 departments, giving them an "unquestionable majority" without stating the number of seats won by the party.<ref name="dione">{{cite news |last1=Dione |first1=Ngouda |last2=Ba |first2=Diadie |title=Senegal's ruling party, opposition both claim victory after legislative vote |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/senegal-votes-legislators-amid-rising-political-acrimony-2022-07-31/ |access-date=1 August 2022 |work=Reuters |date=1 August 2022 |language=en}}</ref> [[Barthélémy Dias]], mayor of Dakar and member of Yewwi Askan Wi immediately disputed Touré's claims, stating "You lost this election at the national level. We will not accept it. This abuse will not pass".<ref>{{cite news |title=Senegal election: Opposition disputes ruling party's victory claim {{!}} DW {{!}} 01.08.2022 |url=https://www.dw.com/en/senegal-election-opposition-disputes-ruling-partys-victory-claim/a-62667182 |access-date=1 August 2022 |work=DW.COM}}</ref> However on 11 August both main opposition coalitions announced that they would not appeal the results, but would keep opposing Macky Sall from inside the National Assembly.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://fr.africanews.com/2022/08/11/senegal-lopposition-acceptera-les-resultats-des-legislatives/ |title=Sénégal : l'opposition acceptera les résultats des législatives |trans-title=Senegal: the opposition will accept the results of the legislative election |language=fr |date=11 August 2022 |access-date=2 September 2022 |work=[[Africanews]]}}</ref> Despite none of the coalitions obtaining a majority of the seats, an agreement over the formation of a new government was reached when Bokk Gis Gis' only elected member, [[Pape Diop]], decided to support Macky Sall, giving the presidential block a one-seat majority.<ref>{{cite web |last=Ollivier |first=Théa |url=https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2022/08/17/senegal-presidential-coalition-achieves-fragile-majority-in-the-national-assembly_5993908_4.html |title=Senegal's presidential coalition forms fragile majority in the National Assembly |date=17 August 2022 |access-date=1 September 2022 |work=[[Le Monde]]}}</ref> However, on 25 September Aminata Touré announced she would no longer sit with BBY in the Assembly, accusing President Sall of promoting Amadou Mame Diop as president of the National Assembly due to "familial ties", resulting in the government losing its majority in the chamber.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ollivier |first=Théa |date=2022-09-25 |title=Sénégal: Aminata Touré claque la porte du groupe présidentiel à l'Assemblée |url=https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20220925-s%C3%A9n%C3%A9gal-aminata-tour%C3%A9-claque-la-porte-du-groupe-pr%C3%A9sidentiel-%C3%A0-l-assembl%C3%A9e |access-date=2022-09-26 |website=RFI |language=fr}}</ref>

{{Politics of Thailand}}

General elections were held in [[Thailand]] on 14 May 2023 to elect 500 members of the [[House of Representatives (Thailand)|House of Representatives]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=20 March 2023 |title=พระราชกฤษฎีกายุบสภาผู้แทนราษฎร พ.ศ. 2566" |url=https://ratchakitcha.soc.go.th/documents/140A022N0000000000100.pdf |access-date=21 March 2023 |archive-date=20 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230320164814/https://ratchakitcha.soc.go.th/documents/140A022N0000000000100.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> The [[Move Forward Party]], led by [[Pita Limjaroenrat]], surprised analysts by winning the most seats, followed by fellow opposition party [[Pheu Thai Party|Pheu Thai]] who had won the most seats in the [[2011 Thai general election|2011]] and [[2019 Thai general election|2019]] elections. Turnout was a record 75.22%.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news |title=Election Commission says MFP won Sunday's election |language=en |work=Bangkok Post |date=15 May 2023 |url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/politics/2570334/election-commission-says-mfp-won-sundays-election |access-date=15 May 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=15 May 2023 |title=Thailand's Election Commission declares victory for Move Forward Party |url=https://www.thaipbsworld.com/thailands-election-commission-declares-victory-for-move-forward-party/ |access-date=16 May 2023 |work=Thai PBS World}}</ref>

The elections were held using a [[parallel voting]] system as in the [[1997 constitution of Thailand|1997]] and [[2007 constitution of Thailand|2007 constitutions]], in contrast to the [[Mixed-member proportional representation|mixed-member apportionment system]] used in 2019. Like in 2019, the elected prime minister did not need to be a member of the House and would be chosen by the full [[National Assembly (Thailand)|National Assembly]], including the 250 military-appointed members of the [[Senate of Thailand|Senate]], for a total 376-seat majority. Due to the structure of the National Assembly, experts had warned of a possible [[Gridlock (politics)|gridlock]] scenario in which the current opposition parties secure more than half of the House votes but are obstructed in the Senate. Additionally, the Election Commission had received criticism over untrustworthiness, unprofessionalism, and bias in its conducting of the voting process.

Sixty-seven parties vied for seats. The ruling conservative [[coalition government]] was composed of the major [[Palang Pracharath Party|Palang Pracharath]], [[Bhumjai Thai Party|Bhumjai Thai]], and [[Democrat Party (Thailand)|Democrat]] parties, and smaller parties including the new [[United Thai Nation Party]], who nominated former junta leader and incumbent prime minister [[Prayut Chan-o-cha]] after his split with Palang Pracharath. The pro-democratic opposition was led by the Pheu Thai and Move Forward parties, the latter being the effective successor of the dissolved [[Future Forward Party]], which had performed unexpectedly well in the [[2019 Thai general election|2019 election]]. Political campaigns focused on the [[Thai economy]], especially its recovery from the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Thailand|COVID-19 pandemic]]. Some parties, most notably Move Forward, also highlighted [[progressivism|progressive]] issues,<ref>{{cite news |title=Thailand's victorious progressive Move Forward Party, 7 allies agree on coalition platform |url=https://apnews.com/article/thailand-election-move-forward-coalition-parties-0380ff3fe653e1e43fcc7e0f7c3c81a1 |access-date=26 May 2023 |work=AP NEWS|first=Jintamas|last=Saksornchai |date=22 May 2023 |language=en}}</ref> and challenged long-held social norms in Thailand.

Pita's Move Forward initially formed a coalition with the other pro-democracy, anti-military parties, which had a majority in the lower house but was unable to form a government after being functionally blocked by allies of the monarchy and military in the Senate. Pheu Thai then assumed the lead, dissolving its alliance with Move Forward and allying instead with conservative, pro-military parties. It then nominated real estate tycoon [[Srettha Thavisin]] as prime minister. He was elected by Parliament on 22 August.<ref>{{cite news|first1=Sui-Lee|last1=Wee|first2=Muktita|last2=Suhartono|title=Thai Parliament Picks Real Estate Mogul as Next Prime Minister|date=21 August 2023|newspaper=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/08/21/world/asia/thailand-thaksin-prime-minister.html|access-date=23 August 2023}}</ref>

On August 7, 2024, Thailand's [[Constitutional Court of Thailand|Constitutional Court]] banned the victors of the election, the Move Forward Party and all of its leaders from politics for its proposal to reform the [[lèse-majesté in Thailand|lèse-majesté law]], arguing it posed a threat to the constitutional order.<ref name="Economist1">{{Cite news |date=7 August 2024 |title=Thailand's top court tramples over the country's democracy |newspaper=The Economist |url=https://www.economist.com/asia/2024/08/07/thailands-top-court-tramples-over-the-countrys-democracy |access-date=17 August 2024 |archive-date=16 August 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240816203416/https://www.economist.com/asia/2024/08/07/thailands-top-court-tramples-over-the-countrys-democracy |url-status=live}}</ref>

==Background==
Following a [[2013–2014 Thai political crisis|political crisis]] in [[Thailand]], the military staged [[2014 Thai coup d'état|a coup d'état in 2014]], ousting [[Yingluck cabinet|the civilian caretaker government]] of [[Yingluck Shinawatra]]. The military junta, known as the [[National Council for Peace and Order|National Council for Peace and Order (NCPO)]], rose to power under the leadership of former army chief [[Prayut Chan-o-cha]] as [[Prime Minister of Thailand|Prime Minister]]. In 2016, the NCPO completed the drafting of [[2017 constitution of Thailand|a new constitution]] and held [[2016 Thai constitutional referendum|a referendum]] to approve it. They banned criticism of the draft constitution and prohibited monitoring of the referendum. Activists against the document were arrested, detained, and prosecuted in military courts,<ref>{{cite web |date=21 June 2016 |title=Thailand: Junta Bans Referendum Monitoring |url=https://www.hrw.org/news/2016/06/21/thailand-junta-bans-referendum-monitoring |access-date=5 July 2016 |website=Human Rights Watch |location=New York |archive-date=21 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220821034003/https://www.hrw.org/news/2016/06/21/thailand-junta-bans-referendum-monitoring |url-status=live }}</ref> whilst voters who expressed their intention to vote against the draft were also arrested and prosecuted by the military regime.<ref>{{cite web |date=17 July 2016 |title=ทนายดังมอบตัวสู้คดีทำผิด พ.ร.บ. ออกเสียงประชามติ |url=http://www.matichon.co.th/news/214333 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160719161817/http://www.matichon.co.th/news/214333 |archive-date=19 July 2016 |access-date=17 July 2016 |website=Matichon Online |publisher={{Interlanguage link|มติชน|th}} |location=Bangkok |language=th}}</ref>

In 2019, after numerous delays, the junta finally held [[2019 Thai general election|a general election]] on 24 March. The elections were seen as a skewed race in which Prayut had an unfair advantage, with the [[Senate of Thailand|Senate]] wholly appointed by the junta and the constituencies redrawn last-minute.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Thai Senate to be appointed at junta's behest |url=https://asia.nikkei.com/Politics/Thai-Senate-to-be-appointed-at-junta-s-behest |access-date=18 March 2022 |website=Nikkei Asia |language=en-GB |archive-date=18 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220318053640/https://asia.nikkei.com/Politics/Thai-Senate-to-be-appointed-at-junta-s-behest |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Rojanaphruk |first1=Pravit |last2=Writer |first2=Senior Staff |date=30 November 2018 |title=Parties Fume Over New 'Gerrymandered' Electoral Map |url=https://www.khaosodenglish.com/politics/2018/11/30/parties-fume-over-gerrymandered-electoral-map/ |access-date=17 March 2022 |website=Khaosod English |language=en-US |archive-date=5 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220605103243/https://www.khaosodenglish.com/politics/2018/11/30/parties-fume-over-gerrymandered-electoral-map/ |url-status=live }}</ref> After the election, the pro-junta [[Palang Pracharath Party|Palang Pracharath party]] formed a [[coalition government]], with Prayut selected by the parliament for another term as prime minister even though his party did not win the most seats.<ref name="WSJ">[https://www.wsj.com/articles/young-harvard-educated-politician-shakes-up-thailands-old-guard-235d1f18?mod=world_lead_pos4 Young, Harvard-Educated Politician Shakes Up Thailand's Old Guard], ''The Wall Street Journal''</ref>

Prayut began his second term as prime minister on 9 June 2019.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Prayut counts on his allies |work=Bangkok Post |date=20 February 2022 |url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/politics/2266927/prayut-counts-on-his-allies |access-date=18 March 2022}}</ref> According to the current constitution, a prime minister can only serve for a maximum of eight years. However, the end of Prayut's term as the prime minister of Thailand is disputed since there are many interpretations about the beginning of his term.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last1=Bangprapa |first1=Mongkol |title=PM defies efforts to oust him from office |work=Bangkok Post |date=7 May 2022 |url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/politics/2305990/pm-defies-efforts-to-oust-him-from-office |access-date=8 May 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Rojanaphruk |first1=Pravit |last2=Writer |first2=Senior Staff |date=30 December 2021 |title=Prawit Says He's Willing to Serve With Prayut Till '2027' |url=https://www.khaosodenglish.com/politics/2021/12/30/prawit-says-hes-willing-to-serve-with-prayut-till-2027/ |access-date=18 March 2022 |website=Khaosod English |language=en-US |archive-date=8 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220408182358/https://www.khaosodenglish.com/politics/2021/12/30/prawit-says-hes-willing-to-serve-with-prayut-till-2027/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=29 December 2021 |title=ฝ่าย ก.ม. ชี้วาระ 8 ปี 'ประยุทธ์' ลากยาวได้ถึงปี 2570 |url=https://www.voicetv.co.th/read/x1s7v7AhM |access-date=18 March 2022 |website=VoiceTV |language=th |archive-date=29 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211229202436/https://voicetv.co.th/read/x1s7v7AhM |url-status=live }}</ref> On 30 September 2022, the [[Constitutional Court of Thailand|Constitutional Court]] finally ruled that Prayut's term began in 2017 along with the new constitution, meaning that he may serve as the prime minister until 2025, if he is selected by the parliament again.

The [[2020–2021 Thai protests|2020–2021 nationwide protests]] started as demonstrations against the premiership of Prayuth but later expanded to include numerous long-overlooked issues in Thai society, and unprecedented demands to reform the monarchy. The Thai royal family is protected by [[Lèse-majesté in Thailand|a lèse-majesté law]]. Even though the protests largely died down due to crackdown, repression, and COVID-19 restrictions, it was anticipated that activism could resurge in this election and afterwards.<ref>{{cite news |title=Thailand: What happened to mass anti-government protests? {{!}} DW {{!}} 19 May 2022 |url=https://www.dw.com/en/thailand-what-happened-to-mass-anti-government-protests/a-61861179 |access-date=8 June 2022 |work=DW |archive-date=5 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220605131101/https://www.dw.com/en/thailand-what-happened-to-mass-anti-government-protests/a-61861179 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The end of 2022 saw the split in the ruling Palang Pracharath Party between Prayut and his close associate [[Prawit Wongsuwon]], after the latter showed accommodation towards the main opposition [[Pheu Thai Party]]. Prayut was expected to join the new [[United Thai Nation Party]] along with his loyalists in the Palang Pracharath Party.<ref>{{cite news |title=Thai Political Parties: No Eternal Allies, No Perpetual Enemies |url=https://thediplomat.com/2022/12/thai-political-parties-no-eternal-allies-no-perpetual-enemies/ |access-date=21 December 2022 |work=The Diplomat |archive-date=21 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221221054816/https://thediplomat.com/2022/12/thai-political-parties-no-eternal-allies-no-perpetual-enemies/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Forty politicians, including 34 incumbent MPs from both coalition and opposition camps, also resigned from their parties to join [[Bhumjai Thai Party]] to increase their winning chances in this election.<ref>{{cite news |title=Former MPs jump ship, join Bhumjai Thai |url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/politics/2462152/former-mps-jump-ship-join-bhumjai-thai |access-date=21 December 2022 |work=Bangkok Post |date=16 December 2022 |language=en}}</ref> On 23 December 2022, Prayut announced his intention to apply for membership of the United Thai Nation Party, as well as becoming the party's sole prime ministerial candidate.<ref>{{Cite web |last=isarin |date=23 December 2022 |title=ด่วน ประยุทธ์ ประกาศสมัครสมาชิกพรรครวมไทยสร้างชาติ |url=https://www.prachachat.net/prachachat-top-story/news-1157022 |access-date=23 December 2022 |website=ประชาชาติธุรกิจ |language=th |archive-date=23 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221223070503/https://www.prachachat.net/prachachat-top-story/news-1157022 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Rumor of a possible coup was circulated long before the election. In September 2022, a cabinet minister, [[Chaiwut Thanakamanusorn]], warned that protesting may result in the cancellation of the election.<ref>{{Cite web |date=24 September 2022 |title="ถ้าเคลื่อนไหวมาก ระวังจะไม่ได้เลือกตั้ง" ชัยวุฒิเตือนม็อบเคลื่อนไหว วันศาล รธน. อ่านคำวินิจฉัยปม 8 ปี นายกฯ |url=https://thestandard.co/chaiwut-thanakamanusorn-240965/ |access-date=27 January 2023 |website=THE STANDARD |language=th |archive-date=27 January 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230127102229/https://thestandard.co/chaiwut-thanakamanusorn-240965/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Electoral system==
[[File:14-05-23 --- a Bangkok polling station for 2023 Thailand General Election - IMG 03.jpg|thumb|right|A polling station in [[Bangkok]] on 14 May 2023, note the two separate boxes for each of the ballots]]
Unlike the preceding [[2019 Thai general election|2019 election]], which used a form of [[mixed-member proportional representation]] with 350 constituency seats and the remaining 150 being [[levelling seat]]s, the electoral system was changed in a 2021 amendment of the constitution which restored the pre-2017 [[parallel voting]] system and removed the [[proportional representation]] mechanism.

Of the 500 members of the [[House of Representatives (Thailand)|House of Representatives]] to be elected, 400 seats were elected from single-member constituencies by [[first-past-the-post voting]] (an increase of 50), and 100 party-list seats—filled separately and no longer serving as leveling seats—are voted on in a separate ballot (unlike in the 2019 election, where only one vote was cast by each voter to determine both constituency and levelling seats).<ref>{{cite news |title=Thai Parliament passes election changes favouring ruling party |url=https://www.businesstimes.com.sg/government-economy/thai-parliament-passes-election-changes-favouring-ruling-party |access-date=26 June 2020 |work=The Business Times |date=10 September 2021 |language=en |archive-date=13 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210913082555/https://www.businesstimes.com.sg/government-economy/thai-parliament-passes-election-changes-favouring-ruling-party |url-status=live }}</ref> The change was criticised by smaller parties as the system benefits larger parties—especially the ruling Palang Pracharath Party and the main opposition party Pheu Thai, who both supported the amendment—at the expense of smaller ones, including the progressive [[Move Forward Party]], whose predecessor [[Future Forward Party|Future Forward]] performed successfully in 2019 thanks to the proportional representation system.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Yuda |first1=Masayuki |title=Thai ruling party irks progressives with electoral tweaks |url=https://asia.nikkei.com/Politics/Turbulent-Thailand/Thai-ruling-party-irks-progressives-with-electoral-tweaks |access-date=23 November 2022 |work=Nikkei Asia |date=16 September 2021 |archive-date=23 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221123102936/https://asia.nikkei.com/Politics/Turbulent-Thailand/Thai-ruling-party-irks-progressives-with-electoral-tweaks |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Prime ministerial candidates ===
The process of selecting a prime minister is still the same as the preceding 2019 election under the [[Constitution of Thailand|2017 Thai constitution]]. Prime ministers may only be chosen from a pre-declared list of candidates. Each party may submit up to three names and must have at least 5% (25 members) in the House of Representatives to receive eligibility. Candidates do not have to be a [[member of parliament]] (MP).

Parliament's vote for prime minister will take place in a joint session with the 250-seat [[Senate of Thailand|Senate]] appointed by the junta, according to the constitution's provisional terms. In 2019, all the senators unanimously voted for then-junta leader Prayut.<ref>{{Cite web |date=5 June 2019 |title=Thailand's military-backed PM voted in after junta creates loose coalition |url=http://www.theguardian.com/world/2019/jun/05/thailand-military-backed-pm-prayuth-chan-ocha-voted-in-after-junta-creates-loose-coalition |access-date=27 January 2023 |website=the Guardian |language=en |archive-date=7 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230407035757/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2019/jun/05/thailand-military-backed-pm-prayuth-chan-ocha-voted-in-after-junta-creates-loose-coalition |url-status=live }}</ref> As the term of the NCPO-appointed Senate lasts until 2024, it is expected to exert influence into this election as well.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Thongnoi |first1=Jitsiree |last2=Jaipragas |first2=Bhavan |title=Thai election a battle royale for junta's Prayuth and the Shinawatras |url=https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/article/3002722/explained-thailands-election-battle-royale-juntas-prayuth-chan |access-date=26 June 2020 |work=South China Morning Post |date=22 March 2019 |language=en |archive-date=28 June 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200628112658/https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/article/3002722/explained-thailands-election-battle-royale-juntas-prayuth-chan |url-status=live }}</ref>

Due to this rule, the anti-junta camp had to secure at least 376 votes in order to select their candidates,<ref name="WSJ"/> while a simple majority in the House could still result in a candidate from the pro-junta coalition winning the selection. If no candidates secured at least 376 votes in the Parliament, it could lead to a deadlock<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/thailand-pro-democracy-candidates-push-to-break-military-grip-in-election-f44a367f?mod=article_inline|title=Thai Voters Back Pro-Democracy Parties in Blow to Military|work=The Wall Street Journal|first=Feliz|last=Solomon|date=14 May 2023|access-date=3 June 2023}}</ref> and pave the way for a person not in the parties' list of candidates becoming prime minister as written in the Constitution. Such a scenario led some to call for [[strategic voting]] for larger anti-junta parties most likely to win in each constituency.

===2022 reapportionment and redistricting===
Due to the increase of the number of members of the House of Representatives elected from single-member constituencies from 350 to 400, a reapportionment of seats and redrawing of electoral boundaries was required. On 1 February 2022, the [[Election Commission of Thailand|Election Commission]] announced its calculations that, from the total registered population of 66,171,439 as of 31 December 2021, there must be 1 member per 165,429 people. This distribution is subject to the approval of the organic law bills currently being considered by the National Assembly.<ref>{{Cite web |title=เปิดจำนวน ส.ส. 400 เขตเลือกตั้งใหม่ กทม.ยังมากสุด 33 คน |url=https://workpointtoday.com/politics-electorate/ |access-date=23 October 2022 |website=workpointTODAY |language=th |archive-date=14 January 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230114211905/https://workpointtoday.com/politics-electorate/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:Map of Bangkok's 28th District for the 2023 Thai General Election.svg|thumb|Some voting districts drawn by the Election Commission, such as Bangkok's 28th district shown above, were atypically composed of various parts of different ''[[List of districts of Bangkok|khet]]''; the commission was accused of [[gerrymandering]].]]

The Election Commission had just finished drawing electoral boundaries in February 2023—just three months before the election, while many candidates had already begun campaigning. The original drawing was challenged in the Constitutional Court as the Commission included non-citizens in the calculation. The Court struck down the drawing, prompting the commission to revise and present another boundary drawing. The second drawing was also challenged in the administrative courts amid the accusation of [[gerrymandering]] by the commission, but the court eventually ruled the drawing was legal in April 2023.<ref>{{cite news |title=ศาลปกครองสูงสุด 'ยกฟ้อง' คดี 'อรรถวิชช์' ฟ้อง กกต. แบ่งเขตเลือกตั้ง ชี้ ชอบด้วยกฎหมาย |url=https://prachatai.com/journal/2023/04/103540 |access-date=10 April 2023 |work=Prachatai |language=th |archive-date=10 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230410153640/https://prachatai.com/journal/2023/04/103540 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Leading up to the election==
Since late 2022, ex-politician [[Chuwit Kamolvisit]] began attacking Prayut whose relative was allegedly linked to Chinese nationals involving drug, gambling and money laundering.<ref>{{cite web|title=China's triads and corrupt Thai cops undermined national security|date=13 March 2023|work=Thai PBS World|url=https://www.thaipbsworld.com/chinas-triads-and-corrupt-thai-cops-undermined-national-security/|access-date=16 May 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Ex-junta leader morphs into political party member|date=10 January 2023|work=Prachatai English|url=https://prachataienglish.com/node/10176|access-date=16 May 2023}}</ref> He later turned to Bhumjai Thai Party, accusing it of corruption regarding [[Orange Line (Bangkok)|Orange Line]] rapid transit planning and promoting unrestricted use of marijuana.<ref>{{cite web|first=Joseph|last=O' Connor|title=Anutin rejects Chuwit's claims about Bangkok's mass transit Orange line and Bhumjai Thai's election odds|date=25 February 2023|url=https://www.thaiexaminer.com/thai-news-foreigners/2023/02/25/anutin-plays-down-chuwit-corruption-claims-orange-line-bangkok/|work=Thai Examiner|access-date=16 May 2023}}</ref>

In January 2023, two youth political activists began a hunger strike calling for the release of political prisoners detained before trial. Many of them were charged with lèse-majesté, which led to another debate on amending or cancellation of the law. Political parties were asked for their stance on the issue.<ref>{{cite web|first=Kaweewit|last=Kaewjinda|title=Thai women activists end hunger strike, vow to keep up fight|date=March 11, 2023|publisher=The Associated Press|url=https://apnews.com/article/thailand-hunger-strike-monarchy-protesters-9d3cb002fc034a8f79ccdd10f667b18a|access-date=16 May 2023}}</ref>

Beginning in January 2023, many civil society organizations called for volunteers to keep their eyes on the election process, citing the untrustworthiness of the Election Commission and its decision not to report the election result in real-time.<ref>{{cite news|title=100,000 volunteers to monitor vote count in upcoming election|date=2 March 2023|work=The Bangkok Post|url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/politics/2518176/100-000-volunteers-to-monitor-vote-count-in-upcoming-election|access-date=16 May 2023}}</ref> As of March 2023, the movement had grown to 50 organizations, including media, who declared they would report the unofficial election result when the commission would not.<ref>{{cite web|title=Media Outlets Form Alliance on Election Results Coverage|date=27 March 2023|publisher=National News Bureau of Thailand|url=https://thainews.prd.go.th/en/news/detail/TCATG230327104419006|access-date=16 May 2023}}</ref>

On 20 March 2023, the House of Representatives was dissolved—three days before the term ended. Due to a legal technicality, the election date was postponed for another week from 7 May 2023. The move also allowed politicians more time to switch parties, which many analysts interpreted as the real motive behind it. Some commentators also noticed that the election day was set during the period of university exams and after a long holiday which could make voting inconvenient for a lot of Thais who have to return to vote in their constituencies.<ref>{{cite news |title=The 2023 General Election in Thailand: Possible Scenarios {{!}} Heinrich Böll Stiftung |url=https://www.boell.de/en/2023/05/09/2023-general-election-thailand-possible-scenarios |access-date=9 May 2023 |work=Heinrich-Böll-Stiftung |language=en |archive-date=9 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230509170212/https://www.boell.de/en/2023/05/09/2023-general-election-thailand-possible-scenarios |url-status=live }}</ref>

In March 2023, a group of hackers posted the personal data of 55 million Thais for sale online. The group called 9Near with a symbol resembling that of the Move Forward Party, also mentioned on their page: "Almost election, choose wisely."<ref>{{cite news |title=GOV'T BLOCKS WEBSITE THAT THREATENS TO LEAK PERSONAL DATA OF 55 MILLION THAIS |url=https://www.khaosodenglish.com/news/crimecourtscalamity/2023/04/01/govt-blocks-website-that-threatens-to-leak-personal-data-of-55-million-thais/ |access-date=1 April 2023 |work=Khaosod English |archive-date=1 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230401080410/https://www.khaosodenglish.com/news/crimecourtscalamity/2023/04/01/govt-blocks-website-that-threatens-to-leak-personal-data-of-55-million-thais/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In May, ex-prime minister [[Thaksin Shinawatra]] tweeted that he was ready to return to Thailand before July 2023 and "enter the legal process". He faced possible prison time from prior convictions.<ref>{{cite news |title=Thaksin wants to come home, 'enter legal process' |url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/politics/2566509/thaksin-wants-to-come-home-enter-legal-process |access-date=9 May 2023 |work=Bangkok Post |date=9 May 2023 |language=en}}</ref>

The Thai economy was still recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic, but it was still struggling with multiple issues, including high energy and electricity costs, the number of employers still fewer than before the pandemic, rising household debts, and falling income growth. Other economic issues such as minimum wage, farm subsidies, and welfare were considered top voting issues. Most political parties campaigned on subsidies and tax exemptions.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Chandran |first1=Nyshka |title=Thailand election: Campaign freebies may be a 'band-aid solution' with fiscal risks |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2023/05/09/thai-polls-economic-populism-takes-center-stage-in-upcoming-election.html |access-date=9 May 2023 |work=CNBC |language=en |archive-date=9 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230509021326/https://www.cnbc.com/2023/05/09/thai-polls-economic-populism-takes-center-stage-in-upcoming-election.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Contesting parties ==

==Overseas and advanced voting==
More than 2 million Thais registered for advance voting, while other 100,000 people registered to vote from overseas.<ref>{{cite news |title=Advance voters queue nationwide as temperatures soar |url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/politics/2565159/advance-voters-queue-nationwide-as-temperatures-soar |access-date=9 May 2023 |work=Bangkok Post |date=7 May 2023 |language=en}}</ref> Thailand's Ministry of Foreign Affairs reported that around 80% of the eligible overseas voters had done so.<ref>{{cite news |title=Overseas voting almost done |url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/politics/2563511/overseas-voting-almost-done |access-date=9 May 2023 |work=Bangkok Post |date=5 May 2023 |language=en}}</ref> Even with high temperatures, some districts still expected a 90% turnout.<ref>{{cite news |title=Big turnout at polling stations for advance voting in Thailand's general election |url=https://www.thaipbsworld.com/big-turnout-at-polling-stations-for-advance-voting-in-thailands-general-election/ |access-date=9 May 2023 |work=Thai PBS World |archive-date=9 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230509163424/https://www.thaipbsworld.com/big-turnout-at-polling-stations-for-advance-voting-in-thailands-general-election/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

The Election Commission's conduct of advance voting drew sharp criticism from the public, especially from numerous cases of incorrect information on ballot envelops. Chuvit Kamolvisit also pointed out irregularities in some Northeastern provinces where unusually high number of voters voted in advance and there were reports of collection of ID cards. More than a million people also signed an [[online petition]] to oust the Election Commission.<ref>{{cite news |title=EC vows poll will be error-free |url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/politics/2566005/ec-vows-poll-will-be-error-free |access-date=9 May 2023 |work=Bangkok Post |date=9 May 2023 |language=en}}</ref>

== Results ==
{{Main|Results of the 2023 Thai general election}}
[[File:Pita celebrating 2023 election victory.png|thumb|[[Pita Limjaroenrat]] of the [[Move Forward Party]] at a press conference declaring victory the day after the election.]]
Final results were announced on 25 May.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=#BREAKING: @EctThailand has released the FINAL OFFICIAL results of #ThaiElection23. |url=https://twitter.com/SaksithCNA/status/1661649873719160833 | author = Saksith Saiyasombut |access-date=2023-05-25 |website=Twitter |language=en}}</ref> The Election Commission endorsed all 500 MPs on 20 June; 67 parties won seats. While there were media reports that 71 MPs-elect in 37 constituencies received election fraud complaints, the commission decided to endorse all the MPs-elect to avoid rushing investigations. They have up to one year to investigate complaints after receiving them.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Sattaburuth |first1=Aekarach |title=MPs endorsed, House to convene within 15 days|date=20 June 2023|work=Bangkok Post|url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/politics/2595144/mps-endorsed-house-to-convene-within-15-days|access-date=20 June 2023}}</ref>

[[File:2023 Thai general election result by camps.svg|thumb|right|350px|Total seats of pro/anti-junta parties]]

The [[Move Forward Party]] won the most seats with 151, including sweeping all but one of Bangkok's seats, outperforming another opposition party, [[Pheu Thai Party|Pheu Thai]], which was considered the frontrunner.<ref name=":1" /> Analysts saw this as a significant political shift, and Move Forward supporters called the results a "wind of change" and the "dawn of a new era".<ref>{{cite news |date=14 May 2023 |title=Thailand elections: Voters deliver stunning win for reform |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-65567781 |access-date=15 May 2023}}</ref> This also broke Pheu Thai's run of being the party with the most MPs since 2001 (including its predecessors, the [[People's Power Party (Thailand)|People's Power Party]] and [[Thai Rak Thai Party]]).<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ratcliffe |first1=Rebecca |date=15 May 2023 |title=Thailand election 2023: opposition delivers crushing blow to military rule |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/may/15/thailand-election-2023-national-elections-opposition-parties-crushing-blow-military-rule-junta |url-status=live |access-date=15 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230514234106/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/may/15/thailand-election-2023-national-elections-opposition-parties-crushing-blow-military-rule-junta |archive-date=14 May 2023}}</ref>

The two main parties connected to the former [[National Council for Peace and Order|military junta]], the [[Palang Pracharath Party]] and its split-off [[United Thai Nation Party]]<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wongcha-um |first1=Panu |last2=Thepgumpanat |first2=Panarat |date=15 May 2023 |title=Thailand opposition crushes military parties in election rout |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/old-rivalries-new-battle-thailand-goes-polls-2023-05-13/ |access-date=16 May 2023 |publisher=Reuters}}</ref> lost half their seats compared to Palang Pracharath's result in 2019. The [[Democrat Party (Thailand)|Democrat Party]], a junior coalition partner, also lost over half its seats. Bhumjai Thai was the only coalition party which gained seats in this election.

Analysts were surprised at Move Forward's performance. It was attributed to a desire for change, dissatisfaction of the Prayuth premiership, and a reluctance to vote for the formerly dominant Pheu Thai. Move Forward's distinctive commitment to reforming the country's [[Lèse-majesté in Thailand|lèse-majesté law]] could also have been an issue that influenced voters.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ratcliffe |first1=Rebecca |date=15 May 2023 |title=Thai election may be turning point as taboo over monarchy fades |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/may/15/thai-election-may-be-turning-point-as-taboo-over-monarchy-fades |access-date=16 May 2023}}</ref> Napon Jatusripitak, a Thai political scientist at the [[ISEAS–Yusof Ishak Institute]], opined that this election indexed a readiness in the country to transcend past political divides and to instead focus on structural reforms "concerning the role of traditional power centers in Thailand".<ref name="DW">{{cite news |title=Thai election: Big win for opposition, but uncertainty looms |language=en |work=DW |url=https://www.dw.com/en/thai-election-big-win-for-opposition-but-uncertainty-looms/a-65628441 |access-date=16 May 2023}}</ref>

With a two-ballot system reinstated in 2021,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-09-10 |title=Thai Parliament approves election system charter change |url=https://apnews.com/article/elections-thailand-constitutions-constitutional-amendments-bangkok-a5fa157501efd0ad115b8211f59f578a |access-date=2025-04-28 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref> vote-splitting led to 186 constituencies having different party-vote winners and constituency winners. The Move Forward Party, Pheu Thai, and United Thai Nation all had higher party votes than constituency votes,<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |date=2023-07-28 |title=One Constituency, Two Parties: Ballot Splitting and Divided Loyalties in Thailand's Election |url=https://fulcrum.sg/one-constituency-two-parties-ballot-splitting-and-divided-loyalties-in-thailands-election/ |access-date=2025-04-28 |website=FULCRUM |language=en-US}}</ref> and were the only party vote winner in all the provinces (excluding [[Pattani province|Pattani]], [[Yala province|Yala]] and [[Narathiwat province|Narathiwat]] where Prachachart won the party vote). Various ''baan yai'' parties ("Big House", wealthy and influential political families in various provinces<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-02-18 |title=Outcome of Recent Thai Provincial Elections Heralds Tighter Race in Next General Election |url=https://fulcrum.sg/outcome-of-recent-thai-provincial-elections-heralds-tighter-race-in-next-general-election/ |access-date=2025-04-28 |website=FULCRUM |language=en-US}}</ref>) and junta support parties managed to win local seats even while those same local seats gave their party vote to Move Forward. The Move Forward Party won the party vote in 34 Bhumjaithai, 23 Palang Pracharath, and 13 United Thai Nation seats, along with entrenched dynasties retaining local seats in Suphanburi, Buriram, Petchabun, Kamphaeeng Phet, and Uthai Thani.<ref name=":4" /> Considering that some dynasties such as the Pitutecha Clan (Democrat Party) in Rayong, along with dynasties in Samut Prakan and Chon Buri lost all their seats, Mathis Lohatepanont and Napon Jatusripitak believe this vote splitting is not a sign of strength for the ''baan yai'', but a struggle for survival against the popularity of the Move Forward Party.<ref name=":4" />

==Government formation==
===<span class="anchor" id="Move Forward-led coalition"></span>Move Forward–led coalition===
The Move Forward party leader [[Pita Limjaroenrat]] announced a six-party alliance with four former opposition parties—Pheu Thai, [[Thai Sang Thai Party|Thai Sang Thai]], [[Prachachart Party|Prachachat]] and the [[Thai Liberal Party]]—and one new party, the Fair Party.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Setboonsarng |first1=Chayut |last2=Wongcha-um |first2=Panu |date=15 May 2023 |title=Thai opposition parties agree to coalition after election success |language=en |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/deals-be-done-thai-opposition-parties-look-form-government-2023-05-15/ |access-date=15 May 2023}}</ref><ref name=bkkpost_15052023>{{cite news|last1=Wipatayotin |first1=Apinya |title=Pita declares six-party coalition with 309 MPs|date=15 May 2023|work=Bangkok Post|url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/politics/2571024/pita-declares-six-party-coalition-with-309-mps|access-date=16 May 2023}}</ref> The coalition would include 310 MPs,<ref name="auto">{{cite news|title=More senators back Pita's bid to be prime minister|date=19 May 2023|work=English|url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/politics/2573517/more-senators-back-pitas-bid-to-be-prime-minister|access-date=20 May 2023}}</ref> more than enough for a majority government in the House of Representatives.<ref>{{cite web|first=Kiki|last=Siregar|title=FAQ: What is the state of play in Thailand as Move Forward attempts to form the government?|work=Channel News Asia|url=https://www.channelnewsasia.com/asia/thailand-election-2023-pita-limjaroenrat-politics-state-play-faq-3489371|access-date=16 May 2023}}</ref> It later grew to eight parties (with Pheu Thai Ruam Palang and the New Social Power Party joining), accounting to 313 MPs.<ref>{{cite news |title=Pita announces 8-party coalition plan |url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/politics/2573332/pita-announces-8-party-coalition-plan |access-date=24 May 2023 |work=Bangkok Post |date=18 May 2023 |language=en}}</ref> On 22 May, the eight parties signed a historic [[memorandum of understanding]] listing 23 policies they agreed on, including restoration of democracy, enacting marriage equality law, and reformation of the security and justice system. However, the issue of lèse-majesté was left out.<ref>{{cite news |title=Thailand Opposition Signs Coalition Agreement, Pledges to Restore Democracy |url=https://www.voanews.com/a/thailand-opposition-signs-coalition-agreement-pledges-to-restore-democracy-/7104063.html |access-date=24 May 2023 |work=VOA |date=22 May 2023 |language=en}}</ref>

Pita needed 376 votes from the complete [[National Assembly (Thailand)|National Assembly]] to be voted prime minister.<ref name=bkkpost_15052023/> Due to the foreseeable gridlock that no senators would vote for a Pita premiership, some started to see Bhumjai Thai, which finished third in the election, a "kingmaker" and allying itself with Move Forward–led coalition, but during campaigning its leader Anutin had ruled out an alliance with parties that seek to reform the lèse-majesté law.<ref>{{cite magazine |title=The Voting in Thailand's Election Is Finished, But the Politicking Is Just Beginning|url=https://time.com/6279758/thailand-elections-move-forward-party-pheu-thai/ |access-date=3 June 2023 |magazine=Time|first=Charlie|last=Campbell |date=15 May 2023 |language=en}}</ref> Some senators said that they would not automatically vote for Pita, while stating that they had the country's best interests at heart;<ref>{{cite news |last1=Bangprapa |first1=Mongkol |title=Senators: PM votes unbiased and in country's best interest |language=en |work=Bangkok Post |date=14 May 2023 |url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/politics/2569862/senators-pm-votes-unbiased-and-in-countrys-best-interest |access-date=16 May 2023}}</ref> however, 15 senators were reportedly gearing to back his bid to be prime minister.<ref name="auto"/> Civil society also began pressuring senators to vote for Pita,<ref>{{cite news |title=Thai senators come under pressure over PM vote |work=Thai PBS World |url=https://www.thaipbsworld.com/thai-senators-come-under-pressure-over-pm-vote/ |access-date=16 May 2023}}</ref> and, on 23 May, organized a rally near the parliament.<ref>{{cite news |title=Move Forward supporters rally to persuade senators to vote for Pita |url=https://www.thaipbsworld.com/move-forward-supporters-rally-to-persuade-senators-to-vote-for-pita/ |access-date=24 May 2023 |work=Thai PBS World}}</ref>

Apart from the full parliament prime minister vote, there was much anxiety of a possible dissolution of the Move Forward party or court rulings against it — the same fate as its predecessor, the Future Forward party. Pita was also accused of owning shares in [[ITV (Thailand)|ITV]], a de-listed television broadcaster since 2008, which could disqualify him from being an MP.<ref name=DW/> After the election, there was a conflict between Move Forward and Pheu Thai over the House speaker seat.<ref>{{cite news |title=Pheu Thai claims House speaker's position |url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/politics/2577580/pheu-thai-claims-house-speakers-position |access-date=29 May 2023 |work=Bangkok Post |date=24 May 2023 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Pita Urges Unity After Thai Coalition Squabbles Over House Speaker Job |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2023-05-26/pita-urges-unity-after-thai-coalition-squabbles-over-house-speaker-job#xj4y7vzkg |access-date=29 May 2023 |work=Bloomberg|first=Patpicha|last=Tanakasempipat |date=26 May 2023 |language=en}}</ref> Some self-proclaimed Pheu Thai supporters also urged their party to leave the Move Forward–led coalition.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Connor |first1=Mitch |title=Pheu Thai supporters urge split from MFP amid House speaker rift |url=https://thethaiger.com/news/national/pheu-thai-supporters-urge-split-from-mfp-amid-house-speaker-rift |access-date=29 May 2023 |work=Thaiger |date=29 May 2023 |language=en}}</ref> Rumors that Pheu Thai could join the old coalition parties from before the election persisted.<ref>{{cite news |title=Thaksin 'flabbergasted' by Chuvit's secret-coalition claim |url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/politics/2580670/thaksin-flabbergasted-by-chuvits-secret-coalition-claim |access-date=29 May 2023 |work=Bangkok Post |language=en}}</ref> The [[Royal Thai Armed Forces]] pledged to respect the results of the general election and not launch a coup.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2023-05-12 |title=Thai Military Rules Out Coup After Election as Campaigning Ends |language=en |work=Bloomberg.com |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2023-05-12/thai-military-rules-out-coup-after-election-as-campaigning-ends |access-date=2023-05-17}}</ref>

On 3 July, the new parliament was opened by [[Vajiralongkorn|King Rama X]], and the coalition agreed to [[Wan Muhamad Noor Matha]] of the [[Prachachat Party]] to be nominated as speaker, paving the way for government formation. Wan previously served as Speaker from 1996 to 2000.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/politics/2604481/move-forward-pheu-thai-clinch-house-speaker-compromise|title=Move Forward, Pheu Thai clinch House speaker compromise|newspaper=Bangkok Post |date=3 July 2023 }}</ref>

On 13 July, the government formation was blocked, as Pita's coalition failed to gain the requisite 375 votes in parliament. While 324 members of parliament voted in favor, 182 voted against and 199 abstained.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/jul/13/winning-thailand-candidate-for-pm-blocked-from-power-pita-limjaroenrat|title=Thailand's winning candidate for PM blocked from power|first1=Rebecca|last1=Ratcliffe|first2=Navaon|last2=Siradapuvadol|work=[[The Guardian]]|location=[[Bangkok]]|date=13 July 2023|access-date=13 July 2023}}</ref> Most of the [[Senate of Thailand|junta-appointed senators]] refused to endorse Pita for [[Prime Minister of Thailand|Prime Minister]], leading to protest and criticism.<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=2023-07-13 |title=Thai Parliament Blocks Pita in First Round of Prime Minister Selection |url=https://time.com/6294351/thailand-prime-minister-parliament-vote-pita/ |access-date=2023-07-13 |magazine=Time |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Ratcliffe |first1=Rebecca |last2=Siradapuvadol |first2=Navaon |date=2023-07-13 |title=Thailand's winning candidate for PM blocked from power |language=en-GB |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/jul/13/winning-thailand-candidate-for-pm-blocked-from-power-pita-limjaroenrat |access-date=2023-07-13 |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>
