{{legend0|#F48984|Republican hold}} {{legend0|#CA0120 |Republican gain}} }} The '''2024 United States House of Representatives elections''' were held on November 5, 2024, to elect the 435 representatives of the [[United States House of Representatives]], as well as 6 [[Non-voting members of the United States House of Representatives|non-voting delegates]] from the [[District of Columbia]] and inhabited [[Insular area|U.S. territories]]. The elections were held together with other federal, state, and local elections, including the [[2024 United States presidential election|U.S. presidential election]] and [[2024 United States Senate elections|elections to the Senate]], as part of the [[2024 United States elections|2024 United States general election]]. The winners of these elections serve in the [[119th United States Congress]], with seats apportioned among states based on the [[2020 United States census]]. The [[House Republican Conference]] has been led by [[Mike Johnson]] since October 2023, following the [[removal of Kevin McCarthy as Speaker of the House]] and the [[October 2023 Speaker of the United States House of Representatives election|speaker election]] that Johnson won. He is the first congressman from [[Louisiana]] to be elected Speaker of the House.{{cite news |last=Hilburn |first=Greg |title=Mike Johnson makes history as Louisiana's first speaker of the House of Representatives |url=https://www.shreveporttimes.com/story/news/2023/10/25/mike-johnson-makes-history-as-louisianas-first-speaker-of-the-house-of-representatives/71313528007/ |access-date=November 2, 2023 |work=[[The Times (Shreveport, Louisiana)|Shreveport Times]] |date=October 25, 2023}} With the election of [[Hakeem Jeffries]] as leader of the [[House Democratic Caucus]], this was the first House election since [[2002 United States House of Representatives elections|2002]] in which the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] was not led by [[Nancy Pelosi]]. Jeffries is the first [[List of African-American United States representatives|African American]] in the history of Congress to serve as leader of either party, and the first congressman from New York to do so since [[Bertrand Snell]]'s retirement in [[1938 United States House of Representatives elections|1938]].{{cite web |title=House Democrats elect Hakeem Jeffries as Congress' first black party leader |first=Nolan D. |last=McCaskill |date=November 30, 2022 |access-date=December 1, 2022 |location=[[Washington, D.C.|Washington]] |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |url=https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2022-11-30/house-democrats-elect-jeffries-as-congress-first-black-party-leader |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221130195253/https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2022-11-30/house-democrats-elect-jeffries-as-congress-first-black-party-leader |archive-date=November 30, 2022}} The election was expected to be highly competitive, with forecasts suggesting less than a five-seat difference between the two parties.{{cite web|url=https://www.270towin.com/2024-house-election/consensus-2024-house-forecast | title = 2024 House Election: Consensus Forecast| access-date = February 5, 2024 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240206045000/https://www.270towin.com/2024-house-election/consensus-2024-house-forecast | archive-date = February 6, 2024 | website= [[270toWin]] }} Events that have occurred during the 118th Congress include the [[January 2023 Speaker of the United States House of Representatives election|January 2023 speakership election]], the [[2023 debt-ceiling crisis]], the [[Removal of Kevin McCarthy as Speaker of the House|removal of Kevin McCarthy from the speakership]], the ensuing [[October 2023 Speaker of the United States House of Representatives election|October 2023 speakership election]], and the [[expulsion of George Santos]]. No party has lost House control after a single congressional term since [[1954 United States House of Representatives elections|1954]]. The Republicans, led by incumbent Speaker [[Mike Johnson]], narrowly maintained control of the House with a small majority of 220 seats (the narrowest [[1930 United States House of Representatives elections|since 1930]]), winning the House popular vote by 4 million votes and a narrow margin of 2.6%.{{cite web|title=Party Divisions of the House of Representatives, 1789 to Present|work=US House of Representatives: History, Art & Archives|url=https://history.house.gov/Institution/Party-Divisions/Party-Divisions/|access-date=December 4, 2024}}{{cite web |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2024-elections/house-results |title=2024 House Results: Republicans keep control |website=NBC News |date=November 13, 2024 |access-date=November 13, 2024}} This resulted in the smallest Republican majority since [[2000 United States House of Representatives elections|2000]]. Democrats made a net gain of 1 seat from the Republicans, which represents the smallest net change in US history in the House of Representatives.{{efn|This does not include the [[2024 New York's 3rd congressional district special election]], which Democrats picked up in February 2024 and held in November.}} The majority was decided by just over 7,000 votes across three congressional districts ([[Iowa's 1st congressional district|Iowa's 1st]], [[Colorado's 8th congressional district|Colorado's 8th]], and [[Pennsylvania's 7th congressional district|Pennsylvania's 7th]]) out of nearly 148 million cast in these elections;{{cite tweet|url=https://x.com/Redistrict/status/1866528527287292405|last=Wasserman|first=Dave|user=Redistrict|number=1866528527287292405|date=December 10, 2024|title=Fact: in 2024, the House majority was decided by just 7,309 votes across three districts (#IA01, #CO08 and #PA07) out of 148 million votes cast nationwide.|accessdate=December 13, 2024}} this was a roughly 2-point bias in favor of Democrats, resulting from Democratic outperformance in swing districts. Despite the Democratic overperformance, the results gave Republicans a [[government trifecta]] for the first time since the [[115th United States Congress|115th Congress]], after the [[2016 United States House of Representatives elections|2016 election]]. These elections marked the first time since [[2016 United States House of Representatives elections|2016]] where Republicans won a majority of the congressional delegation in Pennsylvania and Michigan.{{Cite web |date=2024-11-07 |title=GOP flips 2 US House seats in Pennsylvania, as Republican Scott Perry wins again |url=https://apnews.com/article/pennsylvania-congress-2024-election-perry-mackenzie-bresnahan-3c79f724690fb734cdcc921512165b72 |access-date=2024-11-08 |website=[[Associated Press News]] |language=en}}{{Cite web |last=LeBlanc |first=Melissa Nann Burke, Grant Schwab, Luke Ramseth and Beth |title=Michigan gets two new U.S. House members as Republicans pick up a seat |url=https://www.detroitnews.com/story/news/politics/elections/2024/11/06/michigan-congress-tom-barrett-kristen-mcdonald-rivet-john-james-marlinga-hertel-junge/76098891007/ |access-date=2024-11-08 |website=[[The Detroit News]] |language=en-US}} They also marked the first time since [[2008 United States House of Representatives elections|2008]] in which Democrats won more than one seat in Alabama, and the first time since [[2006 United States House of Representatives elections|2006]] when Democrats won more than one seat in Louisiana. However, both cases were due to new seats created by redistricting.{{Cite web |last=Hagan |first=Victor |title=Democrat Shomari Figures wins Alabama's redrawn 2nd Congressional District |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/elections/2024/11/06/alabama-house-election-shomari-figures/76085783007/ |access-date=2024-11-08 |website=[[USA TODAY]] |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=Ballard |first=Mark |date=2024-11-05 |title=Cleo Fields returns to Congress, along with Louisiana's five incumbent House members |url=https://www.nola.com/news/politics/elections/cleo-fields-and-louisianas-incumbent-house-members-win/article_94dba5ee-9b19-11ef-999f-137314ce5a9e.html |access-date=2024-11-08 |website=[[The Times-Picayune/The New Orleans Advocate]] |language=en}} These elections saw Republicans win the majority of congressional districts in 30 states while the Democrats won a majority in 18 states. Two states (Colorado and Minnesota) elected a split house delegation. [[Sarah McBride]] of Delaware became the [[List of LGBTQ members of the United States Congress|first openly transgender member]] elected to the [[United States Congress]].{{cite news|title=Sarah McBride becomes first transgender person elected to US Congress|url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/politics/sarah-mcbride-becomes-first-transgender-person-elected-to-us-congress/ar-AA1tA7lO?ocid=BingNewsVerp|newspaper=[[USA Today]]|date=November 6, 2024|access-date=November 7, 2024}} This was the third presidential election cycle in a row in which the victorious presidential party lost seats in the House while holding its majority. == Electoral system == Forty-six states used the [[first-past-the-post voting]] plurality-win system to elect their representatives. [[Instant-runoff voting]] was used in two states (Alaska and Maine), and the [[Two-round system|runoff system]] was used in two states (Georgia and Louisiana).{{Citation needed|date=January 2026}} == Results == === Federal === The 2024 election results are compared below to the 2022 election. In 2024, most states used the same districts created in the [[2020 United States redistricting cycle|redistricting cycle following the 2020 census]], which were first used in the 2022 elections. However, maps have changed or would change in several states, often due to legal challenges made on the basis of political or racial gerrymandering. As of May 2024, several states have seen challenges to their [[List of United States congressional districts|congressional district]] maps that were put in place during the [[2020 United States redistricting cycle|redistricting cycle]] brought upon by the results of the 2020 census. In [[2024 United States House of Representatives elections in Alabama|Alabama]], a [[special master]] drew a new map after the [[Alabama Legislature|state legislature]] submitted a map that did not comply with the [[Voting Rights Act]] after the [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]] ruled their original map violated the [[Voting Rights Act]] in ''[[Allen v. Milligan]]'', requiring the creation of a second [[List of majority-minority United States congressional districts|predominantly Black district]].{{cite news |last=Liptak |first=Adam |date=June 8, 2023 |title=Supreme Court Rejects Voting Map That Diluted Black Voters' Power |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/06/08/us/supreme-court-voting-rights-act-alabama.html |url-access=limited |newspaper=[[The New York Times]]}}{{Cite web |last=Chandler |first=Kim |date=2023-09-05 |title=Judges reject Alabama's congressional lines, will draw new districts to increase Black voting power |url=https://apnews.com/article/alabama-redistricting-ruling-black-population-affd7b662f65b0b28da42fb88f72207e |access-date=2023-09-05 |website=[[Associated Press]] |language=en}} Similarly, a judge in Georgia ruled that Georgia's maps were illegally racially gerrymandered and the [[Georgia General Assembly]] drew a new map that added a new predominantly Black district.{{cite news |last=Smith |first=David |date=December 28, 2023 |title=Win for Republicans as US judge upholds Congressional Map |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2023/dec/28/judge-upholds-republican-georgia-voting-maps |newspaper=[[The Guardian]] |agency=Reuters}}{{Cite web |last=Amy |first=Jeff |date=2023-12-28 |title=Federal judge accepts redrawn Georgia congressional and legislative districts that will favor GOP |url=https://apnews.com/article/georgia-redistricting-maps-approved-a5ccc16a870601d9df15d14e8ba15767 |access-date=2023-12-30 |website=[[Associated Press]] |language=en}} In Louisiana, the Supreme Court's decision not to intervene in ''Robinson v. Legislative elections were held in [[Vietnam]] on 23 May 2021 to elect members of the [[National Assembly (Vietnam)|National Assembly]], which would subsequently appoint the Prime Minister, and deputies of People's Councils.<ref>{{Cite web|title=National election slated for May 23, 2021|url=https://en.nhandan.com.vn/politics/domestic/item/9302802-national-election-slated-for-may-23-2021.html|date=18 November 2020|website=Nhân Dân|access-date=3 March 2021|archive-date=16 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210416211226/https://en.nhandan.com.vn/politics/domestic/item/9302802-national-election-slated-for-may-23-2021.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> The election took place on a Sunday in line with local legislation. Results were announced on 10 June.

==Background==
The [[Communist Party of Vietnam]] rules Vietnam as a [[one-party state]] and as such is the only party that can contest the elections. In the [[2016 Vietnamese legislative election|2016 elections]] the party won 475 of the 496 seats, with the rest going to independent members of the government-aligned [[Vietnamese Fatherland Front]].

==Electoral system==
The members of the National Assembly were elected from 184 multi-member constituencies using the two-round system, with a maximum number of 500 candidates to be elected. [[Block voting]] was used, with each district having two or three seats.<ref>{{cite book | chapter-url=https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1515/9781503614758-005/pdf | doi=10.1515/9781503614758-005 | chapter=Two How Elections Work in Vietnam | title=United Front | year=2021 | pages=49–66 | isbn=9781503614758 | s2cid=240967678 }}</ref> Candidates had to receive at least 50% of the vote in the first round to be elected, with a second round held on a plurality basis.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Viet Nam (Quoc-Hoi), Electoral system|url=http://archive.ipu.org/parline-e/reports/2349_B.htm|access-date=2021-05-18|website=Inter-Parliamentary Union}}</ref>

General elections were held in [[Zambia]] on 12 August 2021 to elect the [[President of Zambia|President]], [[National Assembly of Zambia|National Assembly]], [[Mayor|mayors]], council chairs and councillors. [[Hakainde Hichilema]] of the [[United Party for National Development]] was elected president, defeating incumbent [[Edgar Lungu]] of the [[Patriotic Front (Zambia)|Patriotic Front]].<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-08-16|title=Zambian opposition leader Hakainde Hichilema wins presidential election|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/zambian-opposition-leader-hakainde-hichilema-wins-presidential-election-2021-08-16/|access-date=2021-08-16|website=Reuters|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web|title=Zambian opposition leader Hakainde Hichilema wins presidential election|url=https://news.trust.org/item/20210816005527-u600i/|access-date=2021-08-16|website=news.trust.org}}</ref>

On 16 August, Lungu conceded in a televised statement, sending a letter and congratulating Hichilema.<ref name="auto1">{{Cite news|date=2021-08-16|title=Zambia election: Hakainde Hichilema beats President Edgar Lungu|language=en-GB|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-58226695|access-date=2021-08-16}}</ref><ref name="auto">{{cite tweet |number=1426967254986629126 |user=zittokabwe |title=#Zambia President @EdgarCLungu has conceded in a letter sent to now president elect @HHichilema of @UPNDZM. Once ag… |accessdate=2021-08-16 |language=en |date=15 August 2021}}</ref>

==Electoral system==
The President is elected via the [[two-round system]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Machenheimer|first=Sabine|date=9 December 2015|title=Closely fought 2016 election would increase localised violence risks and put pressure on Zambia's austerity plans|url=http://www.janes.com/article/56569/closely-fought-2016-election-would-increase-localised-violence-risks-and-put-pressure-on-zambia-s-austerity-plans|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160408083349/http://www.janes.com/article/56569/closely-fought-2016-election-would-increase-localised-violence-risks-and-put-pressure-on-zambia-s-austerity-plans|archive-date=8 April 2016|access-date=2021-02-14|website=Janes|language=en}}</ref> Of the 167 members of the National Assembly, 156 are elected by the first-past-the-post system in single-member constituencies, with a further eight appointed by the President and three others being ''ex-officio'' members: the Vice President, the Speaker and a deputy speaker elected from outside the National Assembly (a second deputy speaker is chosen from among the elected members). The minimum voting age is 18, whilst National Assembly candidates must be at least 21.<ref>{{Cite web|title=ZAMBIA (National Assembly), Electoral system|url=http://archive.ipu.org/parline-e/reports/2359_B.htm|access-date=2021-02-14|website=Inter-Parliamentary Union}}</ref>

==Candidates==
A total of sixteen candidates registered to run for the presidency. The race was expected to be a close race between [[Edgar Lungu]] of the [[Patriotic Front (Zambia)|Patriotic Front]] and [[Hakainde Hichilema]] of the [[United Party for National Development]]. Both competed in the [[2016 Zambian general election|2016 presidential elections]], which Lungu won by a margin of 50.35% to 47.63%.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2016-09-22|title=2016 National Assembly Elections|url=https://www.elections.org.zm/results/2016_national_assembly_elections|access-date=2021-06-30|website=Electoral Commission of Zambia|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160922215316/https://www.elections.org.zm/results/2016_national_assembly_elections|archive-date=22 September 2016}}</ref>

==Campaign==
On 15 May 2021, [[Electoral Commission of Zambia]] chair [[Esau Chulu]] launched the start of the election campaign.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-05-12|title=ECZ announces date to start campaigns for August 12 general election|url=https://zambianews365.com/ecz-announces-date-to-start-campaigns-for-august-12-general-election/|access-date=2021-08-17|website=ZambiaNews365.com|language=en-US|archive-date=17 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210817005852/https://zambianews365.com/ecz-announces-date-to-start-campaigns-for-august-12-general-election/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-05-12|title=Joint Diplomatic Statement on Start of Zambian Elections Campaign|url=https://zm.usembassy.gov/joint-diplomatic-statement-on-start-of-zambian-elections-campaign/|access-date=2021-08-03|website=U.S. Embassy in Zambia|language=en-US}}</ref> However politicians were advised to minimise large crowd gatherings during campaign meetings due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Zambia|COVID-19 pandemic]]. The [[National Assembly of Zambia|National Assembly]] was dissolved on 12 May by President [[Edgar Lungu]] to provide a level playing field in the campaign.<ref>{{Cite web|work=APA NEWS|title=Zambia dissolves parliament ahead of August polls|url=http://apanews.net/en/news/zambia-dissolves-parliament-ahead-of-august-polls|access-date=2021-08-03|language=en}}</ref> However, Lungu remained in office as per constitutional requirements.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Zambia : Parliament to dissolve on May 12-President Lungu|language=en-GB|work=LusakaTimes.com|url=https://www.lusakatimes.com/2021/04/23/parliament-to-dissolve-on-may-12-president-lungu/|access-date=2021-08-03}}</ref>

===Violence and virus cases rise===
On 26 May Lungu launched his own campaign. He also directed the police service and Ministry of Health to ensure enforcement of the COVID-19 pandemic health regulations and guidelines without fear or favour.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-05-26|title=Zambian president bans campaign rallies to stem COVID-19 spread|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/zambian-president-bans-campaign-rallies-stem-covid-19-spread-2021-05-26/|access-date=2021-08-03|website=Reuters}}</ref> On 3 June, due to the rise in COVID-19 cases, the Electoral Commission suspended campaign rallies again to avoid large crowds.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Bloomberg – Zambia Suspends Election Rallies as Covid Cases Surge|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2021-06-03/zambia-suspends-election-rallies-as-covid-19-cases-surge|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210821150252/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2021-06-03/zambia-suspends-election-rallies-as-covid-19-cases-surge|archive-date=2021-08-21|access-date=2021-08-03|newspaper=Bloomberg.com|date=3 June 2021 }}</ref> On 15 June, the Electoral Commission banned the [[Patriotic Front (Zambia)|Patriotic Front]] and [[United Party for National Development]] from campaigning in [[Lusaka]], [[Mpulungu District|Mpulungu]], [[Namwala District|Namwala]] and [[Nakonde District|Nakonde]] due to political violence. The Commission also banned all roadshows across the country to curb the transmission of COVID-19.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Zambia : ECZ Suspends All campaigns, Including All Road Shows by PF and UPND in Lusaka and three other districts|date=15 June 2021 |url=https://www.lusakatimes.com/2021/06/15/ecz-suspends-all-campaigns-including-all-road-shows-by-pf-and-upnd-in-lusaka-and-three-other-districts/|access-date=2021-08-03|language=en-GB}}</ref> On 1 August Lungu ordered the deployment of the [[Zambian Army|military]] to help the [[Zambia Police Service|police]] fight escalating political violence during the campaign.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Zambia deploys army to curb violence ahead of elections|url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2021/8/1/zambia-deploys-army-to-curb-violence-ahead-of-elections|access-date=2021-08-04|website=www.aljazeera.com|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Zambia president deploys army to quell violence ahead of vote|url=https://www.wionews.com/world/zambia-president-deploys-army-to-quell-violence-ahead-of-vote-402269|access-date=2021-08-04|website=WION|language=en}}</ref>

On 28 July UPND Secretary General [[Batuke Imenda]] released a statement that the party was disappointed with government institutions being used by President Lungu to block UPND presidential candidate Hakainde Hichilema from campaigning.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Zambia : UPND Accuse President Edgar Lungu of blocking HH from campaigning for the August 12 Elections|date=28 July 2021 |url=https://www.lusakatimes.com/2021/07/28/329989/|access-date=2021-08-03|language=en-GB}}</ref> On 30 July, Hichilema and his campaign team were prevented from entering [[Chipata]] and detained on the runway of [[Chipata Airport]]. Before Hichilema's arrival in Chipata, police had teargassed his supporters.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Zambia : Police in Chipata try to block UPND campaigns-HH detained for over 2 hours at the airport|date=30 July 2021 |url=https://www.lusakatimes.com/2021/07/30/330253/|access-date=2021-08-03|language=en-GB}}</ref> On 3 August, police in [[Mbala, Zambia|Mbala]] blocked Hichilema and his campaign team from entering the town, with police claiming that he needed a permit to enter.<ref>{{cite tweet |number=1422660597355798528 |user=HHichilema |title=Now we have been blocked from entering Mbala. They say we need a permit. We don't know which permit, because they a… |accessdate=2021-08-04 |language=en |date=3 August 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-08-04|title=blocked Again But They Are Leaving Office – HH|url=https://www.zambianobserver.com/blocked-again-but-they-are-leaving-office-hh/|access-date=2021-08-04|website=The Zambian Observer|language=en-US}}</ref>

===Campaign tactics===
Hichilema heavily criticised Lungu, claiming he had used state power to interfere with the elections.<ref>{{Cite news|date=2017-08-16|title=Zambia opposition leader Hakainde Hichilema released|language=en-GB|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-40945825|access-date=2021-08-19}}</ref> In a campaign video, Hichilema portrayed Lungu as a morally corrupt individual with a history of monetary mismanagement, while portraying himself as fiscally responsible.<ref>{{Citation|title=The Tale Of Two Professionals [Hh & Edgar]|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ld7vm9Tsv7M|language=en|access-date=2021-08-19}}</ref>

==Conduct==
Three days before the elections the government openly stated there was a possibility of an internet shutdown if citizens failed to use cyberspace responsibly during the electoral process.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-08-10 |title=Zambia : Zambia may shut down internet during voting period if Zambians fail to correctly use cyber space-Malupenga |url=https://www.lusakatimes.com/2021/08/10/government-may-shut-down-internet-during-voting-period-malupenga/ |access-date=2023-12-07 |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Malakata |first=Michael |date=2021-08-11 |title=Zambia backtracks on response to internet shutdown rumours |url=https://itweb.africa/content/lwrKxv3K9nrvmg1o |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=ITWeb Africa |language=en-ZA}}</ref> In response to the initial report, Information and Broadcasting Services Permanent Secretary Amos Malupenga promptly issued a statement dismissing the claims as malicious. However, there was a subsequent reversal in Malupenga's stance, as he admitted that an internet shutdown was a viable option. He emphasised the government's stance on preventing the abuse of cyberspace and warned of potential inconveniences if individuals were found to be engaging in misconduct. Malupenga stressed that the government would invoke relevant legal provisions to maintain law and order and ensure peace and stability during the election period.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Malakata |first=Michael |date=2021-08-09 |title=Zambia’s government slams internet shutdown rumours |url=https://itweb.africa/content/VgZeyvJoOQY7djX9 |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=ITWeb Africa |language=en-ZA}}</ref>

On 12 August numerous [[Twitter]] users took to the platform to express concerns about the apparent shutdown of popular [[social media]] and [[messaging apps]] such as [[Facebook Messenger|Messenger]], [[Facebook]], [[Instagram]] and [[WhatsApp]] in the country.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2021-08-11 |title=Facebook Blocked in Zambia as Voters Flood Election Centers |language=en |work=Bloomberg.com |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2021-08-11/zambian-vote-fairness-questioned-on-eve-of-tight-contest |access-date=2023-12-07}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-08-12|title=Social media and messaging apps restricted in Zambia on election day|url=https://netblocks.org/reports/whatsapp-and-social-media-restricted-in-zambia-on-election-day-18lpLY8a|access-date=2021-08-13|website=NetBlocks|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|author=Samantha Tapfumaneyi, Lauren Kent and Tim Lister|title=Social media and messaging apps appear to be shutdown in Zambia on election day, Facebook says|url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/08/12/africa/zambia-election-social-media-blackout-intl/index.html|access-date=2021-08-13|website=CNN|date=12 August 2021}}</ref> This caused a significant impact as it hindered the flow of information and communication on a vital day for democratic processes.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|date=2021-08-13|title=Zambia counting votes with internet restrictions still in force|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/zambia-counts-votes-internet-restriction-remain-force-2021-08-13/|access-date=2021-08-13|publisher=Reuters|language=en}}</ref> Reports surfaced that internet users resorted to using [[Virtual private network|Virtual Private Network]] (VPN) services as a workaround to bypass the restrictions imposed on WhatsApp and various social media platforms. Despite these efforts to maintain connectivity, the situation raised questions about the accessibility and freedom of expression during the election period.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nkomesha |first=Ulande |date=2021-08-12 |title=Zambia Election Update: Govt shuts down Social Media ahead of vote count |url=https://diggers.news/local/2021/08/12/zambia-election-update-govt-shuts-down-social-media-ahead-of-vote-count/ |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=Zambia: News Diggers! |language=en-GB}}</ref>

In response to the claims, Malupenga refuted the reports, dismissing them as "malicious." He emphasized the government's stance on responsible internet usage, stating that the government would not tolerate any abuse of the internet. Malupenga went on to caution that if any misconduct occurred, the government reserved the right to take legal action to prevent any potential disruption of law and order, particularly during the sensitive election period. His remarks underscored the government's commitment to ensuring a secure and orderly electoral process. Despite Malupenga's statements, the restrictions on social media platforms persisted, creating a challenging environment for citizens to freely express their views and share information. The limitations on the platforms added an additional layer of complexity to an already tense election period, sparking concerns about the implications for freedom of speech and information dissemination in the country.<ref>{{Cite web|title=WhatsApp and other social media platforms restricted in Zambia amidst ongoing elections|url=https://techcrunch.com/2021/08/12/whatsapp-and-other-social-media-platforms-restricted-in-zambia-amidst-ongoing-elections/|access-date=2021-08-13|website=TechCrunch|date=12 August 2021 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":1" />

==Results==
On 16 August Hakainde Hichilema was declared president-elect of Zambia.<ref name=":3" /> At the time of the announcement, 155 out of Zambia's 156 constituencies had been counted, with only [[Mandevu (constituency)|Mandevu constituency]] still to declare. As the votes in that constituency were insufficient to affect the outcome, the electoral commission announced Hichilema's victory.<ref name="trtw_Zamb">{{Cite web |title=Zambia's opposition leader Hichilema wins presidential vote at sixth bid |author= |work=TRT World |date=16 August 2021 |access-date=17 August 2021 |url= https://www.trtworld.com/africa/zambia-s-opposition-leader-hichilema-wins-presidential-vote-at-sixth-bid-49208}}</ref> Edgar Lungu conceded defeat shortly after the announcement.<ref name="auto"/><ref name="auto1"/>

{{Politics of Zimbabwe}}
General elections were held throughout [[Zimbabwe]] on 23 and 24 August 2023 to elect the [[President of Zimbabwe|president]], [[legislator]]s and [[councillor]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |date=31 May 2023 |title=Zimbabwe Presidential Elections Scheduled for Aug. 23|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2023-05-31/zimbabwean-president-sets-presidential-elections-for-aug-23 |access-date=31 May 2023 |website=Bloomberg}}</ref> The main race for presidential office was between two candidates of [[Kalanga people|Karanga]] origin: [[ZANU–PF]]'s [[Emmerson Mnangagwa]] and [[Citizens Coalition for Change]]'s [[Nelson Chamisa]].

The presidential election was won by the incumbent president Mnangagwa, while the governing [[ZANU–PF]] party won a majority of seats in parliament, with observer bodies describing the elections as not being free and fair.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cohen |first=Tim |date=2023-08-28 |title=After the Bell: Were the Zimbabwean elections free and fair? Please, spare me |url=https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2023-08-28-after-the-bell-were-the-zimbabwean-elections-free-and-fair-please-spare-me/ |access-date=2024-08-02 |website=Daily Maverick |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Zimbabwe's Flawed Election Results Meet With Regional Skepticism  |url=https://www.cfr.org/in-brief/zimbabwes-flawed-election-results-meet-regional-skepticism |access-date=2024-08-02 |website=www.cfr.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=SADC Electoral Observation Mission Preliminary Statement to the Harmonised Election to the Republic of Zimbabwe |url=https://www.sadc.int/document/sadc-electoral-observation-mission-preliminary-statement-harmonised-election-republic |access-date=2024-08-02 |website=www.sadc.int}}</ref>

The voter rolls for the election increased to 6.5 million, up from 5.8 million in 2018.<ref>{{Cite web |date=21 June 2023 |title=ZEC records 6.5 million registered voters - New Ziana |url=https://newziana.co.zw/2023/06/21/zec-records-6-5-million-registered-voters |access-date=24 August 2023 |language=en-GB}}</ref>

The [[Zimbabwe Electoral Commission]] spoke about the delays citing that they would compensate for the delays meaning if the polling station was opened at 11{{nbsp}}am, it would close at 11{{nbsp}}pm to ensure that there is 12 hours of voting. There were some reports from the [[Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation]] that about 5 wards in [[Manicaland Province|Manicaland]] people did not manage to vote at all because of logistical difficulties which were faced by the [[Zimbabwe Electoral Commission|ZEC]]. About 35 more were delayed, of which 11 of them were in the capital of the country, [[Harare]], which ultimately lead to ZEC declaring 24 August 2023 to be a second voting day, although voting is supposed to take place within one day according to Zimbabwean law.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Banya |first1=Nelson |last2=Chingono |first2=Nyasha |date=24 August 2023 |title=Zimbabwe sets extra day of voting in selected wards after delays|language=en|work=Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/zimbabweans-vote-hopes-ending-economic-freefall-appear-dim-2023-08-23/ |access-date=24 August 2023}}</ref>

Political parties competed for one presidential seat, 1,970 council seats and 280 parliamentary seats, and 60 senate seats to be elected for a five-year term. As per the [[Constitution of Zimbabwe]], the president is to be elected using the [[two-round system]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Zimbabwe election: Your guide to how the electoral system works|url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2023/8/19/infographic-how-do-the-zimbabwe-elections-work|access-date=24 August 2023|website=www.aljazeera.com |language=en}}</ref>

The general population feared possible violence during the election because both sides have a history of political violence. Preelectoral polls suggested a runoff was likely,<ref>{{Cite tweet |author=Africa Elects |user=AfricaElect|title=Zimbabwe, SABI strategy poll |number=1624235211184545793 |date=10 February 2023 |access-date=23 August 2023 |language=bn, en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Zimbabwe: Poll suggests election headed to a runoff|url=https://www.theafricareport.com/316033/zimbabwe-poll-suggests-election-is-headed-to-a-runoff/ |access-date=23 August 2023 |website=The Africa Report.com |language=en}}</ref> but [[Emmerson Mnangagwa|Mnangagwa]] was elected in a single round with a narrow majority.

==Electoral system==
'''Presidential Election'''

The [[president of Zimbabwe]] is elected using the [[two-round system]].

'''Parliamentary Election'''

The 280 members of the [[National Assembly of Zimbabwe|National Assembly]] consist of 210 members elected in [[List of Zimbabwean parliamentary constituencies|single-member constituencies]] along with 60 women and 10 youth seats elected by [[proportional representation]] in ten seven-seat constituencies based on the country's [[Provinces of Zimbabwe|provinces]]. Voters cast a single vote, which is counted for both forms of election.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ipu.org/parline-e/reports/2361_B.htm|title=Electoral system – National Assembly|website=Inter-Parliamentary Union}}</ref> The 80 members of the [[Senate of Zimbabwe|Senate]] include 60 members elected from ten six-member constituencies (also based on the provinces) by proportional representation using party lists; the lists must have a woman at the top and [[Zipper system|alternate between men and women]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ipu.org/parline-e/reports/2383_B.htm|title=Electoral system – Senate|website=Inter-Parliamentary Union}}</ref> The other 20 seats include two reserved for [[Disability|persons with disabilities]] and 18 for [[Chief of the Name|traditional chiefs]].

'''Local Authority Election'''

The Local Authority elections consist of 1970 members elected in single-member ward along with 603 seats reserved for women elected by proportional representation in local authorities based on an additional 30% of seats in a local authority being reserved for women. Voters cast a single vote, which is counted for both forms of election.

== Presidential candidates ==
The Zimbabwe Electoral Commission approved 11 candidates, but disqualified [[Saviour Kasukuwere]] for failing to meet residency requirements.<ref name=BBC1>{{Cite news |date=12 June 2023 |title=Zimbabwe elections 2023: What you need to know |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-65775996 |access-date=21 July 2023}}</ref> The approved candidates include:<ref name=BBC1/><ref>{{cite news |date=19 July 2023 |title=Elisabeth Valerio Becomes Sole Woman in Presidential Election |work=VOA Zimbabwe|url=https://www.voazimbabwe.com/a/elisabeth-valerio-becomes-sole-woman-in-presidential-election/7187427.html}}</ref>

*[[Emmerson Mnangagwa]] of [[ZANU–PF]] - incumbent [[president of Zimbabwe]] since 2017.
*[[Nelson Chamisa]] of the [[Citizens Coalition for Change]] (CCC).
*[[Elisabeth Valerio]] of the United Zimbabwe Alliance (UZA).
*[[Joseph Makamba Busha]] of the FreeZim Congress (FZC)
*[[Tapiwa Trust Chikohora]] of the Zimbabwe Coalition for Peace and Development Party (ZCPD).
*Blessing Kasiyamhuru of the Zimbabwe Partnership for Prosperity (ZIPP).

== Campaign ==
The main issue of the election campaign was [[inflation]]<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Banya |first1=Nelson |last2=Chingono |first2=Nyasha |date=23 August 2023 |title=Zimbabweans vote but hopes of ending economic freefall look dim|language=en|work=Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/zimbabweans-vote-hopes-ending-economic-freefall-appear-dim-2023-08-23/ |access-date=23 August 2023}}</ref> and the economic crisis which had been exacerbated by the [[hyperinflation]] of the new [[Zimbabwean dollar (2019–2024)|Zimbabwean dollar]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Zimbabwe gears up for 2023 election amid economic woes – DW – 12/30/2022|url=https://www.dw.com/en/zimbabwe-gears-up-for-2023-election-amid-economic-woes/a-64232802 |access-date=23 August 2023 |website=dw.com |language=en}}</ref>

The number of women candidates declined significantly compared to previous elections in 2018.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Patriarchal politics, online violence and silenced voices - The Nordic Africa Institute |url=https://nai.uu.se/news-and-events/news/2023-12-13-patriarchal-politics-online-violence-and-silenced-voices.html |access-date=2024-01-10 |website=nai.uu.se |language=en}}</ref>

==Conduct==
A [[Commonwealth of Nations|Commonwealth]] [[Election monitoring|observer mission]] was invited as part of an attempt to restore Zimbabwe's membership in the Commonwealth.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-africa-66542695|title=Emmerson Mnangagwa - Zimbabwe's 'crocodile' who wants another bite|date=18 August 2023|access-date=23 August 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230822112019/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-africa-66542695|archive-date=22 August 2023|url-status=live|publisher=BBC}}</ref>

Voting was extended for another day after a lack of ballot papers disrupted voting,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Chingono |first=Nyasha |date=23 August 2023 |title=Voting in Zimbabwe general election delayed by lack of ballot papers |language=en-GB |work=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/aug/23/voting-in-zimbabwe-general-election-delayed-by-lack-of-ballot-papers |access-date=23 August 2023|issn=0261-3077}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Chingono |first=Nyasha |date=24 August 2023 |title=Voting in Zimbabwe election extended by another day after ballot delays |language=en-GB |work=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/aug/24/voting-zimbabwe-election-extended-by-another-day-ballot-delays |access-date=24 August 2023 |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> with some voters being forced to queue overnight to cast their ballots.<ref>{{Cite news|first=Jane|last=Flanagan |date=24 August 2023 |title=Zimbabwe elections: Voters queue overnight and polling stations open late|newspaper=[[The Times]] |language=en|url=https://www.thetimes.com/world/article/zimbabwe-general-election-polls-president-voters-2023-6xzq06wt2|access-date=24 August 2023 |issn=0140-0460}}</ref>  There were reportedly delays of up to 10 hours in opposition stronghold areas.<ref>{{Cite web |date=24 August 2023 |title=Voting extended in Zimbabwe election after 'disproportionate' delays in opposition strongholds |url=https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20230824-voting-extended-in-zimbabwe-election-as-incumbent-president-seeks-second-term |access-date=24 August 2023 |website=France 24 |language=en}}</ref> The [[Zimbabwe Electoral Commission]] acknowledged the late distribution of ballot papers at some polling stations and blamed it on printing delays "arising from numerous court challenges".<ref>{{Cite web |date=24 August 2023 |title=Zimbabwe's election extends to a second day after long ballot delays. Some slept at polling stations|url=https://apnews.com/article/zimbabwe-election-mnangagwa-3c354f2928902de8e91fb907c6fb7d40 |access-date=24 August 2023 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref> Forty-one poll monitors were arrested during the election, being accused of illegally attempting to announce results before the state elections body.<ref>{{Cite news |date=24 August 2023 |title=Zimbabwe election: Poll monitors arrested amid election |language=en-GB|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-66604659 |access-date=24 August 2023}}</ref> Accusations of vote rigging were made by the opposition.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Musengi |first1=Kudzanai |last2=Cotterill |first2=Joseph |date=24 August 2023 |title=Zimbabwe election marred by delays and vote-rigging accusations |work=Financial Times|url=https://www.ft.com/content/51c6cd1c-25bf-4120-94ea-6839292f60d7 |access-date=24 August 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Chamisa |first1=Nelson |title=Zimbabwe opposition alleges ‘blatant and gigantic fraud’ in election |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2023/8/28/zimbabwe-opposition-alleges-blatant-and-gigantic-fraud-in-election |access-date=18 June 2025 |agency=Al Jazeera |date=28 August 2023}}</ref>

=== National Assembly ===
The National Assembly has 210 single-member constituencies, the results of which are shown below.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Election Dashboard : Live Update Results 23 August 2023 |url=https://zimbabweelections2023.co.zw/dashboard.html |access-date=2023-08-29 |website=zimbabweelections2023.co.zw}}</ref> The remaining 70 seats comprises 60 seats which are reserved for women, six seats in each province, and 10 seats for youth, one seat in each province, which are filled based on the votes in the single-member constituencies using party-list proportional representation, distributed using the largest remainder method and the Hare quota.

On election day itself ZANU–PF won 136 seats and the CCC 73, with ZANU–PF retaining its rural base and the CCC capturing the urban vote.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Banya |first1=Nelson |last2=Chingono |first2=Nyasha |date=2023-08-25 |title=Zimbabwe braces for close election as early parliamentary results come in|language=en|work=Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/zimbabwe-braces-close-election-early-parliamentary-results-come-2023-08-25/ |access-date=2023-08-25}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-08-25 |title=Early results suggest closely fought Zimbabwe parliamentary polls|url=https://www.dailysabah.com/world/africa/early-results-suggest-closely-fought-zimbabwe-parliamentary-polls |access-date=2023-08-25 |website=Daily Sabah |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-08-25 |title=Partial results suggest ZANU-PF's lead as election observers decry 'climate of fear'|url=https://www.sabcnews.com/sabcnews/partial-results-suggest-zanu-pfs-lead-as-election-observers-decry-climate-of-fear/ |access-date=2023-08-25 |website=SABC News |language=en-US}}</ref> Voting in the [[Gutu West]] constituency was postponed to 11 November after one of the candidates died shortly before the elections.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://nehandaradio.com/2023/07/15/zec-stops-gutu-west-election-after-death-of-retired-soldier-candidate/|website=Nehanda Radio|title=ZEC stops Gutu West election after death of retired soldier candidate|date=15 July 2023}}</ref> Following the parliamentary election in Gutu West, 65.24% of the constituency seats went to ZANU-PF and 34.76% of the constituency seats went to the CCC.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2023 Elections Zimbabwe |url=https://www.pindula.co.zw/elections/2023/ |access-date=2023-08-31 |website=Pindula |language=en}}</ref>
